articles.title: Comment: Should fireworks be allowed on any night but bonfire night?
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's council displays went quiet this year, but residents say fireworks carried on into this week. We look at the law, the harm to people and animals, and what could change.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council chose reduced-noise fireworks for its three bonfire events this year, yet residents say the bangs have carried on well into this week. Is it time to ask whether fireworks should be allowed on any night other than bonfire night?

The council's displays ran on Monday 2 November in Middleton, Tuesday 3 November in Heywood and Wednesday 4 November at Cronkeyshaw Common. None fell on Thursday 5 November itself.

By most accounts the Cronkeyshaw display worked: an eyewitness told Rochdale Daily that the quieter, music-led fireworks were enjoyed by a large crowd with little traffic disruption.

The problem is what happens outside the organised events. Residents have reported fireworks through the weekend and into Monday, after the council displays and bonfire night had both passed.

This is not new. In July and August, households in Shawclough and Healey reported explosions after 11pm on consecutive nights, with parents describing children woken after bedtime and pet owners describing distressed animals.

At full council on 15 October, Councillor Jordan Tarrant-Short raised residents' concerns about fireworks being used throughout the year. Councillor Tricia Ayrton said she had been speaking with partner agencies about a coordinated response, and encouraged councillors to raise the call for stronger national action with their MPs.

What the law actually says

In England, adult fireworks may not be set off between 11pm and 7am under the Fireworks Regulations 2004. The exceptions are bonfire night, when the cut-off is midnight, and New Year's Eve, Diwali and the first day of Chinese New Year, when it is 1am. Council-run and national celebration displays are also exempt.

Outside those nights, nothing stops a private display at 10.59pm on any evening of the year.

Shops without an all-year licence may sell to the public only from 15 October to 10 November, from 26 to 31 December, and in the days before Diwali and Chinese New Year. Retailers with a council licence can sell all year round. Consumer fireworks are capped at 120 decibels, and it is an offence to sell adult fireworks to under-18s.

The curfew is enforced by the police, and breaches can bring a fine of up to £5,000. In practice, proving who lit a firework in a back garden at 11.30pm is difficult, and a short burst of noise rarely meets the threshold for a council statutory nuisance investigation.

Scotland has gone further. The Fireworks and Pyrotechnic Articles (Scotland) Act 2022 restricts public use to 6pm to 11pm, with later cut-offs on the main celebration nights, and lets councils designate firework control zones where fireworks are banned at all times.

The physical harm

NHS England figures reported last month showed 161 firework-related hospital admissions in England in 2025, up from 120 the year before. November alone accounted for 85 admissions, compared with 60 in November 2024.

In 2019 a coalition of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons, the British Society for Surgery of the Hand and the British Burn Association reported 1,936 A&E visits for firework injuries in a single year. Hand surgeons said they often treat people who have lost large portions of a hand, and children made up 31% of admissions.

The coalition pointed to Northern Ireland, where licensing for the more powerful categories of firework was followed by reported injuries falling from 136 in 2001 to 38 in 2002.

Pets, livestock and wildlife

In the RSPCA's 2024 impact survey, 66% of respondents said backyard displays were a major concern. The charity wants consumer fireworks cut from 120 to 90 decibels, sales limited to licensed shops, and firework-free zones near animals and vulnerable people.

The horse charity Redwings gathered more than 45,000 signatures in seven weeks last year for the same 90-decibel limit.

The National Farmers' Union says sudden explosions are one of the main causes of stress and injury in livestock, and has reported a member losing around four acres of wheat to a stray firework. The borough's Pennine farmland sits close to housing in Littleborough, Milnrow and Norden.

Researchers at Anglia Ruskin University reported last year that crows, rooks and jackdaws abandoned their roosts and flew erratically on New Year's Eve, which the authors linked to prolonged stress.

People with PTSD and anxiety

Help for Heroes and Combat Stress surveyed veterans in 2023. Almost a quarter (23%) said fireworks had triggered a negative experience, from feeling jumpy to panic attacks. Some 74% wanted the days and times fireworks can be used restricted further, and 67% wanted fewer days on which they can be sold.

Unannounced displays on ordinary nights give anyone with an anxiety condition no chance to prepare.

Weddings and New Year

Weddings sit in an awkward place. There is no special rule for them: a wedding display follows the same 11pm curfew as any other private use, on any night of the year, using fireworks from an all-year licensed seller.

For the couple it is one night. For neighbours, a busy wedding season can mean several unplanned displays a month, with no warning.

New Year's Eve is already protected in law until 1am, and few would argue against a midnight countdown. The question is whether the nights either side of it, and of bonfire night, should be treated the same way.

The case against tighter rules

There are serious arguments on the other side. Most people who use fireworks do so legally and safely, and displays are a valued part of family celebrations, religious festivals such as Diwali, and community fundraising.

The NFU itself opposes a complete ban on consumer fireworks, preferring quieter products and advance notice for farms. Opponents of tighter rules also argue that restricting legal sales could push buyers towards unsafe, unregulated products. And the curfew is already widely broken, so a stricter law with the same weak enforcement may change little.

What could be done

The Government's consultation, which closed on 7 October 2026, asked whether the consumer noise limit should fall from 120 decibels to 110, 100 or 90, and proposed reserving the loudest fireworks for professional displays. It did not propose limiting the nights on which fireworks can be used, and its response has not yet been published.

Options that would go further include:

Restricting private use to bonfire night, New Year's Eve and recognised religious festivals, with all-year use limited to licensed and notified displays.

Ending or tightening all-year retail licences, so that fireworks are not on sale in July and August.

Requiring advance notice to neighbours and nearby farms for wedding and private displays outside the permitted nights.

Giving English councils the same power as Scottish councils to create firework-free zones around farms, nature reserves such as Healey Dell, and care homes.

Making quieter fireworks, like those used at Cronkeyshaw, the standard for consumer sale.

Rochdale has already shown that a council display can be quieter and still draw a crowd. Whether the rules for everyone else should follow is a decision for Parliament, including the MPs who represent the borough.

Fireworks used after 11pm on non-permitted nights can be reported to Greater Manchester Police on 101 or online.

Sources: Fireworks Regulations 2004; Rochdale Borough Council; Department for Business and Trade consultation (July 2026); NHS England via ITV News; BAPRAS, BSSH and British Burn Association; RSPCA; Redwings; National Farmers' Union; Anglia Ruskin University; Help for Heroes and Combat Stress; Scottish Government. Photograph: reader-supplied, Cronkeyshaw Common, 4 November 2026.

articles.title: Volunteers wanted for Rochdale town centre's Saturday night Safe Haven
articles.excerpt: Community Medics is recruiting welfare volunteers aged 16 and over for its town centre welfare point, which runs on Saturday nights from 10pm to 3am. Training is provided.
articles.content_html:
A welfare point that helps people who feel unwell, distressed or unsafe on a night out in Rochdale town centre is looking for volunteers.

The Safe Haven, run by Community Medics, operates every Saturday from 10pm to 3am.

Volunteers provide a visible, approachable presence and reassure people who need help. They spot when someone needs support and work with the scheme's clinical team to make sure that person gets the right help.

The role is non-clinical: volunteers do not give medical treatment. Community Medics describes it as focused on early support, engagement and escalation.

No previous experience is needed, and full training is provided in safeguarding, vulnerability awareness and conflict management. Volunteers must be 16 or over and can help regularly or occasionally.

People can apply through the Community Medics website at communitymedics.co.uk/welfarevolunteer, by emailing admin@communitymedics.co.uk, or by calling 0161 806 1533.

Source: Community Medics. Photograph: Rochdale Daily library.

articles.title: Free job-search, CV and money advice at Middleton Library today
articles.excerpt: Middleton Library is hosting a free work and skills hub on Monday 9 November, with help for job applications, interviews and managing budgets.
articles.content_html:
People looking for work or help improving their job applications can attend a free work and skills session at Middleton Library on Monday 9 November 2026.

Rochdale Borough Council lists the session from 9.30am until 12.30pm at Middleton Library, Long Street, Middleton, M24 6DU. No booking is needed and adults can simply turn up.

The council says the hub offers advice on finding vacancies and training courses, completing CVs and application forms, preparing for interviews, and managing debt or household budgets.

The session is described as taking place every other Monday, although residents should check the council's events listing for the next confirmed date rather than assuming every fortnightly date will go ahead.

For someone returning to employment, the most useful starting point may be a CV or a specific application they want help with. Anyone seeking support can bring details of the vacancy or course they are interested in, although the council does not state that any paperwork is required.

The council's listing confirms the session is free. For enquiries, contact middleton.library@rochdale.gov.uk.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council event listing, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/579/work-and-skills-hub---middleton-library
articles.image_alt: Free job-search, CV and money advice at Middleton Library today

articles.title: Free Heywood Library friendship group offers a place to meet people this Thursday
articles.excerpt: A free drop-in friendship group at Heywood Library on Thursday 12 November is open to adults, with no advance booking required.
articles.content_html:
People hoping to make new friends or meet others in their community can attend a free friendship group at Heywood Library on Thursday 12 November 2026.

Rochdale Borough Council's event listing gives the time as 1.30pm to 3.30pm at Heywood Library, LCpl Stephen Shaw MC Way, Heywood, OL10 1LW.

The gathering is aimed at people aged 18 and over who want to meet new people or learn skills. The council also lists it as suitable for families with children aged four and over, provided children are accompanied by a responsible adult.

No advance booking is required. Visitors can simply turn up. The listing describes it as a regular Thursday activity and says participants can also find out about joining the library and other activities available there.

For residents who have recently moved to Heywood, work from home or simply want more local company, it offers a straightforward way to meet others without committing to a paid course or membership.

For questions, contact heywood.library@rochdale.gov.uk. Check the council listing before travelling in case arrangements change.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council event listing, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/996/friendship-group---heywood-library
articles.image_alt: Free Heywood Library friendship group offers a place to meet people this Thursday

articles.title: RBH tenants rate landlord in top 25 per cent nationally on all 12 survey measures
articles.excerpt: National figures from the Regulator of Social Housing place Rochdale Boroughwide Housing in the upper quartile of large landlords on all 12 tenant survey measures for 2025/26.
articles.content_html:
Tenants of Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, the borough's largest social landlord, rate it among the top quarter of large landlords in England on every survey measure, new national figures show.

The Regulator of Social Housing published the 2025/26 Tenant Satisfaction Measures on Thursday 5 November, covering 356 submissions from landlords with 1,000 or more homes.

RBH set itself a target of reaching the "upper quartile", the top 25 per cent of landlords nationally, and said all 12 of its tenant survey results are now in that band.

Rochdale Daily checked each of RBH's published scores against the regulator's upper-quartile figures, which are rounded to whole numbers. All 12 clear the line.

Overall satisfaction was 80.5 per cent, against an upper quartile of 80 per cent and a national median of 74.2 per cent.

Satisfaction with repairs was 85.2 per cent (upper quartile 82 per cent), with the time taken to complete a repair 80.4 per cent (79 per cent), and that the home is well maintained 82.9 per cent (80 per cent).

Tenants who said their home is safe stood at 88.2 per cent (85 per cent). Those satisfied that RBH listens and acts on their views were 76.6 per cent (72 per cent), and that it keeps them informed 85.1 per cent (79 per cent).

Agreement that RBH treats tenants fairly and with respect was 85.7 per cent, the narrowest margin, against an upper quartile of 85 per cent.

Among tenants who had complained, 48.6 per cent were satisfied with how it was handled (45 per cent). Satisfaction with communal areas was 77.2 per cent (75 per cent), with RBH's contribution to the neighbourhood 79.2 per cent (74 per cent), and with its handling of anti-social behaviour 74.4 per cent (68 per cent).

In a statement, RBH said: "We are very proud to let you know that, across all 12 tenant satisfaction measures covered by our survey, our customers have placed our performance among the top landlords in the country."

It added: "We have only been able to improve by using the feedback and experience from our customers alongside the hard work and expertise of our team and the support of our stakeholders."

"We're pleased that our customers are telling us we're moving in the right direction, and we're determined to continue to learn and continue to improve," the statement said.

The 12 measures come from a telephone survey carried out for RBH by the independent firm Viewpoint. Every social landlord must ask the same questions, set by the regulator.

The regulator advises comparing landlords that used similar survey methods. Telephone is the most common method nationally, used for 65 per cent of surveys of rental tenants.

RBH's claim covers the 12 survey measures only. The regulator also publishes 10 measures drawn from landlords' own records, where RBH's picture is more mixed.

RBH completed 99.6 per cent of required gas safety checks, below the national median of 99.9 per cent. It answered 93 per cent of stage one complaints within the Housing Ombudsman's timescales, just under the median of 93.8 per cent.

It recorded 29.7 stage one complaints per 1,000 homes, about half the national median of 56.8, and reported that 0.2 per cent of its homes fail the Decent Homes Standard, against a median of 0.6 per cent.

Every RBH score improved on the previous year. Overall satisfaction rose from 76.6 per cent in 2024/25.

The results come nearly six years after the death of two-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in December 2020 after prolonged exposure to mould in an RBH flat.

The regulator downgraded RBH's governance to a non-compliant G3 rating in December 2022. It restored the landlord to a compliant G2 rating in March 2025, after two years of intensive engagement.

RBH's full 2025/26 results and survey method are published on its website, and the regulator's national figures for every large landlord are available on GOV.UK.

Source: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing statement and performance figures; Regulator of Social Housing, Tenant Satisfaction Measures 2025/26. Photograph: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing.

articles.title: Woman dies at Tesco in Rochdale after emergency services called
articles.excerpt: A woman in her 50s has died following an incident at a Tesco store on Silk Street in Rochdale on Saturday afternoon.
articles.content_html:
A woman in her 50s has died after emergency services were called to a Tesco store on Silk Street in Rochdale on Saturday afternoon, 7 November 2026.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) received a call expressing concern for the welfare of a woman inside the supermarket. Eyewitnesses reported that staff initially attended to her before paramedics arrived.

Shoppers were asked to leave the store and the car park to allow emergency services to manage the situation. Video footage showed an air ambulance landing in the car park as part of the response.

Despite the efforts of emergency personnel, the woman could not be saved and was pronounced dead at the scene. A GMP spokesperson confirmed that her family has been notified.

Tesco declined to comment on the incident when approached by the media.

Local readers are encouraged to remain aware of community support services and safety measures.

articles.title: Bikers in red leave Birch Services for 13th Ring of Red ride around the M60
articles.excerpt: Riders were due to set off from the M62 services at 1pm to form a giant poppy around Manchester, raising money for Heywood Veterans Association.
articles.content_html:
Bikers in red were due to leave Birch Services on the M62 at 1pm today for the 13th Ring of Red ride, raising money for Heywood Veterans Association.

Riders gather at the westbound HGV parking area of the services, which sit between Heywood and Middleton, before heading along the M62 and joining the M60 at junction 18.

They then travel clockwise around the whole of Manchester's ring road. With every rider wearing something red, the procession is meant to look like a giant poppy encircling the city when seen from above.

Riders could gather from 8am, and organisers said the westbound lorry park would be closed to HGVs from Saturday night until 2.30pm today. More than 1,000 motorcyclists were expected.

Jeanette "Netty" Kiely, who organises Ring of Red M60, told the source the ride was a way of saying "we remember, we care, and we will never forget".

Ms Kiely said seeing the bikes come together each year reminded organisers why they do it. She also praised the Bridge Supporters who stand on motorway bridges in all weathers to wave and cheer as the riders pass underneath.

She added that after 13 years the event had become a community coming together to remember, rather than simply a motorcycle ride.

The Ride of Respect is free to join and non-competitive. It honours members of the Armed Forces past and present and those who died in service.

Money is raised through sales of official red T-shirts, hoodies and patches, with a separate clothing range for Bridge Supporters. Heywood Veterans Association, this year's nominated charity, supports veterans in Heywood, Middleton and surrounding areas.

The Manchester ride grew out of the original Ring of Red on the M25. Ms Kiely has previously said she agreed to stage a northern version after a phone call from the London organiser.

The M60 event's biggest turnout came in 2022, when 5,986 bikes took part, up from 4,400 the year before. Ms Kiely said at the time: "It was incredible to have our highest turn out yet – with 5986 bikes."

Around 3,000 bikers took part last year, according to the Oldham Times. Previous nominated charities include Veterans into Logistics and Veterans in Communities.

Riders finish back at Birch Services once the lap of the M60 is complete.

Source: Ring of Red M60 organisers via the source. Photograph: supplied.

articles.title: Castleton Remembrance Sunday service draws big crowd but resident asks for a better speaker next year
articles.excerpt: Crowds gathered on Castleton's village green for the Act of Remembrance, but one resident said the words could not be heard.
articles.content_html:
A large crowd gathered on Castleton's village green for the Remembrance Sunday service this morning, but one resident said nobody could hear what was being said.

Castleton's Act of Remembrance began at 10.50am at Castleton Memorial Gardens on Queensway, on the village green. The service was led by St Martin's Parish Church, according to the order of service handed to those attending.

Photographs from the service show people lining the green as the service took place under the trees.

Writing in the Castleton community group on Facebook after the service, Graham Glover said: "Great turnout but please can we invest in a new speaker for next year? You can't hear a word being said."

Castleton's service was one of eight Remembrance Sunday parades and services held across the Rochdale borough today, in Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow, Castleton, Norden and Wardle.

Armistice Day falls on Wednesday 11 November, with the national two-minute silence at 11am.

Source: Castleton community group post supplied to Rochdale Daily; order of service for Castleton's Act of Remembrance; Rochdale Borough Council. Photograph: Graham Glover / Castleton community group.

articles.title: Middleton's Veterans' Walk: the poppy mural honouring the town's service men and women on Remembrance Sunday
articles.excerpt: A wreath has been laid at Middleton's Veterans' Walk, the Middleton in Bloom mural of poppies, a Spitfire and the white cliffs of Dover.
articles.content_html:
A poppy wreath has been laid at Middleton's Veterans' Walk, the town centre mural that Middleton in Bloom created as a tribute to the town's service men and women, on Remembrance Sunday.

The mural runs the length of a wall in Middleton town centre. A Spitfire trails a stream of red poppies across a painted sky, above silhouettes of soldiers standing among giant poppies, a soldier with a horse, the white cliffs of Dover and a warship at sea.

Planters along the foot of the wall are wrapped in a poppy-print banner carrying the words of Laurence Binyon's poem For the Fallen: "They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old."

The wreath sits beneath the Veterans' Walk plaque, in the planter in front of the painted sea.

The plaque records that the installation was officially opened on 8 May 2025, the 80th anniversary of VE Day, by Ted Woolley OStJ, branch chairman of the Middleton branch of the Royal British Legion.

Middleton in Bloom finished the white cliffs of Dover section in time for VE Day last year, the Rochdale Times reported at the time. The wooden panel had to be replaced, so the sea was painted first and the Spitfire and poppies were added afterwards.

Elsewhere in Middleton, a "Lest We Forget" display of two kneeling soldiers either side of a cross has been planted with red cyclamen and poppies.

Middleton's Remembrance Sunday parade assembled at 10.10am on Long Street this morning and marched to Middleton Memorial Gardens on Middleton Old Road for a service at 10.45am.

More about the group's work is published at middletoninbloom.co.uk.

Source: photographs supplied to Rochdale Daily; Veterans' Walk plaque; Rochdale Times; Rochdale Borough Council. Photographs: supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Remembrance walkers cover 22 miles and eight cenotaphs to raise money for veterans
articles.excerpt: Get Together After Serving walkers paid their respects at cenotaphs from Norden to Rochdale, with the Mayor joining them at Milnrow.
articles.content_html:
Walkers from Get Together After Serving (GTAS) have completed a 22-mile Remembrance walk across the borough, stopping to pay their respects at eight cenotaphs along the way.

The Remembrance Walk 2026 was organised to raise money to support veterans. GTAS has now shared photographs from the later stages of the route, which ran from Norden to a final tribute at Rochdale Cenotaph.

After paying their respects at Norden Cenotaph, the group stopped at Denehurst House Café for a brew and a butty before setting off again for Wardle Cenotaph.

The route then took the walkers to Littleborough Cenotaph and on to Milnrow Cenotaph, where the Mayor joined them, before they finished at Rochdale Cenotaph.

The group's photograph shows walkers of all ages, including children, wearing matching green GTAS T-shirts and poppies at one of the war memorials on the route.

In a message to supporters, GTAS thanked everyone who walked alongside the group, cheered them on or helped raise money for veterans.

Donations to support veterans can be made through the GTAS appeal post.

Source: Get Together After Serving post supplied to Rochdale Daily. Photograph: Get Together After Serving.

articles.title: Is there really a secret tunnel under Middleton between the Ring O’Bells and St Leonard’s?
articles.excerpt: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells to St Leonard’s, but formal records and heritage surveys offer no published proof.
articles.summary: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells to St Leonard’s, but formal records and heritage surveys offer no published proof.
articles.body:
Short answer: no published, verifiable evidence has been found that a continuous built tunnel links the Ring O’Bells (St Leonard’s Square) and St Leonard’s Parish Church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

The story is older and more persistent than the proof. For generations Middleton guides, ghost‑tour pages and regional folklore compilations have repeated a neat Civil War image: Royalists meet in the pub cellar, a hidden passage runs under the road to the church and the plotters slip away when the Roundheads arrive. The tale is still used on commercial ghost walks and local history roundups. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

Where the legend runs into trouble is the documentary and professional heritage record. St Leonard’s is a Grade I listed medieval church whose National Heritage List entry sets out its fabric, phases and sensitivity in detail; that entry makes no mention of a connecting passage. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332)) The Middleton Town Centre conservation‑area appraisal kept by Rochdale Council, the document that describes known historic assets and archaeological sensitivity across the square, likewise does not record any mapped or scheduled tunnel between the buildings. ([planning.data.gov.uk](https://www.planning.data.gov.uk/entity/6313525))

Stories of bones, buckles, muskets and a landlord frightened by a flying stone appear repeatedly in popular accounts and in later retellings of a local newspaper item often cited as the Oldham Evening Chronicle, 18 August 1972. Those secondary sources show how the tale has been told and retold, but I could not find a publicly accessible archaeological report, museum accession entry or digitised press copy that records the 1972 item or the claimed finds to the standard used by heritage professionals. In short: there are repeated claims of finds in folklore and tourism material, and an absence of a published excavation report or archive catalogue entry to corroborate them. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

That absence matters. If a brick‑lined or purpose‑built passage had been known, recorded or opened in modern times it would normally appear in at least one of these places: the national listing or schedule, the local conservation appraisal, an archaeological trust report, or a museum accession catalogue for recovered artefacts. None of those formal records I checked lists a continuous tunnel between the pub and the church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

Does that mean there was no subterranean connection at any point in any century? Not necessarily. Old cellars, drains, short escape routes and rubble‑filled voids are common in historic town centres; people over the centuries may have used cellars and alleys in ways oral tradition remembers as a “tunnel”. The distinction between an occasional informal route (a bricked‑up opening, a man‑hole, a drainage culvert) and an intentionally constructed, continuous tunnel is crucial and is where legend and archaeological standards part company. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

If a reader wants to move the story from local memory to proof, the practical steps are straightforward. Search original local‑paper runs (Rochdale Local Studies and the borough archives hold many microfilm runs and can advise on the Oldham Evening Chronicle reference); ask the Local Studies Centre (Sparth / Touchstones) and Middleton Library about any accessioned finds or records from Ring O’Bells cellars; and, if someone locates artefactual material, have it recorded by an accredited archaeologist and offered to a museum or deposited with the borough collection. The local archives are the place to start for newspaper, court and parish records. ([yourtrustrochdale.co.uk](https://www.yourtrustrochdale.co.uk/venues/local-studies-centre/))

For most Middleton people the tunnel story is less a missing map than a useful piece of place‑making: it links real places (a medieval church, an old inn) to real turmoil (the Civil War) and to the town’s habit of telling itself stories about its past. That is worth recording; just not the same thing as saying the tunnel, as described in the tales, has been demonstrated by archaeology or primary documents. Treat the passage as a well‑rooted local tradition with plausible historical context, and—until someone produces an excavation report or archive copy to the contrary—also treat the physical tunnel as unproven. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))
articles.content_html:
Short answer: no published, verifiable evidence has been found that a continuous built tunnel links the Ring O’Bells (St Leonard’s Square) and St Leonard’s Parish Church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

The story is older and more persistent than the proof.

For generations Middleton guides, ghost‑tour pages and regional folklore compilations have repeated a neat Civil War image: Royalists meet in the pub cellar, a hidden passage runs under the road to the church and the plotters slip away when the Roundheads arrive.

The tale is still used on commercial ghost walks and local history roundups. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

Where the legend runs into trouble is the documentary and professional heritage record. St Leonard’s is a Grade I listed medieval church whose National Heritage List entry sets out its fabric, phases and sensitivity in detail; that entry makes no mention of a connecting passage.

([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332)) The Middleton Town Centre conservation‑area appraisal kept by Rochdale Council, the document that describes known historic assets and archaeological sensitivity across the square, likewise does not record any mapped or scheduled tunnel between the buildings. ([planning.data.gov.uk](https://www.planning.data.gov.uk/entity/6313525))

Stories of bones, buckles, muskets and a landlord frightened by a flying stone appear repeatedly in popular accounts and in later retellings of a local newspaper item often cited as the Oldham Evening Chronicle, 18 August 1972.

Those secondary sources show how the tale has been told and retold, but I could not find a publicly accessible archaeological report, museum accession entry or digitised press copy that records the 1972 item or the claimed finds to the standard used by heritage professionals.

In short: there are repeated claims of finds in folklore and tourism material, and an absence of a published excavation report or archive catalogue entry to corroborate them. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

That absence matters.

If a brick‑lined or purpose‑built passage had been known, recorded or opened in modern times it would normally appear in at least one of these places: the national listing or schedule, the local conservation appraisal, an archaeological trust report, or a museum accession catalogue for recovered artefacts.

None of those formal records I checked lists a continuous tunnel between the pub and the church. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

Does that mean there was no subterranean connection at any point in any century? Not necessarily.

Old cellars, drains, short escape routes and rubble‑filled voids are common in historic town centres; people over the centuries may have used cellars and alleys in ways oral tradition remembers as a “tunnel”.

The distinction between an occasional informal route (a bricked‑up opening, a man‑hole, a drainage culvert) and an intentionally constructed, continuous tunnel is crucial and is where legend and archaeological standards part company. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1162332))

If a reader wants to move the story from local memory to proof, the practical steps are straightforward.

Search original local‑paper runs (Rochdale Local Studies and the borough archives hold many microfilm runs and can advise on the Oldham Evening Chronicle reference); ask the Local Studies Centre (Sparth / Touchstones) and Middleton Library about any accessioned finds or records from Ring O’Bells cellars; and, if someone locates artefactual material, have it recorded by an accredited archaeologist and offered to a museum or deposited with the borough collection.

The local archives are the place to start for newspaper, court and parish records. ([yourtrustrochdale.co.uk](https://www.yourtrustrochdale.co.uk/venues/local-studies-centre/))

For most Middleton people the tunnel story is less a missing map than a useful piece of place‑making: it links real places (a medieval church, an old inn) to real turmoil (the Civil War) and to the town’s habit of telling itself stories about its past.

That is worth recording; just not the same thing as saying the tunnel, as described in the tales, has been demonstrated by archaeology or primary documents.

Treat the passage as a well‑rooted local tradition with plausible historical context, and—until someone produces an excavation report or archive copy to the contrary—also treat the physical tunnel as unproven. ([wyrdways.uk](https://wyrdways.uk/sites/ring-o-bells-middleton-sad-cavalier/))

articles.title: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish to hold Remembrance Day service on 8 November
articles.excerpt: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish will hold a Remembrance Day service of Holy Communion on 8 November, officiated by Revd Natty Gray, followed by community refreshments.
articles.content_html:
St Luke’s Church in Deeplish is set to hold a Remembrance Day service of Holy Communion on 8 November at 10.30am, officiated by Revd Natty Gray.

This service will include readings from 1 Thessalonians 4: 13-end and Matthew 25: 1-13, providing a moment for reflection and remembrance.

Following the service, attendees are invited to enjoy tea or coffee and engage in conversation, fostering community spirit among regular members and newcomers alike. This gathering will provide an opportunity for attendees to connect and share their thoughts on the significance of Remembrance Day.

In addition to the Remembrance Day service, St Luke’s Church will host a Bible Study on 11 November at 10am, welcoming anyone interested in exploring the Bible in an informal setting.

Later that day, a Morning Praise service will take place at 11am, led by Reader Sue Horobin, featuring readings from Daniel 5: 13-30 and Revelation 7: 1-4,9-17.

The church is also selling some of its youth group costumes, which have taken up considerable space.

articles.title: Rochdale care leaver behind Little Acts of Christmas explains why no young person should go without a gift
articles.excerpt: Brianna, who grew up in care, started Little Acts of Christmas to give presents to young people in care. Her appeal has passed £900, with more than 30 requests so far.
articles.content_html:
A young Rochdale care leaver has explained why she started Little Acts of Christmas, an independent appeal to make sure children and teenagers in care do not go without a present this Christmas.

Brianna, who grew up in the care system herself, set up the project to provide gifts for young people aged roughly 10 to 18 who are in care, care-experienced or otherwise at risk of missing out. She runs it alone, without a charity, staff or budget behind her, and has built it largely through TikTok alongside a GoFundMe page and an Amazon wishlist.

In a statement supplied to Rochdale Daily, Brianna said: "Christmas is often portrayed as a magical time of year, but for some children and young people, it can be a reminder of the things they don't have, the people they might be missing or the difficult circumstances they're growing up in."

She added: "I didn't want to just sit back and accept that some young people might go without Christmas presents or that they might feel forgotten. Instead, I wanted to do something about it."

Brianna said young people in care, and those leaving it, can feel increasingly overlooked as they get older, and that she wanted to turn her own experience into something positive for others.

"I'm not a big organisation, I don't have a team of employees or a large budget behind me. I'm simply someone who understands how important even the smallest act of kindness can be," she said.

The appeal set out to raise £800 to buy gifts for more than 50 young people. On 2 November it stood at £140, with more than 12 young people having already messaged Brianna through TikTok to ask whether they could receive a present.

Since then the total has risen sharply. Brianna told Rochdale Daily that the appeal had passed £900 by Saturday 7 November, including a £700 donation from a business whose owner is himself a former care leaver.

Requests have grown too, to more than 30. Brianna said she has paused new requests until Thursday 12 November so that she does not promise gifts she cannot deliver. She plans to go shopping that day for the 30 young people already on her list, and will reopen requests if enough money remains.

She also has to cover postage, as she wants the project to reach young people beyond Rochdale.

Brianna is asking for financial donations, brand-new gifts, support from local businesses and organisations, or simply for people to share the fundraiser. She hopes to grow Little Acts of Christmas into a larger initiative across Greater Manchester and beyond, possibly as an independent organisation in future.

"A present might seem like a small thing to some people, but to someone who isn't expecting anything, knowing that somebody has thought about them can mean so much more than the gift itself," she said.

Donations can be made through the Little Acts of Christmas GoFundMe page at gofund.me/be1e51022, and the project can be found on TikTok at @Littleactsofchristmas.

Source: Statement and fundraising update from Brianna, founder of Little Acts of Christmas, supplied to Rochdale Daily. Image: Little Acts of Christmas logo, supplied.

articles.title: Who is the 'Sad Cavalier' said to haunt Middleton's Ring O'Bells?
articles.excerpt: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to St Leonard’s, but the formal record does not confirm a continuous, built tunnel.
articles.summary: Local tradition says a Civil War escape‑passage ran from the Ring O’Bells’ cellars to St Leonard’s, but the formal record does not confirm a continuous, built tunnel.
articles.body:
If you ask pub regulars and local guidebooks who the Ring O'Bells' ghost is, they'll give you a tidy answer: the Sad Cavalier, nicknamed Edward, a Royalist in plumed hat and cloak who haunts the old inn and its cellars. That account — a betrayed cavalier fleeing through a secret tunnel, murdered at a church exit, and buried under the pub's flagstones — is the version most often repeated in tourism and folklore write-ups, and it is the story behind ghost-hunt events now advertised for the building on St Leonard's Square. (Visit Rochdale’s local history/what’s-on page summarises the tradition in full.)

But legend and archive are not the same thing. What survives in contemporary and older printed sources is two separate threads: first, Middleton's documented seventeenth‑century politics and local gentry; second, a body of later folklore, local recollections and modern tourism copy that stitches a named cavalier to the Ring O'Bells. The reliable historical picture is straightforward: Middleton and its leading families were active in the Civil Wars and, as local histories explain, many local men and some gentry supported Parliament. Nineteenth‑century accounts of the town (for example, Edwin Waugh’s Lancashire Sketches) record Ralph Assheton and others raising men for the parliamentary cause and the wider county’s contested loyalties in the 1640s. Those sources show the town was very much a theatre of seventeenth‑century political division — which makes it an easy setting for a Royalist-versus-Roundhead ghost story.

The Stannycliffe name that appears in the Ring O'Bells tale also exists in the documentary record. County and diocesan antiquarian material mention a house or hall near Middleton called Stannycliffe (older printed collections record people “of Stannycliffe Hall” and deaths there). Those references confirm Stannycliffe as a historic local place‑name and social unit, not a modern invention of ghost tours. They do not, however, identify an “Edward” who was killed at the pub or provide a contemporary 1640s account of the gruesome ambush the legend describes.

What the tradition adds — and what we cannot yet verify from primary records — are the grisly details: a secret tunnel linking the Ring O'Bells' cellar to St Leonard’s church; the discovery of Civil War‑period pikes, buckles or helmets beneath the cellar flagstones; several skeletons dug up and identified as seventeenth century; and a 1972 newspaper report of violent cellar phenomena. These claims are regularly echoed in guidebooks and paranormal sites and are summarised on Visit Rochdale’s event listing, but I could not locate a contemporary archaeological report, museum accession record or an accessible copy of the cited 1972 Oldham Evening Chronicle item while researching this piece. In short: the colourful physical evidence cited in the story appears in modern folklore sources, but I found no published excavation report or council record confirming human remains or a formal 17th‑century burial under the pub.

That distinction matters for readers: Middleton’s seventeenth‑century division and the existence of Stannycliffe give the story a historically plausible frame, but plausibility is not proof. If you want to pursue the matter further, the borough’s Local Studies and Archives holds parish registers, newspapers, maps and estate papers that are the right places to look for contemporary mentions (the Rochdale Local Studies Centre and Middleton library collections are the starting points listed by the council). A verified archaeological report or an indexed newspaper copy would settle whether the cellar finds and the 1972 incidents are documentary facts or later accretions to the tale.

So who is the Sad Cavalier? In Middleton today he is, quite plainly, a figure of folk memory: a Royalist gentleman named in local story, given the friendly if mournful nickname Edward by landlords and guide‑writers. The deeper, verifiable facts are less dramatic — a documented history of local Parliamentary activity in the 1640s and the historic place‑name Stannycliffe — and no clear primary record tying a named Royalist corpse to the Ring O'Bells' cellar has been located in the sources checked for this piece. The legend will keep drawing in curiosity; for readers who prefer evidence to atmosphere, the archives at Touchstones/Rochdale Local Studies and the parish papers are where the next, verifiable chapter would appear.

Sources consulted: Visit Rochdale’s Ring O'Bells entry and event listing for the pub’s folklore; nineteenth‑century local histories recording Middleton’s Civil War activity; and diocesan/antiquarian material that attests to a historic Stannycliffe near Middleton. Where modern guides repeat finds of helmets, pikes and skeletons beneath the cellar I have flagged those claims as unverified pending archival or archaeological confirmation.

articles.title: 103-year-old D-Day veteran shares his story at Rochdale church event
articles.excerpt: A 103-year-old D-Day veteran will share his experiences at a local event, highlighting the importance of remembering wartime stories.
articles.content_html:
A 103-year-old D-Day veteran will be sharing his remarkable experiences at an upcoming event in Rochdale. The event aims to honour the stories of World War II veterans, particularly those who are part of the rapidly disappearing generation that fought in the war.

Gary Bridson-Daley, a passionate storyteller and poet, is behind the initiative. His project, Debt of Gratitude, has been dedicated to preserving the memories of veterans through storytelling and poetry.

Bridson-Daley has been actively involved in promoting these narratives for over eight years, creating a platform for veterans to share their experiences.

The event will take place at a local church, where Bridson-Daley will also discuss his latest book, Poetry and Portraits, which features moving poetry and images that pay tribute to veterans.

This book has been well-received and is recommended for anyone interested in the subject or those who appreciate compelling storytelling.

Local residents are encouraged to attend and participate in this meaningful event.

articles.title: The Baum Rabbit: the ghostly white hare that belonged to St Mary in the Baum
articles.excerpt: A local boggart in the shape of a white rabbit was a fixture of Rochdale folklore around St Mary in the Baum; nineteenth‑century guides and dialect collections record how families used the story as a warning and a joke.
articles.summary: A local boggart in the shape of a white rabbit was a fixture of Rochdale folklore around St Mary in the Baum; nineteenth‑century guides and dialect collections record how families used the story as a warning and a joke.
articles.body:
You can still stand outside St Mary in the Baum on St Mary’s Gate and see how easy it would have been, in the years before the town filled the fields, to imagine something uncanny stirring among the tombstones. The church on this site was founded as a chapel of ease in the 1740s; today’s building dates to 1909–11. Local history collections record that the graveyard and its approaches were long the stage for a phantom known in the Lancashire dialect as the Baum Rabbit (or Baum Rappit). That, at least, is what the nineteenth‑century parish histories and later compilers say. (Facts about the church’s foundation and listing come from Historic England and the National Churches Trust; the folkloric note is recorded in local parish history.)

The simplest, best‑documented point is this: “Baum Rabbit” was a local name for a ghost story said to haunt the vicinity of St Mary’s Chapel (Cheetham Street). The entry in a standard history of the parish plainly describes the name and the traditional belief that a white rabbit haunted the chapel yard. That is a recorded piece of local tradition, not proof of anything supernatural. The primary value of the story is cultural: it shows what people around Rochdale saw, said and passed on about the town’s edges. (The parish history that records the entry is available in the local historical compilation.)

What do we know about how people used the tale? Nineteenth‑century and later printed sources and dialect collections suggest the Baum Rabbit behaved like other British “bogies” — a cautionary figure. Writers who collected local anecdotes and dialects quote the rabbit in short exchanges and refer to it as a thing to frighten children or explain odd noises. Folklorists and local historians have shown the phrase “baum‑rappit” used in speech as a shorthand reaction to something unlikely or imagined. In other words, for many Rochdale families the Baum Rabbit was a piece of verbal culture: a nursery bogey, a joking local mascot in dialect tales and an item of town gossip recorded in journals and collections.

How early is the story on the record? The church was established in the 1740s and the graveyard was part of a densely inhabited area by the mid‑nineteenth century; the Baum Rabbit appears in nineteenth‑century parish and dialect material and in local journals and sketches from that period. Later folklorists and a modern survey of local traditions have gathered those nineteenth‑century mentions into a recognisable thread. There is no reliable documentary evidence that the story is medieval; the available scholarship treats the rabbit as an eighteenth‑/nineteenth‑century urban graveyard boggart rather than an ancient relic.

Which details are uncertain or unverified? Several colourful claims turn up in later retellings — that the beast grew to enormous size, that it was shot and the shot passed through its body, or that clergy recorded sightings in parish registers. Those claims appear in popular retellings and should be treated cautiously; the surviving primary texts (parish history, dialect entries and contemporary newspapers cited in later studies) do not substantiate sensational particulars. Where a specific newspaper or diary entry names a date or witness, scholars either quote it precisely or mark it as anecdote; where no such original is found, the safer judgment is that the detail is part of oral amplification.

Why did Rochdale keep telling the story? The Baum Rabbit seems to have worked on several levels: as a practical warning (keep children from the graveyard at night), as a local joke in dialect that marked belonging and identity, and as material for the town’s storytellers and periodicals. As urban Roche‑dale replaced fields and closed off some old shortcuts in the later nineteenth century, those physical changes also altered the story’s stage; yet the name survives in local memory and even in pub names and tourist notes.

If you’re after a next step: the best primary places to follow the trail are the parish history entries that note the Baum Rabbit and the official record on the church’s history and listing. Those give you the verifiable facts — where the chapel stood, when the present building dates from and that a ghostly rabbit was part of local tradition — and let you read the folklore in its proper, human context.

articles.title: Rochdale to commemorate Remembrance Sunday with local events on 8 November 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale will host several events for Remembrance Sunday on November 8, 2026, honouring those who served in the armed forces.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale will observe Remembrance Sunday on 8 November 2026, with various events planned to honour those who have served in the armed forces. This day is part of a nationwide commemoration that culminates in a two-minute silence at 11am on 11 November, marking Armistice Day.

The local events will include a parade featuring veterans, military personnel, and cadets, who will march to the town's cenotaph. This procession is expected to draw community members together to pay their respects and remember the sacrifices made by service members.

In addition to the parade, local churches and community centres will hold services throughout the day, providing opportunities for residents to participate in remembrance activities. The events aim to foster a sense of community and reflection among attendees.

As the date approaches, residents are encouraged to engage with these events and consider purchasing a poppy to show their support.

The significance of Remembrance Sunday lies in its ability to unite communities in gratitude and remembrance, making it an important occasion for Rochdale and its residents.

articles.title: Did goblins move Rochdale Parish Church up the hill?
articles.excerpt: A long-told local tale says unseen workers carried building stones overnight to the top of the hill; the record shows a medieval church, later Victorian work, and a 19th‑century storyteller rather than supernatural masons.
articles.summary: A long-told local tale says unseen workers carried building stones overnight to the top of the hill; the record shows a medieval church, later Victorian work, and a 19th‑century storyteller rather than supernatural masons.
articles.body:
The short answer is: no, there is no evidence that goblins or other supernatural creatures physically moved the stones of St Chad’s Church. That story belongs to Lancashire folklore, best known from the 19th‑century collector John Roby, while the documentary and architectural record shows a long‑standing church site with medieval fabric and later restorations. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

Roby’s version of the tale — titled “The Goblin Builders” in his Traditions of Lancashire — describes a Saxon thane, piles of building stone laid by the river, and those materials mysteriously transferred overnight to the hill where St Chad’s now stands; Roby also notes the famous flight of steps (he records 124) leading up to the church. That account is a clear piece of local storytelling rather than a contemporary record of building work. Roby wrote in the 19th century as a folklorist and compiler of oral tradition; his retelling preserves how people in his era understood the place, not the legal or archaeological history of its masoning. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

The documented history of the building is plain and far less sensational. Historic England lists St Chad’s as Grade II* and describes medieval and post‑medieval construction phases: a thirteenth‑century tower, fourteenth‑century arcade columns and arches, a clerestory dated 1557, and substantial Victorian restorations and additions in the 19th century. Those layers — Norman and medieval masonry altered, repaired and refashioned over centuries — explain the church’s position and appearance more plausibly than an overnight relocation by invisible hands. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

Why on the hill? Practical and symbolic reasons usually guided medieval siting. A high position overlooks the river and the town, keeps the building clear of floodplain, and gives the church civic and visual prominence; these are the kinds of factors architectural historians use when they discuss hilltop parish churches, and they match the description of St Chad’s occupying high ground above the River Roch. The building’s long use as the mother church of the ancient parish of Rochdale — serving a large rural parish for many centuries — also favoured a prominent site. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

That is not to say the legend has no local value. Roby’s telling and other versions preserve a communal memory that the church’s siting felt important enough to explain with a story; the goblin motif is widespread in English folklore as a way to name unexplained or surprising events. Local guides and walking routes still point out the steps and repeat the tale; it’s part of how Rochdale people have talked about their church across generations. But folklore and documentary history are different tools: the former explains meaning, the latter records evidence. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

If you want to check the facts in person: the parish continues to use St Chad’s as Rochdale Parish Church, and the building, its steps and the churchyard are publicly accessible; the parish’s information pages list services and contact details. The short answer is: no, there is no evidence that goblins or other supernatural creatures physically moved the stones of St Chad’s Church.

That story belongs to Lancashire folklore, best known from the 19th‑century collector John Roby, while the documentary and architectural record shows a long‑standing church site with medieval fabric and later restorations. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

Roby’s version of the tale — titled “The Goblin Builders” in his Traditions of Lancashire — describes a Saxon thane, piles of building stone laid by the river, and those materials mysteriously transferred overnight to the hill where St Chad’s now stands; Roby also notes the famous flight of steps (he records 124) leading up to the church.

That account is a clear piece of local storytelling rather than a contemporary record of building work.

Roby wrote in the 19th century as a folklorist and compiler of oral tradition; his retelling preserves how people in his era understood the place, not the legal or archaeological history of its masoning. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

The documented history of the building is plain and far less sensational.

Historic England lists St Chad’s as Grade II* and describes medieval and post‑medieval construction phases: a thirteenth‑century tower, fourteenth‑century arcade columns and arches, a clerestory dated 1557, and substantial Victorian restorations and additions in the 19th century.

Those layers — Norman and medieval masonry altered, repaired and refashioned over centuries — explain the church’s position and appearance more plausibly than an overnight relocation by invisible hands. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

Why on the hill? Practical and symbolic reasons usually guided medieval siting.

A high position overlooks the river and the town, keeps the building clear of floodplain, and gives the church civic and visual prominence; these are the kinds of factors architectural historians use when they discuss hilltop parish churches, and they match the description of St Chad’s occupying high ground above the River Roch.

The building’s long use as the mother church of the ancient parish of Rochdale — serving a large rural parish for many centuries — also favoured a prominent site. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1045812))

That is not to say the legend has no local value.

Roby’s telling and other versions preserve a communal memory that the church’s siting felt important enough to explain with a story; the goblin motif is widespread in English folklore as a way to name unexplained or surprising events.

Local guides and walking routes still point out the steps and repeat the tale; it’s part of how Rochdale people have talked about their church across generations. But folklore and documentary history are different tools: the former explains meaning, the latter records evidence.

([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/15271/15271-h/15271-h.htm))

If you want to check the facts in person: the parish continues to use St Chad’s as Rochdale Parish Church, and the building, its steps and the churchyard are publicly accessible; the parish’s information pages list services and contact details.

For the architectural inventory, Historic England’s official list entry gives the formal description and dating used by planners and conservators.

If any reader is curious about the Roby story itself, his Traditions of Lancashire is available in full online as a 19th‑century account of local legend. ([rochdalecommunity.org.uk](https://rochdalecommunity.org.uk/sites/saint-chad-rochdale-parish-church/))

articles.title: Rochdale Leisure Centre small pool closed for repairs
articles.excerpt: The small pool at Rochdale Leisure Centre is closed until further notice due to a technical issue with its movable floor, affecting scheduled sessions.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Leisure Centre has announced the closure of its small pool due to ongoing technical issues with the movable floor. The facility is currently awaiting assistance from a specialist external contractor to resolve the problem.

As a result of this closure, all scheduled sessions for the small pool on Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays, Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays have been cancelled until further notice. The management has expressed apologies for any inconvenience this may cause to users.

This closure affects local residents who rely on the small pool for swimming lessons, recreational swimming, and other aquatic activities. The leisure centre is a key facility for health and fitness in the Rochdale area, making this closure significant for the community.

The management is working to restore normal service as quickly as possible and appreciates the patience and understanding of its users during this time.

articles.title: Does a boggart still haunt Clegg Hall?
articles.excerpt: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.summary: Clegg Hall’s stone house and its Grade II* listing are facts; the boggart is a long‑lived story with no contemporary record to prove the medieval murder it’s said to haunt.
articles.body:
Short answer: the house at Clegg Hall is real; the boggart belongs to folklore.

Clegg Hall stands on Clegg Hall Road, near Smithy Bridge (Milnrow) about two miles north‑east of Rochdale. The building you can see today is a protected, Grade II* listed house whose main fabric dates to about 1610; Historic England records that listing (List Entry 1309615, first listed 10 August 1951) and gives the architectural description and location. Those are verifiable, recent and public facts. The “boggart” stories are an older, oral and literary tradition layered over that solid record. 

What the documents say: local and county histories trace the place-name and family back to the medieval era but do not confirm the grisly crime the legend describes. Victorian county compilers and parish historians — the sources relied on by Historic England — record that the medieval Clegg family held land here, but that their holding had changed hands by the late 1200s and that later documentary evidence for a family murder is absent. In short: there is no surviving contemporary legal or parish record that corroborates the tale of an uncle murdering heirs by throwing them into a moat. (These points are set out in the local histories cited in the Historic England listing and in the History of the Parish of Rochdale.)

What the storytellers say: the best‑known version of the boggart appears in 19th‑century folklore collections. John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and other collectors printed lively accounts of a “Clegg‑Hall Boggart” — a malign household spirit variously called “Noman” in retellings — and filled them with theatrical incidents: a boggart chamber, a conjuring scene that includes the mock‑baptism of a fowl, and a supposed murderous plot to seize an inheritance. These tellings are valuable as folklore — they show how local people and writers shaped place and memory — but they are literary and oral sources written long after the events they describe. They do not stand in for primary legal evidence.

How historians and archivists treat the story: county historians and the Victoria County History tradition treat the Roby‑style tales as imaginative reconstructions rather than archival reportage. That judgement matters: antiquarian and folkloric writers of the 18th and 19th centuries enthusiastically collected local stories, but they also embroidered and adapted them for drama and moral lesson. Where a claim concerns a violent death or other serious matter, historians look for surviving deeds, court rolls, wills or parish registers. For Clegg Hall, those contemporary anchors for the boggart narrative are missing in the published local record.

Does anybody claim to have recent proof of a haunting? No. There is no official inspection, police finding, archaeological report or archival discovery published in primary sources that confirms the supernatural elements of the Clegg Hall tales. The house remains private property and its architectural listing is the public record that governs what the council and the public can rely on. If anyone hopes for an authoritative update (for example a newly found medieval deed or a published archaeological survey), that would need to appear in named archival catalogues, a local authority report or a recognised academic publication before it could alter the basic separation between folklore and documented history.

What readers can do and where to look next: if you want the verifiable facts about the building and its legal status, start with Historic England’s National Heritage List entry (List Entry 1309615). For the folklore side, read the contemporary printed collections such as John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and the 19th‑century county histories (often available in digitised form). If you want archival confirmation one way or another, Rochdale local studies and archives and the county record offices hold the primary material historians would consult; ask them for searches of deeds, manorial records and parish registers for Clegg/Clegg Hall — but be clear: until such primary documents are published or cited, the boggart remains a durable piece of local storytelling rather than a documented historical fact.

Verdict for the reader: Clegg Hall’s building and location are verifiable; its boggart lives in the region’s printed and oral folklore. That’s not the same as proof of a haunting or of a medieval murder supported by contemporary records. For now, the boggart is a good story worth retelling — and a reminder to treat nineteenth‑century folklore as a literary and cultural source, not a court roll.

articles.excerpt: The event will take place in Rochdale Town Centre, starting at Rochdale Train Station, featuring stories of hope and community.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Town Centre will host an engaging audio walk event titled 'Stories We Tell: Rochdale' on a date yet to be confirmed. This unique experience aims to connect participants with local community stories, exploring themes of belonging, change, and hope.

The audio walk will begin at Rochdale Train Station, where volunteers will assist participants throughout the route. The event is designed for all ages, encouraging community engagement and participation.

Hayley Garner, a street mural artist, has contributed to the project, enhancing the experience with her artistic perspective. Participants are advised to dress appropriately for the weather and wear suitable footwear for the walk.

Further details regarding the event date and registration will be announced soon.

articles.title: Rochdale Asda worker's kindness a 'breath of fresh air' for widowed customer
articles.excerpt: Shaheda times her help around an older customer's shopping trips after the woman lost her husband, scanning and packing her shopping and stopping for a chat.
articles.content_html:
A worker at Asda's Rochdale store has been praised for looking out for an older customer after the woman was widowed.

Shaheda first noticed something had changed when the customer, who used to shop with her husband, stopped coming in for a while. When she next saw her, the woman was shopping with her daughter, and the pair told her what had happened.

The daughter lives in London and was worried about how her mother would cope on her own. Shaheda promised to look after her and told her which days she works, so the customer could time her visits for when Shaheda would be there.

Now, when the customer comes in, Shaheda scans and packs her shopping, fetches her a chair and makes time for a chat.

The customer told the store's customer manager, Dave, how much the help meant to her. Dave said: "The lady told me that ever since she lost her husband three months ago, Shaheda has been like a breath of fresh air in her life every time she shops – not just because of the help she offers, but as an emotional support and somebody to chat to."

Shaheda said: "I used to see the lady come in with her husband all the time and then didn't see her for a while. Then I saw her shopping with her daughter, and they told me what had happened. I told her to come and see me every time she came in... and she does. We have a good chat and I help her, as she does struggle a bit."

She added: "She thanks me every single time and I go, 'no, you don't need to thank me'. It's sweet, though. I like to think that somebody would do that for my own mum. I always think too that one day I could be in that position. It doesn't cost anything to be pleasant and kind, does it?"

For someone adjusting to life alone after a bereavement, a familiar face on a weekly errand can make a real difference, and the help Shaheda gives costs nothing but a little time.

Source: account supplied to Rochdale Daily. Photograph: supplied.

articles.title: Middleton care worker celebrated after 27 years at Langfield Care Home
articles.excerpt: Karen Haycock, who joined Langfield Care Home in Langley in May 1999, was surprised by colleagues and residents marking what the home calls 10,000 days of service.
articles.content_html:
A support worker at a Middleton care home has been celebrated by colleagues and residents after more than 27 years of looking after people at the home.

Karen Haycock, a specialist support worker at Langfield Care Home on Wood Street, Langley, was surprised with gifts, flowers and cards at a gathering on 27 October.

The home is marking the occasion as 10,000 days of service. Karen joined the home’s operator, Orchard Healthcare Group, in May 1999 — roughly 10,000 days ago — so the milestone reflects the length of her time with the home rather than a count of individual shifts.

Over her career Karen has worked across residential care, dementia care and nursing. She now works in the home’s Reconnect dementia community, which supports residents living with advanced dementia.

Along the way she completed an NVQ Level 2, took part in Orchard’s Step Up programme and undertook specialist Dementia Promise training. The group says she has seen the sector change considerably in that time, with better specialist training, equipment and more individual approaches to caring for people with dementia.

For Karen, though, the job is still about people. “I love spending time with the residents. They become your family,” she said.

Asked what she would tell anyone thinking about a career in care, she said: “You need to give it 100% to be able to make a difference to people, and that’s the best part.”

Home manager Lisa-Marie Hutchinson said: “Karen’s 10,000 working days is a fantastic achievement, and we were delighted to celebrate this special milestone with her and show her how much she is appreciated.”

Long service of this kind is increasingly rare in adult social care, where staff turnover is high and many homes rely on a changing workforce. For residents living with dementia, a familiar face who has known the home for decades can make a real difference to day-to-day life and to families choosing care for a relative.

Langfield is one of 23 care homes run by Harrogate-based Orchard Healthcare Group across the North of England and the Midlands. The group says the home holds a Good rating from the Care Quality Commission.

Source: press release from Orchard Healthcare Group, supplied to Rochdale Daily. Photograph: Orchard Healthcare Group.

articles.title: Free play sessions for young children in Littleborough and Middleton this week
articles.excerpt: Littleborough Library has a free under-fives session on Tuesday 3 November, while Junction Library in Middleton is advertising Saturday Lego and Duplo play for children aged two and over.
articles.content_html:
Families looking for free activities with young children this week have two council-listed library sessions to consider in Littleborough and Middleton, with no advance booking required for either.

Littleborough Library, at Hare Hill Park, OL15 9HE, is advertising Library Time for Tuesday, 3 November 2026, from 9.15am to 10.15am. The session is aimed at children under five with their parents, carers or childminders. It offers toys, puppets, simple crafts and a chance to meet other families. The council describes Library Time as an every-other-Tuesday activity, and says visitors can simply turn up.

In Middleton, Junction Library on Grimshaw Lane, M24 2BW, is advertising Lego and Duplo play on Saturday, 7 November, from 10am until noon. It is a free weekly activity for families with children aged two and over. No booking is needed. The council explains that it is informal creative play rather than a structured Lego class; children can choose to have their creations displayed at the library.

The two sessions serve different age groups and take place on different days. Parents should check the council's current event listings before travelling, particularly if a session is affected by an unexpected change to library opening or staffing.

The libraries also offer books and other reading activities, and the council maintains a wider events directory for families who cannot attend either session. A free library session does not require families to buy materials or tickets for the activities described above.

Official details: Littleborough Library Time, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/258/library-time---littleborough-library; Junction Library Lego and Duplo play, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/503/lego-and-duplo-play-on-saturdays---junction-library. The council's listings show the next dates as 3 and 7 November respectively.

articles.title: Rochdale remembers as community gathers for Remembrance Day services
articles.excerpt: Members of the public are invited to attend the Remembrance Day services on 8 November 2026, supported by the council.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale will hold Remembrance Day services on 8 November 2026, inviting members of the public to join in honouring those who served in the armed forces. The services will take place across various locations in the borough, providing an opportunity for reflection and remembrance.

The council is actively supporting all members of the armed forces community, ensuring that the sacrifices made by service personnel are recognised and commemorated. This initiative aims to foster a sense of unity and respect within the community.

The phrase 'Lest we forget' will resonate throughout the events, reminding attendees of the importance of remembering those who have fought for their country. The council encourages participation from residents to pay tribute to the fallen and show support for veterans.

As the date approaches, further details about specific locations and times for the services will be made available. Residents are encouraged to mark their calendars and participate in this significant occasion.

Lest we forget.” The Royal British Legion is holding its annual poppy appeal until Sunday, November 8, raising money to support British servicemen and women and their families. articles.title: Birthday cards for Wendy: family’s heartfelt appeal ahead of her 79th birthday
articles.excerpt: Wendy Bamford turns 79 on Wednesday 4 November, and her birthday wish is simple: cards filled with kind words.
articles.content_html:
A family is inviting the community to help make Wendy Bamford’s 79th birthday special by sending her a card filled with a few kind words.

Wendy turns 79 on Wednesday 4 November. Her son Stephen Bamford shared the appeal after she moved to Springhill Hospice in Rochdale.

When he asked his mum what she wanted for her birthday, or whether there was anything she would like to do, her answer was simple: lots of birthday cards, so she could sit and read the lovely messages inside. It is the only thing she has asked for, Stephen said.

A little kindness could mean so much

Stephen is welcoming cards from people who know Wendy and those who have never met her but would like to brighten her day.

“A few kind words might seem like a small thing, but they would mean the world to her right now,” he wrote.

In an update, Stephen thanked everyone for their comments and messages, explaining that the response had become too large for him to answer individually. He shared two addresses where cards can be sent.

Where to send a birthday card

Cards can be addressed directly to Wendy at:

Wendy Bamford, Room 10, Springhill Hospice, Broad Lane, Rochdale

Alternatively, cards can be sent to Stephen through the Littleborough collection address:

For Wendy Bamford, care of Stephen Bamford, Cryers Butchers, 39 Victoria Street, Littleborough, OL15 8BA

Stephen has promised to make sure his mum receives them, ready to open and enjoy on her birthday. Anyone wishing to take part is encouraged to allow time for delivery.

Source: Stephen Bamford’s public birthday appeal and follow-up, supplied to Rochdale Daily. Photograph supplied with the appeal.

articles.title: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish announces upcoming services and community events
articles.excerpt: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish will hold a Morning Praise service on November 1, followed by a series of community activities throughout the month.
articles.content_html:
St Luke’s Church in Deeplish is set to hold a service of Morning Praise on November 1 at 10am, officiated by Reader Sue Horobin. This service will be followed by tea and coffee, providing an opportunity for attendees to socialise and connect with one another.

On 4 November, the church will host a Bible Study at 10am, followed by another Morning Praise service at 11am, officiated by Revd Natty Gray. The church welcomes both regular members and newcomers to join their friendly congregation.

Last Sunday, the church celebrated Holy Communion, officiated by Revd Ian Butterworth, and will continue with communion next week, led by Kirsten Rutherford. After each service, refreshments will be available, allowing for fellowship among attendees.

In addition to the services, the church is selling some of its youth group costumes, which have attracted interest from societies worldwide, including buyers from Germany, Italy, Norway, and America.
