articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing Limited (RBH) has awarded a contract for the provision of VAT services to S3TAX Limited. The contract, valued at £14,750 excluding VAT, will run from November 1, 2026, to October 31, 2029.

The contract award is part of RBH's ongoing efforts to enhance its financial operations and support its housing services in the Rochdale area. By securing expert VAT services, RBH aims to improve its financial efficiency and compliance.

articles.title: Eight winners honoured at Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Diversity Awards celebrated eight winners for their contributions to equality and community cohesion at a ceremony attended by over 350 guests.
articles.content_html:
More than 350 guests gathered at Rochdale Town Hall on 30 October 2026, for the Rochdale Diversity Awards, which recognised eight winners for their outstanding contributions to equality, diversity, and community cohesion across the borough.

Organised by the Kashmir Youth Project (KYP), the awards celebrated the achievements of individuals and organisations that have made significant impacts in promoting inclusivity. This year, the event received over 130 nominations, showcasing the breadth of community engagement in Rochdale.

Among the winners, Rochdale Science Initiative C.I.C. received the Breaking Barriers Award, while its founder, Mohammed Attaur Rahman, was honoured with the Outstanding Achievement in Diversity Award.

Other notable recognitions included the Diversity in Public Sector Partnership Working Award, awarded to Petrus and the Rochdale Community Safety Team for their Town Centre Outreach Initiative.

The awards, which KYP has delivered since 2012, highlight the importance of fostering a diverse and inclusive community.

articles.title: The priest, the chicken and the shoe: Rochdale’s strangest boggart story
articles.excerpt: A gruesome Lancashire legend — a priest who answers a spirit’s demand for “a body and a soul” with the body of a cock and the sole of a shoe — belongs to nineteenth‑century folklore, not to court records.
articles.summary: A gruesome Lancashire legend — a priest who answers a spirit’s demand for “a body and a soul” with the body of a cock and the sole of a shoe — belongs to nineteenth‑century folklore, not to court records.
articles.body:
The memorable trick — produce a cock’s body and a shoe’s sole, burn them and send the boggart packing — is the line that keeps the Clegg Hall story alive in the district. It’s vivid, comic and a touch grotesque; it is also a motif from folk-tale collections rather than a contemporaneous legal record. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/25256))

Clegg Hall itself is not fiction. The stone house on Clegg Hall Road, Little Clegg (near Milnrow) survives as a Grade II* listed building; its main fabric dates to the early seventeenth century and the National Heritage List entry records its architectural details and sources. The building was first listed on 10 August 1951. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

The tale as most readers expect it appears in Victorian folklore collections: a household is tormented by a “boggart” or household spirit said to be bound to the hall after a crime against children. When a priest is summoned and the spirit demands “a body and a soul,” the cleric produces a cock and the sole of a shoe, burns them and so lays the spirit — at least temporarily. This version is preserved in John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire and in nineteenth‑century compilations that drew on Roby’s material. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/25256))

There is more than one way the story was told. Collectors printed dramatic variants and local ballads: William Nuttall of Rochdale supplied a ballad that elaborated characters and violence; county compilers quoted local proverbs that used the boggart’s name to mean something hard to get rid of. Those repeated tellings are useful evidence of how the story circulated and changed in speech and print. ([iapsop.com](https://iapsop.com/ssoc/1867__harland_wilkinson___lancashire_folk-lore.pdf))

When historians look for a contemporaneous crime to match Roby’s narrative they come up short. A late‑nineteenth‑century parish history that inventories local houses and families explicitly describes Roby’s account as “pure imagination” while acknowledging a ghost‑tradition and a local proverb — “As ill as Clegg Hall boggart” — that show the tale’s hold on local speech. There are no surviving court or parish records that confirm the dramatic murders narrated by folklorists. ([your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com](https://your-content.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/04145039/chapter-xvii-old-houses-and-old-families-butterworth-pages337-389.pdf))

The cock‑and‑shoe bargain is not unique to Clegg Hall. Folklorists have long noted motifs in which a spirit demanding a body and soul is tricked with a bird’s body and an inanimate “soul” substitute; such formulas are part of a wider European folk repertoire that nineteenth‑century collectors drew on, adapted and localised. That diffusion helps explain why the image is so durable: it is cultural shorthand for outwitting a restless presence. ([readingroo.ms](https://readingroo.ms/4/8/1/2/48123/48123-h/48123-h.htm))

For readers who prefer facts to fable: the architectural and documentary record gives Clegg Hall a clear place in local history — its list entry cites the Victoria County History and a late‑nineteenth‑century parish account for owners, dates and structural description — but the lurid murder narrative is a product of oral tradition and Victorian compilation, not surviving trial papers. The place name, the proverb and the ballad verses are the evidence we have of the boggart’s cultural life. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1309615))

That leaves the Clegg Hall boggart where it belongs for most purposes: in folklore, not the record of criminal proceedings. The story is worth keeping — as an example of how a local proverb and a single telling can grow into a regional legend — but readers should treat the cock, the shoe and the priest as part of Lancashire storytelling rather than a literal local history. If you walk past Clegg Hall on a dull afternoon you may still hear the tale; just don’t expect to find the court papers that prove the dark centre of the story.

articles.title: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing updates on Representative Body developments
articles.excerpt: Andrew Johnson has been re-appointed as Chair of the RBH Representative Body, with Rachael Ray as Deputy Chair, as they work to improve services for residents.
articles.content_html:
Andrew Johnson has been re-appointed as Chair of the Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) Representative Body during a meeting held last week. He welcomed Rachael Ray as the new Deputy Chair and acknowledged the contributions of outgoing Deputy Chair Rob Dyson. This update was shared on October 27, 2026, and highlights the ongoing commitment of the Representative Body to enhance services for residents.

During the meeting, the Representatives approved RBH's Annual Report to Customers, which is available on the RBH website. Johnson expressed satisfaction that the Representatives were able to provide additional oversight before the report's publication.

The body also approved the findings of a recent scrutiny review aimed at improving customer feedback regarding the investment programme.

The scrutiny review resulted in six out of seven recommendations being accepted, including tailored approaches for gathering feedback from different customer groups.

Johnson thanked the panel members and RBH staff for their efforts in this review, which aims to enhance how the organisation interacts with its customers and manages services.

Membership in RBH allows residents to have a voice in shaping the services that affect their homes and communities.

Johnson encouraged those not yet members to sign up, emphasizing that their involvement strengthens the organisation and ensures it remains responsive to the needs of the community.

articles.title: Free benefits checks at Littleborough and Wardle libraries on Monday and Tuesday
articles.excerpt: Council advisers will offer free, no booking needed benefits checks at Littleborough Library on 26 October and Wardle Library on 27 October, from 10am to noon.
articles.content_html:
Residents unsure whether they are receiving all the financial support available to them can speak to council advisers at two free library drop in sessions this week. The sessions are particularly relevant to pensioners, carers, disabled residents and people worried about household costs, but the council says they are open to adults generally.

The first is at Littleborough Library in Hare Hill Park, Littleborough OL15 9HE, on Monday 26 October 2026 from 10am until noon. The second takes place at Wardle Library, 448 Birch Road, Wardle OL12 9LH, on Tuesday 27 October, also from 10am until noon. No appointment is needed for either event.

The council says advisers can check potential entitlement to Pension Credit, explain Attendance Allowance, review Council Tax Support eligibility and give information about Winter Fuel Payments, Blue Badge applications and other cost of living assistance. They can also signpost residents to organisations offering further help, including Citizens Advice and Age UK. Attending does not guarantee entitlement to a benefit or an immediate payment: decisions depend on the relevant eligibility rules and application process.

Anyone attending is asked to bring details of their income, pensions, savings and benefits already received, so advisers can offer a more accurate check. Those visiting on behalf of a family member should bring relevant information if available. Take care with personal documents and give sensitive details only to the advisers at the official session.

Both sessions are advertised by Rochdale Borough Council as free and do not require booking. Anyone unable to attend can use the council's published events information to find its contact details and check for other advice sessions.

Official event details: Littleborough Library https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/1484/pension-credit-awareness-drop-in-event---littleborough-library and Wardle Library https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/1485/pension-credit-awareness-drop-in-event---wardle-library.

articles.title: New book showcases unseen 1930s photographs of Rochdale's Norden Riviera
articles.excerpt: A new book featuring 600 unseen photographs captures the essence of 1930s Rochdale, including the lost Norden Riviera lido, highlighting the area's historical significance during a transformative decade.
articles.content_html:
A new book titled "Britain in the 1930s" by Steven Brindle and Maureen Hill features 600 previously unseen photographs, including images of Rochdale's lost Norden Riviera lido.

This collection captures the essence of Greater Manchester on the brink of World War II, showcasing the stark contrasts of the era.

The Norden Riviera, which opened in 1935, was a popular outdoor swimming pool located off Edenfield Road in Norden. It provided a seaside experience for local families who could not afford to travel far. The facility included diving boards, slides, and spectator stands, surrounded by gardens and sports fields, making it a cherished local attraction during the 1930s.

The book highlights the economic challenges faced by the north of England during this decade, with unemployment rates soaring due to the decline of traditional industries.

However, it also reflects a time of joy and resilience, as communities sought leisure and enjoyment amidst the hardships of the Great Depression and the aftermath of World War I.

"Britain in the 1930s" is available for £50 and covers various regions, including parts of the old Lancashire, now Greater Manchester.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Unseen pictures of 1930s from Manchester's Ritz to Rochdale 'Riviera' - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news Unseen pictures of 1930s from Manchester's Ritz to Rochdale 'Riviera' From Rochdale's lost "Norden Riviera" lido to an almost deserted East Lancashire Road, a remarkable new book featuring 600 unseen 1930s archive photographs captures Greater Manchester on the brink of WWII. View 8 Images Cashier at the Ritz Dancing Hall. Manchester, on Boxing Day 1938 Add to preferred sources Comments News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 05:53, 26 Oct 2026 Storm clouds were gathering again globally. But on Boxing Day 1938 she captured, vivaciously, just one aspect of that decade. Crimson-lipped the cashier of the Ritz Dancing Hall in Manchester reflected the population's determination to find joy after the dark days of the First World War, the Great Depression, and unemployment. The 1930s led novelist and broadcaster JB Priestley to his famous vision of "three Englands" – the ancient country of cathedrals and villages, the blackened and scarred industrial Britain created by the Victorians, and the Americanised new consumer world of suburbs, cinemas and motorcars. He came to the conclusion after travelling the country with his suitcase and a typewriter to find material for his book "English Journey" published in 1934. ‌ Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter The decade in Britain saw a nation in transition. The north was hit hard by economic turmoil with unemployment levels soaring above the national average due to the collapse of industries like coal mining and shipbuilding. However, seaside cities became alive in the 1930s, thanks to the expansion of cheap rail travel and the emerging concept of paid holidays with thousands of working-class families flooding to the coast during their “Wakes Weeks” But the south and the midlands had seen a growth in new industries, notably car making, and electrical goods, and were able to withstand the economic fallout which the book says were distributed in a "grotesquely uneven way". ‌ A picture of a young, very well dressed couple, on Oxford Street, London, shows how affluence thrived in parts of the country while elsewhere, like the Lancashire George Orwell (pen name for Eric Blair) discovered in his travelogue "The Road to Wigan Pier" working class communities were decimated by the decline of traditional industries. View 8 Images A Wigan street decorated with washing, 1930s. The land as a place of marked contrasts is captured in a new book, Britain in the 1930s by Steven Brindle and Maureen Hill from Atlantic Publishing, price £50. It features 600 unseen black and white historic photographs of the UK. Counties covered by the book include parts of the old Lancashire, which are now in Greater Manchester, Cheshire, Yorkshire, Lancashire, and Northumberland. ‌ Images include an outdoor swimming pool in Rochdale in 1936 known as the Norden Riviera; soldiers clearing snow from the Manchester to Sheffield railway line; and a busy Deansgate in December 1930. A now lost Rochdale lido gave Mancunians a chance to enjoy a seaside experience without having to travel to the coast or abroad. The Norden Riviera opened in 1935 during when open air swimming was booming in Britaian. Located just off Edenfield Road in Norden, it was 'Rochdale by the sea' for many who could not afford a longer journey or who preferred something nearer to home. The pool was heated and came equipped with diving boards, slides and spectator stands. It was surrounded by attractive gardens, a cafe, a sports field with horse riding facilities, fences for show jumping, cricket pitches and areas for ball games. ‌ View 8 Images The "Rochdale Riviera" - the open air pool as it was at Norden in 1936. The Manchester Guardian newspaper on August 17, 1935. described the facility. It said: "The Norden pool, which measures 80ft by 40ft and is from 2ft 6in deep to 9ft deep is situated in the grounds of what, before the war, was Tenter House, just beyond the bleachworks at Norden, and the stables, where horses are kept for hire, belonged to this residence." "It is surrounded by green deckchairs and by an outdoor café, where one may have tea (or other meals) under green and yellow umbrellas. All around are delightful woods, beyond which one can see a shoulder of hill - but not the three factory chimneys lower down the valley. "A round paddling-pool satisfies the children too young to swim, and the conservatory of the old house has been turned into a ballroom. Next season, tennis courts, a gymnasium, a miniature golf course, and a children's playground will be added to the attractions of the Norden Riviera. ‌ View 8 Images A well-dressed couple in Oxford Street in 1932. "Bathing in the warmed water often continues till late by the light of powerful electric lamps." Other images in the book include Manchester's Cenotaph in St Peter's Square in 1935 in its original location before it was dismantled and reconstructed by Manchester City Council in 2014 at the northeast corner of the square next to the town hall to make way for the expansion of the Metrolink tram service. The memorial was first unveiled on July 12th 1924 by the Earl of Derby assisted by a Mrs Bingle, a local resident, whose three sons all died in the First World War. ‌ View 8 Images Manchester's Cenotaph in St Peter's Square pictured in 1935. A street in Wigan is pictured decorated with washing strung out across it. A Liverpool policeman directing traffic is seen standing in a protector box. These days the East Lancashire Road can be a notorious spot for traffic chaos. But a 1933 picture of the then "Liverpool to South East Lancashire Road" shows just eight vehicles over a half mile distance. The 27 mile highway was built at a cost of £3m. Britain was on the cusp of change in the 1930s. A world that would soon be transformed forever by the Second World War. ‌ Photographs in the book cover every county and city at that time, revealing a nation poised between tradition and modernity. View 8 Images A busy Deansgaate, Manchester in December 1930 The 1930s marked the golden age of the British seaside. Packed beaches, bustling promenades, pleasure piers and elegant hotels lured millions. Blackpool and Morecambe became synonymous with summer holidays. Camping, walking and boating holidays grew in popularity, while lidos, dance halls and pavilion theatres reflected a new culture of recreation and entertainment. ‌ Beyond the towns and cities, much of rural Britain appeared little changed from previous centuries. Medieval market squares, village greens and ancient churches dominated the landscape, while agricultural shows, livestock markets and seasonal fairs continued to shape everyday life. The decade was a world where horses and carts still shared roads with motorcars, and where quaint picturesque villages, market towns and centuries-old buildings remained at the heart of British identity. Co-author, Steven Brindle, is an historian and conservationist from Blackburn. He studied History at Oxford and spent almost forty years with English Heritage in a variety of roles as a historian and Inspector of Ancient Monuments. He has published extensively on architectural and engineering history. The photographs in the collection are from the archive of Associated Newspapers, plus contrbutions from many distinguished photographers. ‌ View 8 Images Holidaymakers on the sea front in Blackpool 1930s. They include: James Dixon-Scott, a photographer who wanted to record landscapes and ways of life that he felt were vanishing. He travelled around Britain taking pictures of buildings and rural scenes with exceptional compositions. Anthony Frank Kersting was a leading British architectural photographer. He was a Londoner who studied at Dulwich College where he developed his creative interests. His work featured a wide range of subjects from industrial landscapes to village life across the country. He was one of the leading architectural photographers of his generation and a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. Will F Taylor was known for photographing sweeping panoramic landscapes across Britain from the end of the Victorian period right through the 1930s. His work has featured in many social history collections. ‌ The book is published on November 5th. View 8 Images The book Britain In The 1930s will be published on November 5th. articles.title: Upcoming services and events at st Luke’s Church, Deeplish
articles.excerpt: St Luke’s Church in Deeplish is hosting several community events this week, including a Holy Communion service and a women’s breakfast.
articles.content_html:
St Luke’s Church in Deeplish is set to hold a service of Holy Communion on October 25 at 10am, officiated by Revd Sylvia Barron. Following the service, attendees are invited to enjoy tea or coffee and engage in conversation, fostering a sense of community among participants.

On 28 October, the church will host a Bible study group at 10am, welcoming anyone interested in exploring the Bible in a friendly and informal setting.

Later that day, at 11am, there will be a Morning Praise service led by Reader Sue Horobin, open to both regular members and newcomers.

This morning, the church is also hosting a women’s breakfast from 9am to 10:30am in the parish room. This event offers a chance for women to connect with friends and meet new people, with breakfast provided free of charge.

The main service on 29 October will begin at 10:30am, focusing on Matthew, chapter nine, verses 18 to 24. The church encourages anyone who hasn’t attended before to come as they are, with refreshments available after the service.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council awards £1.1 million contract for young people's accommodation
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract worth over £1 million to Stepping Stone Projects for a new supported accommodation service for young people at risk of homelessness.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has awarded a contract valued at £1,108,081 to Stepping Stone Projects for the Rochdale Team Around the Young Person Accommodation Model (TAYPAS). This initiative aims to provide supported accommodation for young people aged 18 to 25 who are at risk of or experiencing homelessness. The contract will run from November 2, 2026, to November 1, 2029.

The TAYPAS model will deliver specialist, psychologically informed support within a newly developed, purpose-built facility that will feature 28 self-contained units. The service will offer 24/7 support and management, ensuring that young residents receive the assistance they need to transition into independent living.

This development is significant for the local community as it addresses the pressing issue of youth homelessness in Rochdale.

By providing a safe and supportive environment, the council aims to improve the life chances of vulnerable young people in the area, helping them to build skills and confidence.

The next steps involve the construction and operational setup of the accommodation, which is expected to be completed in the coming months.

articles.title: The Healey Dell prophecy: Eleanor Byron, Mother Bagden and what the records actually show
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.summary: A short guide to the strange local tale that a Lady Eleanor was “maid, wife and widow in one day” — what early collectors wrote, what the Heritage Centre tells visitors, and what survives as documentary fact.
articles.body:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge — the Thrutch — is one of Rochdale borough’s most durable story‑places. The best‑known version of the tale says a local noblewoman, usually called Lady Eleanor (later linked by tellings to the Byron family), visited a fortune‑teller named Mother Bagden; the woman predicted Eleanor would be a maid, a wife and a widow all in one day, and on her wedding night the bridegroom was killed. That dramatic sequence appears in the earliest printed collections of Lancashire lore and in the Dell’s modern visitor material, but the story’s status changes sharply once you separate nineteenth‑century collectors from contemporary medieval records. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

The oldest printed witness we can point to is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire, a book of collected oral tales published in the early 1800s; Roby preserves a long, romance‑style narrative set at Healey that includes a miller, a ‘Fairies’ Chapel’, a talisman and the fatal wedding night that fulfils the prophecy. Roby’s purpose was to record local storytelling rather than to provide documentary proof of medieval events, and his account reads as literary folklore rather than archival history. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/25256/pg25256-images.html))

Local antiquarians and guidebooks of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries amplified Roby’s version. The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s trail guides and a short history leaflet reproduce the same outline: Ralph the miller, a messenger, Mother Bagden who claims intimate contact with a Fairy Queen, and the prediction that Eleanor will be “maid, wife and widow” in one day, followed by the death of her groom in a family feud. Those local guides attribute their narrative to older local histories such as William Robertson’s writings. The Heritage Centre presents the material as local myth and interpretation, alongside explanations of the Dell’s geology and industrial archaeology. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

What is demonstrably factual? Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve and visitor attraction at 121 Dell Road, with industrial archaeology (old mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Victorian railway viaduct that now forms part of a riverside trail. The viaduct is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those physical and administrative facts are public and documentable. articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The tale of Lady Eleanor, Mother Bagden and the Fairies’ Chapel at Healey Dell is well attested in local printed collectors — but it survives as folklore, not as a documented medieval event.
articles.summary: The tale of Lady Eleanor, Mother Bagden and the Fairies’ Chapel at Healey Dell is well attested in local printed collectors — but it survives as folklore, not as a documented medieval event.
articles.body:
Ask a local where the Fairies’ Chapel is and they’ll point you down the steps from Station Road, into the ravine by the River Spodden. Ask whether fairies live there and the practical answer is simple: no verifiable evidence supports the existence of fairies; what the records do show is a named rock formation, a cluster of old stories collected in the nineteenth century and a long history of people visiting the site because the place feels, to many, a little uncanny. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

Those are not trivial facts. Healey Dell is a designated Local Nature Reserve and an area of industrial archaeology that straddles borough boundaries; part of the valley was legally made a statutory LNR in April 1976. The most dramatic built feature is the Healey Dell Viaduct, a high, eight‑arched sandstone railway viaduct that is a Grade II listed structure on the National Heritage List for England. Those designations are documentary and can be checked. ([rossendale.gov.uk](https://www.rossendale.gov.uk/download/meetings/id/4148/e2_appendix_2))

The Dell’s historical record is everyday, material and useful. The valley contains the remains of nineteenth‑century mills and the disused Rochdale‑to‑Bacup railway line; archaeological and conservation surveys catalogue those features and guide how the reserve is managed for wildlife and visitors. Management is led locally by Rochdale (and neighbouring Rossendale) authorities and by volunteer groups; published ecological reports and neighbourhood plans reference Healey Dell when mapping green infrastructure for the area. That is the part of the story that affects readers’ lives—path repairs, parking signage, listed‑building consent for the viaduct—because those are things the council, landowners and statutory consultees can change. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

The Fairies’ Chapel and the Healey Dwarf belong to a different archive: folklore. Nineteenth‑century writers and local collectors, notably the county antiquarian tradition and later local compilers, set down tales about a natural recess in the rock that looked a little like an altar and could be called a chapel. Early print references—quoted in modern guides—describe a hidden pulpit‑like formation revealed when a flood washed away a covering ledge; later colourful retellings add a Fairy Queen, a Fairy King and a bewitched dwarf or witch‑figure, motifs common to British fairy lore. Those stories come from literary and folkloric sources rather than parish registers, court records or archaeological excavation reports; they are valuable for what they tell us about local imagination and nineteenth‑century reading habits, not as evidence of the supernatural. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/history/Fairies-Chapel-final.pdf))

You can still see the place‑name on the ground. Local walking leaflets and heritage trails mark a route down to the feature and signposts to a ‘Fairy Chapel’ appear on nearby footpaths and at the steps off Station Road. Community events and the Tearooms’ heritage material reproduce the old legends for visitors, which keeps the stories alive. None of these modern references change the distinction: a name, an attractive rock formation and repeated storytelling are not proof of otherworldly residents. ([whitworth.gov.uk](https://www.whitworth.gov.uk/uploads/walkingdocuments/files/WALK%206%20Healey%20Dell%20-%20captioned%20viaduct.pdf))

What remains uncertain—and worth noting—is provenance. Some of the best‑known versions of the Healey tales were shaped by nineteenth‑century collectors and local storytellers; when folklore circulates in print, oral tradition and tourism literature it can harden into ‘local history’ in popular memory. Where claims involve specific historical persons, dates or events, they should be tested against archival material; in the case of the Fairies’ Chapel, the archive records the place and the stories about it, not supernatural events. If you want proof, visit the council‑maintained reserve, look up the Historic England listing for the viaduct and read the nineteenth‑century sources for yourself—then decide whether the place’s atmosphere does the rest. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784))
articles.content_html:
Healey Dell’s narrow gorge, the Thrutch, has long been a place that invites stories.

Visitors still stand under the Victorian viaduct, follow the path to the small pool visitors call the Fairies’ Chapel, and hear the familiar local version: a fortune‑teller called Mother Bagden prophesied that a noblewoman, usually named Lady Eleanor (later linked with the Byron family), would be a maiden, a wife and a widow in one day; on her wedding day the bridegroom was slain and the prophecy fulfilled.

That dramatic sequence is not a modern invention. The earliest printed form widely available to readers comes from the 19th century: John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire preserves a long, romance‑style account set at Healey that gives the tale its shape and characters. Later local antiquarians — notably William Robertson in his regional histories — recycled and amplified the narrative, and modern site interpretation at Healey Dell Heritage Centre follows that printed tradition when it tells visitors the Fairies’ Chapel story.

What is verifiable fact? Healey Dell is a named Local Nature Reserve and visitor attraction at Dell Road, with recognisable industrial archaeology (mill sites, lodges) and a prominent Grade II listed viaduct built for the Lancashire and Yorkshire extension railway in 1869–70. Those are public, documentable features you can still see. The Heritage Centre publishes its own guides that describe the gorge, the so‑called Fairies’ Chapel and the local legends; Rochdale Borough Council lists the reserve, its address, opening details and facilities. The viaduct is recorded on the National Heritage List for England. These are the things you can check on official records and by visiting.

What is folklore? The supernatural elements — a Fairy Queen who issues prophecies, a witch‑fortune‑teller who communes with her, or the idea that a named medieval Lady Eleanor’s fate is attested in contemporary legal or parish records — belong to oral tradition and antiquarian storytelling.

Roby, Robertson and later guide‑book writers recorded what people were telling in their own times rather than producing medieval documents. Local interpretation today openly presents the story as legend rather than as archival history.

How the story changed over time is itself revealing. Roby’s early 19th‑century text gives a literary, sometimes florid narrative with named characters: a miller, a talisman, Oliver Chadwyke and a Lady Eleanor.

Later retellings folded in local family names (Byron, Chadwick) and local topography (the Thrutch, the Fairies’ Chapel).

The Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s material adapts those versions when it points visitors to the rock formation and to the flood of 1838 that altered the gorge and submerged some of the features said to be the ‘chapel’.

That lineage — oral tale into printed folklore into heritage interpretation — is a common path for many English place legends.

What cannot be shown from surviving records is the medieval documentary backbone the story implies.

I found no contemporary 15th‑century court rolls, parish registers or legal documents that confirm a wedding‑night killing, a named Lady Eleanor Byron of the period, or a recorded prophetic witch in Healey Dell.

Where claims cannot be matched to contemporary archives, the careful historian treats them as tradition and story. The result is not dismissal but classification: good material for local imagination, caution for anyone treating it as proven history.

If you want to see the story’s sources for yourself: read John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the early printed tale, inspect the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s guide for the way the tale is now presented on site, and consult Rochdale Borough Council and the National Heritage List for England for the reserve’s practical and architectural facts.

The prophecy endures because place, geology and a few dramatic printed versions make for memorable storytelling. That is a valuable local inheritance — so long as readers keep legend and archive in separate pockets.

Practical details: Healey Dell Nature Reserve and the Heritage Centre are listed by Rochdale Borough Council (address Dell Road, Healey). The viaduct is Grade II listed on Historic England’s National Heritage List.

For maps, opening times and the Heritage Centre’s explanatory leaflets, use the council and the centre’s published material.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council invites feedback on proposed Customer Access strategy
articles.excerpt: Residents are encouraged to share their views on the proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy, which aims to enhance how the public interacts with the Council over the next five years.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has launched a consultation inviting residents to provide feedback on its proposed Customer Access & Experience Strategy for the next five years. The strategy aims to simplify how residents contact the Council and ensure they receive consistent support, whether online, by phone, or in person.

The Council has identified six priorities for enhancing customer access and nine pledges detailing what residents can expect from the service. The aim is to create a seamless experience for users, allowing them to receive assistance without needing to navigate the Council's organisational structure.

The Council emphasises the importance of making it easy for individuals to access the right help, especially during challenging times.

Residents can review the draft strategy and related documents, including the Equality Impact Assessment and Sustainability Impact Assessment, on the Council's consultation hub. The Council is keen to know if the proposed priorities resonate with the community and whether any aspects have been overlooked.

The consultation documents are available for review and can be accessed through the Council's website.

The consultation is open now, and residents are encouraged to participate to help shape the final version of the strategy. Feedback can be submitted through the Council's website until the consultation period closes.

This initiative represents an opportunity for the community to influence how the Council interacts with its residents over the coming years.

articles.title: Residents face uncertainty as Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks undergo safety review
articles.excerpt: The future of Rochdale's Seven Sisters tower blocks remains uncertain as residents prepare to relocate amid safety concerns and ongoing housing limbo.
articles.content_html:
Residents of Rochdale's College Bank estate, known for its iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks, are facing significant uncertainty as they prepare to move out due to safety concerns. The landowners, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH), informed 229 households in October 2025 that they would need to vacate the premises. Currently, only about 90 households remain in the blocks, with many residents already relocated as part of a safety review process.

Claire Lord, a long-term resident of the Mardyke block, expressed her reluctance to leave her home, citing the security and community she has enjoyed for over a decade.

She is currently waiting for a move to a nearby bungalow, but delays in renovations have left her without a confirmed moving date.

Claire's situation reflects the broader anxiety among residents, many of whom are concerned about losing their established support networks and the uncertainty surrounding the future of the tower blocks.

The safety review has raised questions about whether the blocks will be demolished or refurbished, with no clear timeline provided by RBH. Residents have reported receiving conflicting information about the future of their homes, leading to a climate of speculation and concern.

Christine Hartley, another resident, is still awaiting a suitable replacement for her two-bedroom flat, which she fears may not be possible due to the size constraints of available options.

As the situation develops, the local community is left grappling with the implications of these changes. The uncertainty surrounding the Seven Sisters highlights the ongoing challenges of housing safety and the need for clear communication from housing authorities.

Residents are encouraged to maintain regular contact with RBH for updates on their housing situation.

evidence_sources.captured_text: The secret safety battle over Rochdale’s Seven Sisters - Manchester Evening News ‌ ‌ Skip to main content Manchester Evening News: Number one for news, opinion, sport & celebrity news The secret safety battle over Rochdale’s Seven Sisters SPECIAL REPORT: As clutter boxes pile high in the living rooms of the 90 remaining households on Rochdale's College Bank estate, an M.E.N. investigation uncovers BSR building safety notices, £1.7m empty council tax bills, and the human cost of a decade-long housing limbo. George Lythgoe reports. View 7 Images Town Mill Brow tower block on College Bank with a wonky R (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) Add to preferred sources Comments News George Lythgoe Local Democracy Reporter and Stephen Topping Senior reporter 07:07, 25 Oct 2026 Claire Lord sits alone in her living room surrounded by head-high boxes. The small space between her sofa and TV is the only bit of the flat not crowded by cubes of clutter. To answer the door she has to clamber over yet more plastic tubs filled to the brim with her worldly possessions. The 56-year-old is ready to move out of her flat in Rochdale ’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks. She’s been ready for weeks. ‌ Claire was one of 229 households told they had to leave by landowners Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) in October 2025. Since then, droves have been moving out of the blocks. Only an estimated 90 households are still left in Seven Sisters - actually named College Bank. RBH says this has been done for safety reasons. View 7 Images College Bank tower blocks in Rochdale known as the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) The tower blocks face an uncertain future, with the question of demolition or refurbishment still on the table after a decade of limbo. No matter the decision, it is understood all residents will have to move out whilst work is done - whether that work is to decorate or destroy. ‌ Claire is one of the latest to be exiting the estate, but it’s not a move she really wanted to do. When describing the day when RBH told her they'd found some new digs for her, she said she was ‘gutted’. The security, the views, proximity to healthcare professionals and the community are the things she cherishes most about her flat. Claire will be moving to a bungalow across the road, behind Lidl. “There has been a delay because the lady who lived in the bungalow hadn't done work on the place for some time,” Claire explained. “They’ve had to do painting and decorating, rewiring, putting new doors on and a fresh kitchen. ‌ “So they’ve been getting it ready for me. RBH told me about four months ago that I’d be moving and were waiting for the date. “Every time I’ve gone down they’ve come up with more work and more work to do. I’ve been down every week to ask. “It’s always the same story - ‘something is being done’. I’ve still not got a move-in date, I think I’ll be told about a move-in date in four weeks. “I do love living here. The security is good and there isn’t much chance of you getting burgled. ‌ “It’s close to the shops in the town centre, my mental health team is nearby and my GP is just down the road. “But my biggest fear of moving is losing that security. I’ve been here (in Mardyke block) for 12 years and I've never had any trouble, it’s a good community. “If I could stay I would. It’s not good for my mental health. I don’t know whether I’m coming or going. “Being stuck halfway is no good as I just don’t know. They’re just going to plonk a day on me.” ‌ View 7 Images Claire Lord, Mardyke resident on the Seven Sisters estate in Rochdale (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) Claire has credited RBH with supporting her through the transition. She has regular contact with housing officers, but that doesn’t mean the transition process has been easy for her. Like many of the tenants, she just wants to know what’s happening with the blocks. Claire added: “We’ve had so many rumours about what is happening. We’ve heard they’re bringing in migrants in; that three are staying up and four are coming down; then we’ve had that they’re all staying up; then we’ve had they’re all coming down and they’re building 250 houses. ‌ “Nothing is set in concrete and they won’t tell us. It’s all just rumours.” Her friend Christine Hartley, who has lived in the Tentercroft block for 14 years, hasn’t accepted any new accommodation from RBH. She is still waiting on a 'like for like replacement', which she admits isn’t really possible due to the size of her two-bed flat. The 67-year-old said: "You know there is someone you can rely on in the blocks. We often ring each other, pop in and check on each other as there are loads of people that have known each other for years. “When we were fighting the campaign, you’d nip to the shop and an hour later you’d get hope because so many people would stop us to ask what is happening with the flats. We’re still getting that now. ‌ “It’s a good question. What is happening with the flats? I'd ask RBH. “They sent a letter last week saying they’ve still not made a decision. But I think they have made a decision, but they just don’t want us to know what it is. “Why should we have to move out when they won’t tell us what they’re doing with the flats? It doesn’t make sense. “You can’t tell me they don’t know what they’re doing. It wouldn’t be the case if they didn’t let them get into this state. ‌ “It’s very quiet on the estate now, even during the day. It never used to be like this, it used to be bustling.” “Why can’t they just tell us what they’re doing? It’s more than due time to tell us now. “We’ve suffered long enough and it plays with your mental health. I’ve cried, I’ve been angry. “Just give us a bit of truth, we deserve that. We deserve some respect, it’s ridiculous.” ‌ View 7 Images College Bank tower blocks in Rochdale known as the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) This is a fair question to ask if you’re being forced to leave your home. Although a number of former College Bank residents have expressed their happiness with the new digs sorted for them by RBH. Christine and her partner Roy Kitcher thought their Tentercroft flat was going to be their forever home. They love life on Seven Sisters and see no reason to move. Speaking on why he is adamant on staying, Roy told the M.E.N : “We moved in here and we were at risk of becoming homeless. We thought this was going to be forever. We love it here. ‌ “It’s right next to the town centre, the doctors are down the road, the chemist is down the road. It’s spacious and we have everything we need right here. Why should we have to move? “When people move out of here RBH are getting reduced rates to move. Those are going to go up and people who’ve moved out could get into dire straits. “When we’re coming back from the holiday or a trip to the lighthouse, I point at the blocks and say ‘home’s over there’. Or coming down the motorway, as soon as I see the Seven Sisters, we’re almost homes now. “Before I moved in I told people I would never move into College Bank, because I didn’t like the look of them. Moving in changed my mind.” The pair are both part of the Save the Seven Sisters (ST7S) campaign that has been going ever since the intention to demolish came knocking. They feel like RBH is disrespecting residents by not explaining why they have to move, or showing the findings of the surveys that sparked the mass exodus in October 2025. ‌ There has been a long history of mistrust between tenants and their landlord, which goes back over a decade. The Manchester Evening News first reported on the possibility of the Seven Sisters being bulldozed by RBH in November 2016. At the time, the housing provider said it would consider proposals for College Bank and Lower Falinge the following spring ‘at the earliest’. RBH spoke of ‘reduced demand for flats as a result of recent welfare reforms’. But in the 10 years since, the picture has changed dramatically. According to Greater Manchester Combined Authority’s (GMCA) housing market monitor, 43 per cent of the 7,892 households on Rochdale’s active social housing register required a one-bedroom property in 2024-25, while 29 per cent needed a two-bedroom property. Campaigners argue that College Bank’s roughly 670 empty flats would make a significant dent in that waiting list. ‌ View 7 Images College Bank tower blocks in Rochdale known as the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) Plans unveiled by RBH in June 2017 would have seen four of the Seven Sisters towers knocked down - Mitchell Hey, Dunkirk Rise, Tentercroft and Town Mill Brow - to make way for up to 120 new homes. The three remaining blocks would have been modernised. Demolition notices were handed out to tenants in March 2019 , but residents refused to give up their homes without a fight. Rochdale councillors and then-mayor Andy Burnham also raised concerns , with local politicians going on to step up their scrutiny of RBH in the years to come. In 2020, a tragedy elsewhere in Rochdale that would bring national scrutiny to RBH and send shockwaves across the country. Awaab Ishak, who lived in a flat on the Freehold estate with his mum and dad, died aged two in December 2020. ‌ His parents had made repeated requests for help with a damp and mould issue at their home, but the issue was not properly addressed. Coroner Joanne Kearsley ruled that exposure to mould at the flat led to Awaab’s death, as she described the tragedy as a ‘defining moment’ for the housing sector . Before Awaab’s inquest took place, an M.E.N investigation in summer 2022 revealed that issues of damp and mould were widespread on the Freehold estate . Other families reported having children with breathing difficulties while living in the same conditions that Awaab’s family faced. The scandal sparked the successful campaign for Awaab’s Law , while RBH went on to be downgraded by the regulator and had their ability to generate private funding frozen. Gareth Swarbrick, the chief executive who had overseen plans to knock down the Seven Sisters, initially refused to resign before being ousted by the social landlord’s board in November 2022 . His interim replacement, Yvonne Arrowsmith, signalled a new era for the beleaguered housing provider. In March 2023, RBH announced a review into the plans for College Bank, before Ms Arrowsmith told the M.E.N in June 2023 that the landlord hoped to save the tower blocks from demolition . ‌ The social landlord entered into an exclusivity agreement with Legal and General Affordable Homes to ‘explore alternative options’, including a full refurbishment of all seven towers. But in October 2024, one year after Amanda Newton had taken over as RBH chief executive, the exclusivity agreement came to an end - with demolition brought back to the table . Andy Burnham launched a mayoral taskforce in an attempt to raise funds for the refurbishment of the Seven Sisters the following month. The Greater Manchester Mayor was joined on that taskforce by strategic partners such as the local council, people from the housing industry, tenants union and political representatives. Housing and regeneration boss at Rochdale council , Coun Danny Meredith, said: “We remain fully committed to our involvement in the taskforce, and with a new Mayor of Greater Manchester now in post, we can continue the joint work that began under the previous Mayor. “Rochdale is still in a housing emergency, and as the council is not a housing stock–holding authority, we must rely on RBH and our partners to build new homes and bring existing stock back into use. ‌ “Right now, 363 households, including 245 families, are living in temporary accommodation. Many of these families have been waiting years for a permanent home. This is not sustainable, and it is not acceptable during a housing emergency. “This is why resolving the situation at Seven Sisters and Lower Falinge is absolutely critical. Across those sites, more than 800 homes currently stand empty. Unlocking those homes is one of the single biggest steps we can take to reduce the pressure on temporary accommodation and give residents the stability they deserve. “We need a clear, deliverable plan from RBH for these sites so that residents can finally have a home for life. I hope we can reach a resolution soon because residents of Rochdale Borough cannot afford further delay.” View 7 Images Mark Slater, campaign organiser for Save the Seven Sisters (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) ‌ Mark Slater has been a leading figure in the ST7S campaign group since its inception and is a member of the taskforce, now chaired by new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig. He feels that RBH have deliberately overseen the degradation of the blocks - what he described as ‘managed decline’. Mark said: “I am frustrated to the point of anger that we’ve got a situation where we are listening to RBH saying no decision has been made. But everything is pointing towards a decision under the radar and proceeding with a demolition agenda. “We’re speaking to colleagues, residents and tenants who are also concerned. We’ve lived with this since 2016 and have this Sword of Damocles dangling over our heads. “For whatever reason RBH have decided to go down a route of ‘lets find out a reason for them to be demolished. That’s the way it feels for people on the estate. ‌ “I’m sure Bev Craig will be looking at those comparisons with an emphasis on retaining social housing and building social housing. Those will be scrutinised very closely. “For an organisation to say ‘we’re transparent, we want to communicate, listen to what people are saying’ but they give us this story that the flats aren’t safe. But some people have lived here for decades. “We know they’ve suffered from the managed decline RBH have pursued with these blocks. It seems to us they’re using these surveys to justify an agenda of demolition.” RBH have vehemently denied this accusation on numerous occasions. The social housing provider has repeatedly claimed they are committed to supporting all residents in their transitions from the 1960s blocks. ‌ In Mark Slater’s eyes, money has been the driving force behind RBH’s decision making this whole time. Because of the way funding works in social housing, it is much easier to get government funding for building projects in social housing as opposed to retrofit. Homes England focus mainly on housebuilding rather than refurbishment projects, which would mean going to the private market for funding in the case of refurbishment of the Seven Sisters. For RBH, that was not an option for a long time due to them being placed in special measures back in 2022 in the wake of Awaab Ishak’s death, who lived on the Freehold estate also operated by RBH. Being put in special measures meant RBH had a freeze on funding in the private sector, therefore unable to fund a potential refurbishment project at College Bank. Mark added: “As far as housing is concerned, one of the things Andy Burnham said at the Labour Conference was looking at giving councils powers to repossess homes that have been kept empty for a period of time. We are pressing for details on that and to see if there is any potential we could use that policy decision to do what we need to do on College Bank. ‌ “Everyone is talking about the need to build social housing, but we’re not looking for solutions in estates like this. We are looking at reasons to demolish and it just doesn’t make sense. “Ever since 2016 one of the things that hundreds of people have asked is ‘why do they need to demolish them’. The reason is because there is funding available for new build projects, but no funding available for refurbishments. “That, in one fell swoop, could change the whole process. If Homes England could produce money for refurbishmentment, I would be very interested to see whether RBH could take advantage of that.” Hannah Fleming, director of regeneration and asset improvement at Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, said: “We have been transparent with our customers that the long-term safety of the buildings in their current state cannot be confirmed, and that any solution would require all customers to move out for at least a decade. ‌ “In the meantime, our focus remains on supporting our customers into their new homes. We have already made significant progress, with just under 90 households left to find their new home and most customers already settled in their new homes. “We are working individually with each household to ensure their move is as simple and straightforward as it possibly can be. We know that this is a significant change for many customers and we are working with each household individually to find them a home that meets their needs and requirements. “In some cases, the new homes have required additional work from our empty homes team before they are ready for our customer to move in. Where this is the case, our team keeps our customers fully informed and supported throughout.” View 7 Images Tentercroft residents Roy Kitcher and his partner Christine Hartley (Image: Jason Roberts /Manchester Evening News) ‌ When to expect a decision on the future of the blocks? A decision on the future of the Seven Sisters has been up in the air ever since demolition was put back on the table in 2024 - when the new regime at RBH came in. The social housing provider say they have conducted surveys that suggest there are a number of structural issues with the blocks and have costed up options for various forms of refurbishments and also demolition. Despite the surveys being completed near the end of 2025, no decision was made by RBH. It is understood that the taskforce designed to shape the future of Seven Sisters, created by former Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham, wasn’t allowed full access to the surveys. So the taskforce agreed with RBH to have an independent review of the surveys. It is understood this was part of due diligence from a local authority point of view, with Rochdale council, Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), the tenants union and the local MP represented on the taskforce. ‌ The findings from that review are expected to be produced in the coming weeks and will be presented to the next taskforce meeting. After that, a decision on the future of the blocks will be made by RBH, but the taskforce will get a say in the matter. It is clear that all parties want to find a solution and have a decision. Campaigners claim that RBH have pushed the managed decline of the blocks in order to pursue demolition; the cost on RBH to keep so many flats empty is eyewatering. RBH have admitted it costs them £1.7m every year in council tax payments. The cost is astronomical because council tax bills increase the longer a property is empty. ‌ Empty homes council tax multipliers range from 100 per cent of the standard bill (double) in the first year, up to 300 per cent after five years of being empty and 400 per cent after 10 years of being empty. RBH executive Ms Fleming added: “It’s important that we make the right decision on the future of College Bank; not necessarily the fastest decision. Our focus throughout has been on doing the right thing for current and future customers, ensuring we can provide safe, warm, affordable homes that meet housing needs for generations to come. “The length of time this has taken reflects our commitment to working with our partners, as well as the complexity of the decision and the need to consider detailed surveys. As part of that process, Rochdale Borough Council and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority commissioned an independent review of the evidence, and we will discuss the findings of that work with partners before the RBH Board makes a decision on the future regeneration route for College Bank.” Rochdale MP Paul Waugh said: “Tenants have been left in limbo for far too long and I hope that they can be given the answers they need about the safety and the future of their homes. ‌ "I urge RBH to act as swiftly as possible to bring this to a conclusion on behalf of all Rochdale residents during a housing emergency. Each day these flats are left empty is another missed opportunity to support the many thousands of Rochdalians living in temporary or unsuitable accommodation. "The council and GMCA have confirmed their commitment to resolving this longstanding and emotive issue, and I will continue to work with colleagues across government to ensure the best quality housing in Rochdale is realised." The latest findings on the tower blocks’ structural integrity In summer 2020, extensive investigations on properties at College Bank uncovered serious problems with ‘compartmentation’ at Seven Sisters flats, which is supposed to prevent fire from spreading between apartments. RBH says a 24-hour waking watch was introduced as a result, plus bespoke fire alarm and evacuation alarm systems. Since then, the Building Safety Regulator (BSR) issued enforcement notices against RBH on four of the tower blocks - Dunkirk Rise, Mitchell Hey, Tentercroft and Town Mill Brow. ‌ In the notices, issued last summer and seen by the M.E.N following the release of documents under the Freedom of Information Act, the BSR said the landlord had failed to ‘take proportionate measures to manage the risk of spread of fire created by compartmentation issues’. Months later, Seven Sisters residents were told they would need to leave . Last October, RBH cited safety concerns regarding structural and electrical issues, problems with the water pumping system, roof damage and increasing costs to heat and light the properties as reasons for the move. The Mitchell Hey block was then evacuated in March 2026 , when a water pipe burst. Campaigners - backed by Rochdale councillors - say they are still yet to see the concrete evidence of why they need to leave the College Bank flats. A spokesperson for the Save the Seven Sisters campaign said: “Despite numerous requests by residents, campaigners and local politicians, RBH still refuse to share any surveys they claim show potential long term safety issues requiring the blocks to be emptied. RBH have pushed to clear the estate of residents since October 2025, all while still claiming that no long term decision on the future of the estate has been made.” ‌ In the meantime, RBH has communicated its concerns over the Seven Sisters to the BSR. Correspondence released under the Freedom of Information Act, seen by the M.E.N, said: “Surveys have identified that although the buildings are currently safe, there are a number of issues which will deteriorate over time. This deterioration means that the long-term safety of the buildings in their current state cannot be confirmed as the issues with building repairs and condition are becoming more pressing as they continue to age. “We have therefore been closely considering the options for how we address this in the short to medium term, as any refurbishment option will take a number of years to plan and commence, and an estimated 12 years to complete across all seven buildings. We are fully cognisant of our duty to keep the buildings and our residents safe during that time, and also to protect the well-being of those residents and their quality of life.” After the M.E.N was given sight of the documents released by the BSR, Siobhan McCoy, director of property services at RBH, said: “The safety of our customers is our absolute priority. We wrote to all College Bank customers about these notices when they were first issued by the BSR more than a year ago, setting out what they meant and offering opportunities for people to speak directly with us. We also posted copies of the notices within each of the buildings together with information on safety and how to contact us about concerns. "The notices concerned ongoing structural surveys and a historic fire safety issue linked to refurbishment work carried out in the 1990s. This issue was identified by RBH in 2020 and a range of additional safety measures were put in place, including a 24-hour waking watch, bespoke fire alarm and evacuation alarm systems, and support for any customers who may need assistance in an emergency. ‌ "We have continued to work constructively with regulatory agencies to manage building safety risks and address regulatory requirements.The decision to rehouse our customers was informed by a range of factors, including structural investigations, the scale of the works that will be required in all regeneration scenarios and - primarily – customer safety. It was not the result of the enforcement notices. "We strongly reject any suggestion that there has been a managed decline at College Bank. articles.title: Jolly Josh Christmas Ball sells out as Rochdale businesses urged to help
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is asking businesses to sponsor a table for £50 or donate raffle and auction prizes ahead of its December ball at Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh has filled the guest tables for its Jolly Jingle Christmas Ball and is now asking local businesses to help turn a full room into vital funding for families.

The ball takes place at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 11 December at 7pm. With guest places filled, the charity is inviting businesses across Rochdale and Greater Manchester to sponsor tables for £50, donate raffle or auction prizes, or discuss other ways to support the evening.

A contribution does not have to be extravagant. Vouchers, meals, products, experiences and services can all help boost the fundraising total.

Based at Ensor Mill on Queensway in Castleton, Jolly Josh says it supports more than 300 families of children and young people with complex medical needs, physical disabilities, life limiting conditions, and profound and multiple learning disabilities.

Its purpose built centre offers hydrotherapy, rebound therapy, sensory activities, youth social groups, accessible after school provision and support for parents and carers.

The charity says it receives no regular government funding, making grants, donations, community fundraising and business support essential to keeping its services running.

Rose Hutchings, Lead Fundraiser at Jolly Josh, said:

“We’ve been absolutely delighted by the response to this year’s Jolly Jingle Ball and to see the tables fill. What we’d really love now is for the wider Rochdale business community to help us make the night as successful as possible for our families.

“A £50 table sponsorship or a donated raffle or auction prize might feel like a relatively small contribution to a business, but when lots of local organisations get behind us those contributions quickly add up.

“Jolly Josh doesn’t receive regular government funding, so fundraising and community support genuinely help us continue providing a safe, accessible place where children and young people with complex needs and their families can connect, access opportunities and feel part of a community.”

The appeal comes as demand for the charity’s specialist services continues to grow. Jolly Josh says its hydrotherapy provision has previously run at least 42 sessions a week and experienced waiting lists, with strong demand for other services too.

Businesses interested in a £50 table sponsorship, donating a raffle or auction prize, or offering other event support can email Rose Hutchings at rose@jollyjosh.co.uk or call 01706 399141.

Further information about Jolly Josh, registered charity number 1178116, is available at https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

Source: Jolly Josh press release supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Upcoming events in Rochdale: Circus theatre and Celebrity secrets
articles.excerpt: Discover the latest events in Rochdale, including a circus theatre performance and insights from a Celebrity Traitors contestant, starting October 21.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale will host a vibrant family show titled "The Hideout," which combines circus, parkour, and storytelling. The performance explores the complexities of friendship through the characters Luca and Maya, who transform a fallen tree into a playground filled with daring adventures.

This engaging production aims to resonate with children by addressing the anxieties surrounding friendships in a visually captivating manner.

In addition to the theatrical performance, Julie Hesmondhalgh, known for her role in the BBC series "The Traitors," will share behind-the-scenes stories and secrets from her time on the show.

This event promises to offer fans an insider's perspective on the popular reality series, making it a must-attend for enthusiasts.

Both events are set to take place starting 21 October, providing an exciting opportunity for local families and fans of the show to engage with the arts and entertainment scene in Rochdale.

For those interested in attending, further details about the venue and ticketing information can be found on local event listings. This is a great chance for residents to enjoy quality entertainment and connect with the community.

articles.title: Rochdale’s £5m crisis support fund: what help is available this winter and how to ask
articles.excerpt: The council lists help with sudden financial emergencies, housing costs and essential goods. Different schemes have different rules; an award is not automatic.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale residents struggling to afford essentials can ask about support through the council's Crisis and Resilience Fund as winter approaches.

The £5 million programme runs from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027, using Department for Work and Pensions funding. It replaced the Household Support Fund in April. The £5 million is the borough-wide programme budget, not an amount available to each household.

The council lists several routes: Crisis Payments for sudden financial difficulty; Housing Payments for emergency rent or housing costs; the Discretionary Crisis Fund for goods; and Healthy Homes grants for eligible vulnerable residents needing help such as boiler repairs or essential appliances. Each route needs its own eligibility check.

For Crisis Payments, eligible residents can receive a voucher worth up to £75 towards food and energy. Applicants must live in Rochdale borough, be at least 16 and have nobody receiving Child Benefit for them. Applications are allowed once every six months. Apply by calling 01706 923685; the published hours are Monday to Friday, 9am–5pm. Examples of a crisis include fire, flooding, a health emergency or losing employment.

The separate Discretionary Crisis Fund is described as last-resort support. It provides goods rather than cash. Its contact number is 01706 532222 and its email is StrategicHousing@rochdale.gov.uk.

Check the route that matches your circumstances before applying. The main fund page also mentions food vouchers only through the end of the 2026 summer holidays; that wording does not establish a winter voucher entitlement.

Official programme and scheme guidance: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund

articles.title: Rochdale Sleep Out raises funds for homeless support
articles.excerpt: Fundraisers gathered at Crown Oil Arena for the annual Sleep Out, raising awareness and funds for homelessness initiatives in the community.
articles.content_html:
Fundraisers spent a night outdoors at Rochdale's Crown Oil Arena to raise awareness and vital funds for people experiencing homelessness. This event, the second annual Sleep Out organised by Petrus Communities and RAFC Community Trust, saw supporters from across the borough come together for a common cause.

The money raised will support the Changing Lives initiative, a football programme designed to assist individuals facing homelessness or living in supported accommodation.

The initiative aims to enhance participants' mental health, physical well-being, and social inclusion through free football sessions, while also providing personal development opportunities, including pathways into volunteering, education, and employment.

Louise Scriven, Fundraising and Partnerships Coordinator at Petrus, emphasised that the Sleep Out is not about pretending to experience homelessness, but about standing in solidarity with those facing housing insecurities. She noted that last year's event significantly impacted participants, helping them rebuild confidence, forge new friendships, and develop skills to become active community members.

The funds raised from this year's Sleep Out will continue to provide essential accommodation, support, advice, and opportunities for those experiencing homelessness and disadvantage in Rochdale, Oldham, and Burnley.

Donations are crucial for sustaining these services and making a difference in the lives of vulnerable individuals in the community.

articles.title: Harvest Thanksgiving service to be held in Rochdale on 17 October
articles.excerpt: A Harvest Thanksgiving service will take place in Rochdale on October 17, inviting the community to celebrate and support local foodbanks.
articles.content_html:
A Harvest Thanksgiving service is scheduled for Sunday 17 October, at 10.30am in Rochdale. The event aims to celebrate the abundance of creation and raise awareness of the need to support those less fortunate in the community.

Led by Rev’d Ben Somervell, the service will include a sermon based on Psalm 126. Attendees are encouraged to bring donations of tinned and dry packaged foods for the local foodbank, highlighting the importance of community support during challenging times.

The service is designed for all ages and will feature performances from the day school choir, who will sing a selection of songs. Following the service, refreshments including coffee and tea will be served in the parish room, providing an opportunity for fellowship and conversation.

Everyone is welcome to attend, regardless of their previous church experience or beliefs. The evening will also include a relaxed prayer meeting, offering a space for reflection and preparation for the week ahead.

articles.title: Broadfield Park Slopes renovation celebrated at Rochdale Town Hall
articles.excerpt: A special event at Rochdale Town Hall recognised the contributions of volunteers and partners involved in the restoration of Broadfield Park Slopes, highlighting the project's community impact and heritage significance.
articles.content_html:
A celebration was held at Rochdale Town Hall to honour the individuals and groups who contributed to the renovation of Broadfield Park Slopes.

This historic site, located between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church, has undergone significant restoration, thanks to the efforts of local volunteers and funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund.

The event, organised by Polly Brant, Cultural Engagement Officer for Rochdale Council, brought together volunteers, partners, and community members to acknowledge their roles in the project. Guests were treated to a series of films by local filmmaker Jack Grindrod, showcasing the stories and heritage associated with the park's transformation. The films captured the community involvement that played a crucial role in the renovation process.

The evening featured poetry readings by Alende Amisi, a local poet and former young poet in residence, who shared his personal reflections on Rochdale's heritage.

His contributions added a personal touch to the event, which celebrated not only the park's restoration but also the community spirit that drove the project forward.

The renovation has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, and introduced new heritage interpretation.

The lower lawn has been terraced to create a natural amphitheatre, providing a new space for activities and events, enhancing the park's role as a community hub.

evidence_sources.captured_text: Town celebrates the people and stories behind Broadfield Park Slopes renovation - Rochdale Times Skip to content LATEST NEWS Town celebrates the people and stories behind Broadfield Park Slopes renovation The people who helped bring Rochdale’s historic Broadfield Park Slopes back to life were celebrated at a special event at Rochdale Town Hall. The celebration, arranged by Polly Brant, Rochdale Council Cultural Engagement officer, brought together volunteers, partners and people who have been involved in the project to recognise what has been achieved and, importantly, the contribution local people have made along the way. Guests watched a series of films created by Rochdale filmmaker Jack Grindrod and Breaking Barriers, capturing the people, stories, heritage and community involvement behind the transformation. The evening also featured poetry readings from Alende Amisi, a poet who grew up in Rochdale and was a young poet in residence during Rochdale’s Town of Culture. Passionate about the town and its heritage, Alende brought a personal perspective to an evening which was as much about Rochdale’s people as its history. A special thank you was also given to the many volunteers who have supported the project, giving their time to archaeological digs, activities and events and helping uncover and share the history of this important part of the town. The Grade II listed Broadfield Park Slopes sit between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church and have been restored through a project delivered by Rochdale Development Agency working with Rochdale Borough Council, with funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund. The work has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, lighting and CCTV, and introduced new heritage interpretation. The lower lawn has also been terraced, creating a natural amphitheatre and new space for activities and events. READ MORE: Customers flock to opening of new Peacocks store Archaeology and community participation have been a major part of the project. Excavations have uncovered the footings of Charles Kershaw’s 19th century Central Corn Mill, cobbled trackways and the former public weigh station, alongside finds including ceramics, clay smoking pipes, animal bones and glass bottles. Four archaeological digs have taken place, with the wider programme involving schoolchildren, students, volunteers and members of the public. It has included 28 work placement students, 12 archaeological volunteers and a two year schools programme involving 715 pupils. Cllr Sue Smith, portfolio holder for Communities and Co-operation at Rochdale Council, said: “This was a wonderful opportunity to celebrate not just the transformation of the Broadfield Park Slopes, but the people who have made this project so special. “Our volunteers deserve a huge thank you. They have given their time, enthusiasm and energy to this project and have helped us uncover and share more of Rochdale’s history. “It was fantastic to see those stories captured in the films created by Jack Grindrod and Breaking Barriers, and to hear from Alende Amisi, whose passion for Rochdale and its heritage really reflects what this project is about. “The Slopes have been part of Rochdale for generations. We have protected an important part of our heritage, opened it back up for people to enjoy and, crucially, involved our communities in doing it.” The Broadfield Park Slopes are now open to the public, creating a restored green space at the heart of Rochdale’s historic town centre.
