articles.title: Young people inspire £85,000–£100,000 Castleton pump track proposal
articles.excerpt: A site beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road is being explored for a Castleton bike track, with young people helping shape the idea. Funding and approvals remain outstanding.
articles.content_html:
A new pump track costing an estimated £85,000 to £100,000 is being explored for Castleton after local young people asked for somewhere closer to home to ride their bikes.

Councillor Dave Jones said an area beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road had emerged as a promising potential location following discussions with council officers and youth workers.

The proposal remains at an early stage. No funding or final site approval has been announced, and there is no confirmed construction timetable.

In an update shared with Rochdale Daily, Cllr Jones described a positive meeting with Environmental Management, township officer Caroline and Jasmin from the Youth Work Team to discuss the concept.

Several possible locations were considered. According to the councillor, young people suggested the Manchester Road site because it feels safe. Its existing play area and car park could also make it convenient for families with children of different ages.

The idea is for younger children to use the playground while older children and teenagers could enjoy a nearby bike track, bringing different activities together in one central location.

Cllr Jones said those at the meeting supported involving young people in the design process. They also discussed whether contractors could explain how the track is built and explore suitable opportunities for young people to participate.

A bike repair hub was another suggestion. Local young people have spoken about their interest in repairing bicycles and sharing those skills with others. Secure bike storage lockers were also raised during the discussions.

The councillor said some young people currently travel to tracks elsewhere in the borough, including Littleborough, and expressed concern about the busy roads those journeys can involve. He believes a Castleton facility could offer a more convenient option and reassurance for families.

Funding is the main obstacle. Cllr Jones put the initial estimated cost at between £85,000 and £100,000 and said several processes and approvals would need to be completed before any scheme could proceed.

Council officers are now exploring possible funding sources, according to his update. A further meeting is planned to discuss potential designs and ensure any future proposal reflects what local young people want.

Cllr Jones also thanked Keane, the young person who first approached him with the idea, and praised young residents for taking an active role in improving their community.

He cautioned: “It's important to stress that projects like this take time, and there is still a long way to go.”

The potential location, repair hub, storage lockers and construction involvement are all ideas under discussion rather than confirmed features of an approved scheme.

articles.title: Rochdale Council celebrates achievements of over 200 cared-for children at annual awards
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council hosted its annual awards ceremony at Matthew Moss High School, recognising the achievements of more than 200 cared-for children with medals and a day of entertainment.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council held its annual awards ceremony on 16 October at Matthew Moss High School, celebrating the achievements of over 200 cared-for children. The event, known as 'Our Big Day', recognised the resilience and determination of young people in care, with hundreds of medals awarded to honour their individual successes.

The council received 273 nominations from carers, teachers, and social workers, highlighting the inspiring journeys of children up to the age of 12. Awards were given for exceptional progress in education, sporting achievements, acts of kindness, and positive attitudes in the face of adversity.

The day included a variety of entertainment, such as trampolines, funfair rides, and face painting, allowing families to create joyful memories together.

Councillor Rachel Massey, cabinet member for children’s services and education, expressed her pride in the achievements of the children, stating, "They are all exceptional young people and show phenomenal determination to be their very best. This doesn’t go unnoticed by those around them."

The event aimed to provide public recognition for the hard work and accomplishments of these young individuals.

Local businesses sponsored the celebration, contributing to the activities and entertainment provided for families. Notable sponsors included A&T Surfacing Ltd, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing, and Rochdale Hornets, among others. This community support helped create a memorable day for the children and their families.

articles.title: Jolly Josh welcomes Rochdale families with inclusive play, music and activity sessions
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with weekly sessions and bookable activities.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with a programme of inclusive activities and support.

Based at 2 Ensor Mill in Castleton, Rochdale, OL11 2NU, the centre welcomes children and young adults aged from birth to 19.

The charity says finding activities where a child is welcomed, understood and supported can be difficult, and wants more parents, carers, relatives and professionals to know what is available.

Its programme includes music and signing, themed play sessions, an after-school club, a youth group and activities that families can book directly with the centre.

Weekly sessions

Sing And Sign runs every Wednesday from 10.30am to 12.30pm, bringing together music, songs and signing to make communication fun.

Themed Stay And Play takes place every Tuesday and Saturday from 9.30am to 12.30pm. Sessions offer activities, friendship and a different theme each week.

Sensory Touch And Music runs every Thursday from 10am to noon, offering a relaxing sensory session.

The After School Club takes place every Wednesday from 4pm to 7pm, with inclusive activities and a light tea offered for every child.

The Youth Group meets every Thursday from 5pm to 8pm, giving young people a welcoming space to socialise, take part in activities and build friendships.

Activities available to book

Hydrotherapy sessions can be booked for families or with the centre’s Hydro Lead.

Private sound bath sessions are also available by contacting the centre, offering an opportunity to take time out of a busy schedule.

Rebound Therapy provides supported movement and sensory experiences using a trampoline, with sessions bookable through the centre.

How to get in touch

Parents, carers, family members and professionals supporting a child with complex medical needs are invited to contact Jolly Josh to learn more about its sessions.

Call 01706 399141, email sarah@jollyjosh.co.uk or visit https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

The centre asks anyone planning to visit to contact the team first so an appointment can be arranged.

Families can contact the centre to discuss which sessions suit their child and ask about booking, availability and charges.

The charity is also encouraging people to share its appeal with families who may not yet know about the support available.

Source: Jolly Josh session information supplied to Rochdale Daily; centre details confirmed through https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

articles.title: Volunteers urgently needed at Hollingworth Lake to help Rochdale Sea Cadets
articles.excerpt: GTAS is appealing for volunteers and a donated skip to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets on Saturday 24 October, meeting at 10am.
articles.content_html:
GTAS has issued an urgent appeal for volunteers to help clear an overgrown storage area for Rochdale Sea Cadets this Saturday, 24 October.

Anyone able to lend a hand is asked to meet at Hollingworth Lake council car park at 10am. Organisers say help would be welcome for any length of time, whether volunteers can spare an hour or stay for the day.

The group describes the clearance as a big task and is asking people to bring sturdy gardening gloves if they have them. Spades, shovels, loppers, other gardening tools and wheelbarrows would also be useful.

Local businesses are being asked to support the effort too. GTAS is looking for a skip or waste company willing to donate a skip for a few hours to help with the clearance.

The volunteer day is an opportunity for residents and businesses to give practical support to Rochdale Sea Cadets by helping bring the overgrown space back into use.

Anyone who can volunteer or help provide a skip should message GTAS directly through the group’s appeal post.

Source: GTAS community appeal supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Volunteers and council team tackle overgrown areas at Middleton’s Jubilee Park
articles.excerpt: The Friends of Jubilee Park and council staff have joined forces for the second phase of work to manage overgrown shrubs and care for the park’s rhododendrons.
articles.content_html:
Work to open up overgrown shrub areas at Jubilee Park in Middleton has entered its second phase, with volunteers and council staff joining forces to improve the grounds.

The Friends of Jubilee Park have been working alongside Rochdale Borough Council’s Environmental Management team, carrying out maintenance that includes caring for the park’s collection of rhododendrons.

The group says the work will encourage healthy new growth over the next couple of seasons, improve views and sight lines, and help visitors feel safer.

Opening up densely planted areas is intended to create a brighter, more welcoming park while supporting the long-term health of its shrubs.

Visitors may notice that some sections look temporarily untidy as the work progresses. The Friends have asked for patience, explaining that the maintenance is intended to bring lasting improvements.

“These improvements will bring lasting benefits for visitors and help Jubilee Park continue to thrive,” the group said.

The Friends describe Jubilee Park as a Gold Medal-winning Green Flag park and thanked visitors for their understanding while volunteers and staff care for the grounds.

The latest work forms part of an ongoing effort to maintain the much-loved Middleton green space for everyone who uses it.

Source: Friends of Jubilee Park update supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Inclusive roundabout and zip line feature in plans for new Falinge Park play area
articles.excerpt: Mayoress Iram Faisal has unveiled plans for new play equipment at Falinge Park, including a wheelchair-accessible roundabout, an inclusive seesaw and a double cableway zip line.
articles.content_html:
Plans for a new play area at Falinge Park have been unveiled, with wheelchair-accessible equipment among the attractions proposed for children and families.

Mayoress Iram Faisal shared details of the project, describing it as a deeply personal undertaking in the park where she played as a child.

The proposed equipment includes a double cableway zip line with ramps; a toddler multi-play unit; toddler and junior swings; an inclusive seesaw; a Crazy Gander springer; and a wheelchair-accessible roundabout.

In her announcement, Mrs Faisal said inclusivity had been central to the vision, with the aim of helping more children enjoy the park together.

“Every child deserves the opportunity to play, explore and enjoy their childhood,” she said.

For the Mayoress, the plans also carry memories of her own upbringing.

“Having lived here and played in this very park myself, to now be in a position to play a part in transforming it for the next generation has been an incredibly emotional journey,” she said.

She thanked councillors Faisal Rana and Amber Nisa, Rochdale Borough Council and its Environmental Management Team, alongside everyone involved in bringing the project forward.

Mrs Faisal said the improvements were about investing in children and creating a space where families could make memories together.

“From playing in Falinge Park as a child to helping shape its future, this really is a full-circle moment,” she added.

The announcement refers to a hoped-for start towards the end of February, with work continuing into March, subject to final arrangements. It does not specify the year or confirm an opening date, so that timetable remains to be clarified.

Residents have been invited to share their views on the proposals.

Source: announcement by Mayoress Iram Faisal, supplied to Rochdale Daily and published on her public Facebook page: https://www.facebook.com/iram.faisal.5095/posts/1764829918060894/

articles.title: Rochdale social worker Nneamaka Uti shortlisted for national award
articles.excerpt: Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Council’s adult care service, is a finalist in the Social Worker of the Year Awards, with winners announced on 22 October.
articles.content_html:
A social worker helping adults in Rochdale has been shortlisted for a national award recognising outstanding work in the profession.

Nneamaka Uti, who works in Rochdale Borough Council’s adult care service, is a finalist for Newly Qualified Adult Social Worker of the Year at the 2026 Social Worker of the Year Awards.

The winners will be announced on Thursday 22 October, at an awards reception in London. The organisers have confirmed that the afternoon event will run from 2pm to 5pm.

Councillor Shah Wazir, the council’s cabinet member for adult care, welcomed the recognition.

He said: “This is lovely and deserved recognition for Nneamaka and showcases Rochdale’s caring side at its very best. Following adult care’s good CQC rating this underlines the high-quality care and support the council is delivering for residents across the borough. Best of luck to Nneamaka at the awards ceremony.”

The council’s announcement links Nneamaka’s shortlisting with the adult care service’s good Care Quality Commission rating, highlighting the contribution of staff supporting residents across the borough.

Now marking their 20th anniversary, the Social Worker of the Year Awards recognise achievements across children’s and adult social work in England. This year, the organisers have named 64 finalists across 14 categories.

Nneamaka is one of six finalists in the newly qualified adult social worker category. The shortlist recognises practitioners at the beginning of their careers, giving Rochdale a representative among those in contention for national recognition.

Gold and silver award recipients will be announced at the October reception.

Rochdale Daily wishes Nneamaka the best of luck.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Announces Free Bonfire Night Events for November 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will host three free firework displays across the borough in early November, featuring reduced noise fireworks for accessibility.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has confirmed a series of free firework displays to celebrate Bonfire Night in November 2026. The events will take place at three locations across the borough, including Middleton, Heywood, and Syke, with festivities beginning on Monday 2 November.

The first event will be held at Bowlee Community Park, located on Heywood Old Road in Middleton, starting at 6pm. The bonfire will be lit at 7pm, followed by fireworks at 7.30pm. The second display will occur on Tuesday 3 November, at Queen’s Park Road in Heywood, with the same timings. The final council-run event will take place on Wednesday 4 November, at Cronkeyshaw Common in Syke, also starting at 6pm.

In addition to the council events, Milnrow Cricket Club and Lobden Golf Club in Whitworth will host their own firework displays on Saturday 7 November. The Milnrow event will charge £7 for adults and £11.25 for families, while the Lobden Golf Club display will cost £5 for adults and £3 for children.

Rochdale Council has introduced reduced noise fireworks this year to make the displays more accessible for all attendees. The council advises visitors to walk or use public transport due to limited parking at the venues. Alcohol, fireworks, and sparklers are prohibited at all council-run events, and no toilet facilities will be available.

The council confirms the Rochdale display is on Wednesday 4 November 2026: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/events/event/481/rochdale-bonfire-and-fireworks-display

articles.title: Pacific, Mangos and Empire until morning: remembering Rochdale’s strip
articles.excerpt: Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—remembering Rochdale’s strip, its familiar faces and the venues keeping the town alive today.
articles.content_html:
Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—Rochdale’s nightlife in the 2000s and early 2010s was a whole chapter of growing up. And places such as Empire are still helping the town make memories.

There was a time when a night out in Rochdale came with its own wardrobe, soundtrack and familiar faces.

Box-dye red hair. Chinos. Ed Hardy. The infamous Rihanna jumper. Outfits that, looking back, were remarkably close to business casual—worn with complete confidence for a night on the strip.

Rihanna and Eminem provided the soundtrack. Ordering a Jägerbomb felt like an event. Pacific, Mangos, Litten Tree and Empire were names woven into the weekend.

Between the bars, the dancefloors and the eventual search for a taxi, Rochdale felt wonderfully alive.

One former glass collector and barmaid remembers an incredible scene: heaving venues, wonderful bouncers and, in her experience, few fights. When the night finally ended, queues for taxis could mean waiting for hours into the early morning.

The people who made the strip

Ask someone about their old nights out and they might start with a club. Before long, they will be talking about a person.

A favourite barmaid. A reassuring face on the door. Someone you always bumped into, whether you had arranged to meet or not.

Among those familiar faces was the man affectionately known to revellers as “the gas man”, remembered sitting at the corner of the strip.

The former bar worker recalls people stopping to hug him and give him money. Despite the difficult circumstances she remembers him facing, he was a beloved presence, recognised and greeted with affection.

His circumstances were his own, and a nickname cannot tell his whole story. But the warmth with which he is remembered belongs in the history of those nights, alongside the music and the venues.

The strip’s character came from its people.

From the glass collector’s side of the dancefloor

Working through those nights meant seeing what customers sometimes missed.

Collecting glasses through a crowded room. Keeping the bar moving. Watching the door team manage another wave of arrivals while friends tried to find one another inside.

The former worker remembers the bouncers warmly. Her account offers a different perspective from the assumption that a busy nightlife scene must have been defined by trouble: what stays with her is how enjoyable it was, how few fights she encountered and how much life filled the town centre.

That is a personal recollection, rather than a claim that every night passed without incident. But it captures something worth preserving—the pleasure of working somewhere everyone wanted to be.

What happened to Pacific, Mangos and Litten Tree?

Pacific, at 8 South Parade, is now listed as closed. An archived council entry records a premises-licence suspension beginning in July 2013 for non-payment of an annual fee or levy. That record does not, by itself, establish the venue’s final trading date or the full reasons it closed.

Sources: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/204/Detail?APP_ID=80078 and https://www.pubsgalore.co.uk/areas/rochdale-central/greater-manchester/

Mangos’ connection to a later venue remains visible in the paperwork. The council’s licensing record for Trinity retains conditions referring to the operating plan for Mango Bar at 3 King Street. The familiar address acquired another identity, although the sources reviewed do not establish the complete changeover story.

Source: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/203/Detail?LIC_ID=6700

Litten Tree’s premises at 10 Fleece Street subsequently became Yates and are now Courtyard Rochdale. CAMRA records its reopening under the Courtyard name in March 2024. For former regulars, the sign has changed, but the address remains somewhere people can meet for a night out.

Source: https://camra.org.uk/pubs/courtyard-rochdale-rochdale-153361

Empire: the night that kept going

Then there was Empire.

In the former bar worker’s memories, it was the infamous destination where the night could stretch towards 6am. Leaving meant discovering that the early morning had arrived while everyone was still enjoying themselves.

Empire remains part of Rochdale’s nightlife today. Its presently advertised Friday and Saturday hours run until 4am, with live bands and performances central to its programme.

Source: https://empirerochdale.co.uk/

Its contribution extends beyond an ordinary weekend. The council’s 2026 Feel Good Festival programme included performances throughout the day at Empire, followed by a midnight DJ slot.

Source: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/rochdale-feel-good-festival/indoor-venues

That continuing activity deserves recognition. Venues such as Empire give people a reason to come into Rochdale, meet friends, hear music and spend an evening in their own town.

The old strip cannot be recreated exactly. Its customers have grown older; their wardrobes, responsibilities and stamina may have changed.

But the affection remains—for the songs, the people, the staff who looked after everyone and the nights nobody wanted to finish.

Rochdale’s next great night out needs people willing to make it happen. Empire and the town’s other active venues are keeping that possibility alive.

What do you remember about the strip? Pacific or Mangos? Litten Tree before Empire?

articles.title: QTS Group hosts first safety Jamboree in Rochdale with over 350 attendees
articles.excerpt: The QTS Group's inaugural safety Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale attracted more than 350 participants, focusing on health, safety, and innovation in the rail industry.
articles.content_html:
National rail contractor QTS Group hosted its first safety-focused Jamboree at Ashworth Valley Scout Camp in Rochdale, bringing together over 350 colleagues, supply chain partners, and activity hosts.

The two-day event, which took place recently, was designed to promote health, safety, and innovation within the rail industry through interactive demonstrations and hands-on activities.

Attendees had the opportunity to engage with new technology and best practices from various suppliers and specialists. Jamie Marks, HSQE Manager at QTS Group, stated that the event aimed to foster knowledge sharing and strengthen relationships across the industry.

He noted the positive feedback received and expressed enthusiasm for making next year's event even larger and more impactful.

Demonstrations included the Elios 3 drone for aerial mapping, virtual reality experiences simulating drone flights, and a confined space training simulator provided by Eurosafe.

Participants also tested their skills on an excavator simulator from Flannery Plant Hire and witnessed mock aerial rescue demonstrations conducted by IRATA-trained teams.

QTS Group plans to build on this success for future events, aiming to further enhance safety practices in the rail industry.

articles.title: Hollingworth Lake to host Wave of Light walk remembering babies and children
articles.excerpt: Families affected by baby or child loss are invited to meet at Hollingworth Lake's beach at 6.30pm on Thursday 15 October for a remembrance walk and 7pm candle-lighting, with bereavement charities and helplines available for support.
articles.content_html:
Families and friends affected by the death of a baby or child are invited to gather at Hollingworth Lake in Littleborough on Thursday 15 October for a candlelit remembrance walk at the end of Baby Loss Awareness Week.

The community invitation asks people to meet at the beach at Hollingworth Lake at 6.30pm. The group plans to walk together around the lake, pausing approximately halfway round at a scenic point to light candles at 7pm as part of the worldwide Wave of Light.

The invitation is open to anyone who has experienced miscarriage, stillbirth, neonatal death, the death of a baby or the loss of a child at any age, as well as relatives, friends, neighbours and others wishing to show their support.

One of the people behind the gathering said that every year they light a candle for the babies they remember. This year, rather than marking the occasion alone, they hope people can come together for a shared moment of remembrance.

Baby Loss Awareness Week takes place each year from 9 to 15 October. At 7pm on 15 October, families around the world take part in the Wave of Light by lighting candles in memory of babies who have died. The Hollingworth Lake walk extends a welcome to those remembering children of all ages.

Those attending can bring a candle or battery-operated light, dress warmly for an October evening and carry a torch for the walk. Please keep a safe distance from the water, take care on paths after dark, never leave flames unattended, and take all candles and materials home rather than leaving them by or in the lake. Details of accessibility arrangements have not been provided in the original invitation.

EVENT DETAILS: Thursday 15 October 2026. Meet at 6.30pm at the beach at Hollingworth Lake, Littleborough, Rochdale, OL15 0AQ. Walk together and stop to light candles at 7pm. This article reports a community invitation; the charities listed below are support resources and are not described as organisers or sponsors of the event.

WHERE TO FIND HELP AFTER BABY OR CHILD LOSS

Grief can affect parents, partners, siblings, grandparents and friends, sometimes long after the death. No one has to attend the walk or speak about a loss to deserve support. The following verified organisations offer specialist information, listening services and, in some cases, counselling or local peer groups.

Sands — confidential help for anyone affected by pregnancy or baby loss, including bereaved relatives and friends. Free national helpline: 0808 164 3332; email: helpline@sands.org.uk; website: https://www.sands.org.uk/support-you/how-we-offer-support/helpline. Telephone hours are Monday to Friday 10am–3pm and Tuesday to Thursday 6pm–9pm, excluding bank holidays.

Child Bereavement UK — support for parents and carers when a baby or child dies, and for bereaved children and young people. Free helpline: 0800 02 888 40, Monday to Friday 8am–8pm, excluding bank holidays. Text or WhatsApp: 07418 341 800 (WhatsApp support for ages 13 and over). Website: https://www.childbereavementuk.org/.

Finding Rainbows — Greater Manchester peer support for families affected by early pregnancy loss or the death of a baby or child. Email: finding.rainbows@outlook.com; website: https://www.findingrainbows.org/.

Tommy's — specialist midwife-led advice on miscarriage, stillbirth, pregnancy after loss and pregnancy-related wellbeing. Free helpline: 0800 0147 800, Monday to Friday 9am–5pm. Email: midwife@tommys.org; website: https://www.tommys.org/. This is a non-urgent advice line.

The Lullaby Trust — specialist bereavement support after the sudden and unexpected death of a baby or young child. Free helpline: 0808 802 6868; website: https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/bereavement-support/find-support/. Phone support is available Monday to Friday 10am–2pm and weekends and public holidays 6pm–10pm.

Antenatal Results and Choices (ARC) — confidential, non-directive support after difficult antenatal test results, fetal diagnosis and pregnancy loss following a decision to end a pregnancy for medical reasons. Helpline: 020 7713 7486, Monday to Friday 10am–5.30pm. Text: 07908 683004; email: info@arc-uk.org; website: https://www.arc-uk.org/.

Miscarriage Association — information and support for anyone affected by miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or molar pregnancy. Website: https://www.miscarriageassociation.org.uk/.

Petals — specialist counselling for people affected by pregnancy loss, stillbirth or neonatal death, subject to service eligibility and referral arrangements. Website: https://www.petalscharity.org/.

4Louis — bereavement support resources and memory boxes for families following the death of a baby or child. Website: https://www.4louis.co.uk/.

SUDC UK — information, bereavement support and research relating to sudden unexplained death in childhood. Contact: 07880 350942, Monday to Thursday 9am–5pm; email: info@sudc.org.uk; website: https://sudc.org.uk/.

Greater Manchester NHS PETALS Perinatal Trauma and Loss Service — assessment and therapeutic support for people experiencing trauma related to birth, pregnancy or baby loss. A healthcare professional can make a referral. Telephone: 0161 271 0188 (option 4), Monday to Friday 9am–5pm; website: https://www.gmmh.nhs.uk/petals.

If you need somebody to talk to now, Samaritans offers free emotional support day and night on 116 123 (https://www.samaritans.org/). For urgent mental health support in England, contact NHS 111 and select the mental health option. Call 999 if someone is in immediate danger.

Whatever their age, and however much time has passed, every child deserves to be remembered. Those planning to attend are encouraged to offer one another kindness and space during the gathering.

articles.title: Rochdale Sleep Out raises almost £10,000 as organisers make final appeal
articles.excerpt: Supporters spent the night outdoors at the Crown Oil Arena for Petrus Community and Rochdale AFC Community Trust, with the annual charity Sleep Out now close to its £10,000 fundraising milestone.
articles.content_html:
Supporters from across Rochdale spent Friday night outdoors in solidarity with people experiencing homelessness, helping an annual charity Sleep Out raise almost £10,000.

The event, organised by Petrus Community and Rochdale AFC Community Trust, took place on Friday 9 October at the Crown Oil Arena. Participants were joined in the fundraising effort by donors and local businesses.

Petrus said the total was now approaching the £10,000 milestone and appealed for one final push to reach it. The figure is a provisional amount reported by the organisers, rather than a confirmed final total.

The Sleep Out aimed to raise awareness of housing insecurity and homelessness while giving participants a limited insight into the practical challenges of spending a night without a comfortable bed. Organisers stressed that taking part for one night cannot replicate the uncertainty and difficulties faced by people who have no safe place to call home.

Money raised will help sustain vital support for people experiencing homelessness and disadvantage. Petrus provides accommodation, housing advice, outreach, wellbeing support and opportunities to help people rebuild stability across Rochdale, Oldham and Burnley.

The partnership between Petrus and Rochdale AFC Community Trust also supports the Changing Lives programme, which uses football, wellbeing activities and pathways into education, volunteering and employment to help people experiencing homelessness or living in supported accommodation.

Last year's Sleep Out raised £7,875.52 for the two organisations. This year's organisers have thanked everyone who slept outdoors, donated or helped make the event possible.

Petrus is encouraging Rochdale residents who wish to support the final fundraising push to donate through its official website: https://www.petrus.org.uk/.

articles.title: Who
articles.excerpt: A short guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel, showing what the oldest printed witnesses say and what is verifiable today.
articles.summary: A short guide to the small ginger‑bearded figure tied to Healey Dell’s Fairies’ Chapel, showing what the oldest printed witnesses say and what is verifiable today.
articles.body:
Walkers who know Healey Dell will recognise the narrow cleft of the Spodden called the Thrutch and the little rock alcove that has long been known locally as the Fairies’ Chapel. The “Healey Dwarf” is the best‑known supernatural figure attached to that place: in local telling a tiny, ginger‑bearded person — sometimes imagined as a stone sentinel in the river — who belongs among the fairies. But the dwarf, like other elements of the Dell’s story‑map, belongs to folklore rather than to the archive of verifiable events.

The oldest printed witness for the tale that survives in wide circulation is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire. Roby collected and published local romances and legends in the early nineteenth century (his Lancashire volumes first appeared in 1829–31), and his chapter often cited as “The Fairies’ Chapel” gathers the characters and episodes — a cavern‑like cleft, a miller, a Fairy Queen and a small figure associated with the place — that later writers repeated and reshaped. Roby’s work is a primary source for the story as it was told in his era, but it must be read as a collector’s and storyteller’s account: it records oral tradition and contemporary retelling rather than offering documentary proof of supernatural events.

Later Victorian and local writers elaborated Roby’s material. A small book published in 1882, Healey Dell, or The History (in Verse) of Fairies: Meetings of the Fairy Queen and Healey Dwarf in the Fairy Chapel, gives a fully dramatised and poetical version in which a character called Healey (often pictured with a ginger beard in these retellings) is offered a place among the fairies and imagined as a stone guardian in the river. These later accounts are useful for tracking how the dwarf’s image — costume, beard and behaviour — became fixed in local imagination, but they are literary treatments rather than independent contemporary testimonies.

On the ground today the concrete facts are straightforward and separate from the stories. Healey Dell is a managed nature reserve with visible industrial archaeology — mill remains, waterfalls and the Victorian viaduct — and a heritage centre that presents the site’s history and folklore for visitors. The rock formation that inspired the name Fairies’ Chapel is a water‑worn niche; the site was altered by extreme flooding in the 1830s, and the physical features visible now are not identical to those seen by earlier visitors. Local authorities and the heritage centre present the dwarf and related tales as part of the Dell’s living folklore rather than as documented historical personages.

What we can say with confidence: the Healey Dwarf is a figure of local tradition preserved in nineteenth‑century printed collections and in later local retellings. The earliest reliable printed appearance is John Roby’s collection; later writers — including the 1882 verse volume — shaped the dwarf’s popular image. What cannot be verified from official records is any claim that a living dwarf or a supernatural guardian actually inhabited the Dell: there are no archival documents, legal records or contemporary official investigations that establish such a thing as historical fact.

If you want to explore the sources, read Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire for the earliest widely available printed version and the Healey Dell Heritage Centre’s material and Rochdale Borough Council’s site listings for the reserve’s geology, industrial remains and how the folklore is presented to visitors today. The story of the Healey Dwarf is best approached as local folklore — a useful lens on how people in and around Healey have imagined their landscape over two centuries — and as an example of the way place, geology and human storytelling become entangled.

Visiting the Dell remains the most direct way to meet the tradition: the rock alcove, the Thrutch, the viaduct and the heritage displays are all real; the dwarf lives in the stories people tell there.

articles.title: Ten years without answers: the continuing search for Rochdale’s Jack Stewart
articles.excerpt: Jack Stewart vanished from Spotland on 8 February 2016. His missing-person appeal remains listed a decade later. Here are the original clothing details, what the community did, and how to report information safely.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Daily | Missing persons appeal | 12 October 2026

Ten years after Jack Stewart disappeared from Spotland, a national missing-person charity continues to carry his photograph and an appeal for information. Jack was last reported seen at about 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, at his home on Ings Lane in Rochdale. What happened next remains unknown in the public appeal. For anyone who remembers that morning, or who notices something potentially significant while walking in the area, information can still be passed directly to the police.

Jack's appeal is currently listed by the independent charity Missing People, with reference 16-000774. The charity records him as 68 when he went missing; some original police reporting described him as 69. The important details are the date, location and identifying information, rather than trying to resolve that inconsistency without original records.

Official Missing People appeal: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

THE MORNING JACK WAS LAST SEEN

At around 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, Jack was seen at his home on Ings Lane, Spotland. Police said his disappearance was extremely out of character, noting that he liked routine in his life. That detail matters because those familiar with his everyday movements may be able to distinguish an ordinary journey from a change in habit. The information available publicly does not establish which direction he travelled, what happened after 8am or why he disappeared.

Contemporary reports describe Jack as a white man, approximately 5ft 9in tall, with brown-and-grey hair worn in a distinctive 'teddy boy' style. His clothing was described in early coverage as a BLACK QUILTED JACKET, BLACK JEANS, STRIPED SOCKS and a DARK-COLOURED CHECK SHIRT. These are the last publicly reported clothing details, not proof that any item would remain recognisable today. Colours, fabrics and descriptions may change over time. The police are best placed to assess the significance of any discovery.

Sources: original 2016 Greater Manchester Police appeal, reproduced in subsequent MEN coverage https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/police-new-appeal-over-missing-10871344; later account with clothing description https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas; charity appeal https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

HOW ROCHDALE RESPONDED

Local people helped to look for Jack soon after he disappeared. Later reporting records that around 60 members of the public joined a search organised from Brotherod Community Centre, near his home. The response reflected a community unwilling to let a neighbour vanish without notice. Those efforts did not produce a publicly confirmed resolution in the records reviewed for this report.

Source: Manchester Evening News coverage of historic missing Greater Manchester residents https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas

JACK AS A PERSON, NOT JUST A MISSING PERSON

Jack was known to police as someone who valued routine. That is one small glimpse of the life behind the appeal: a man whose ordinary day was sufficiently familiar that his absence immediately stood out. Rochdale Daily has not been able to verify specific hobbies, employment history, or details about a wife, partner, children or surviving relatives from reliable public sources. We will not speculate about them or print supposed family memories without permission.

Anyone close to Jack who wishes to share family-approved memories of his interests, favourite places, the things that made him laugh or his daily routine may contact the newsroom. There is no expectation that relatives should speak publicly. Their privacy and wellbeing come first, and the missing-person appeal does not require the family to relive events for others' curiosity.

TEN YEARS ON: NO CONCLUSIONS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

Jack's continued listing on Missing People means the public appeal has not been withdrawn on the charity's site at the time of this report. It does not establish that he died, that he was harmed by another person, or that the police are pursuing any particular theory. The precise investigative status, searches undertaken since 2016 and any new leads have not been confirmed in a current statement from Greater Manchester Police.

A decade passing does not turn an unverified theory into fact. Whether someone remembers a sighting, has a dated photograph or recalls an unusual circumstance, even a detail that seemed insignificant at the time may be worth submitting to the officers responsible.

IF YOU ARE WALKING YOUR DOG AND FIND SOMETHING CONCERNING

If you come across clothing, personal effects, bones or other material that might be connected to a missing-person case, DO NOT try to decide yourself whether it belongs to Jack. Many items will have entirely unrelated explanations.

If you suspect you have found human remains or a scene requiring an urgent police response, call 999. Do not touch, move, uncover, collect or take anything home; do not dig or disturb the surrounding ground. Keep children and dogs away and avoid walking through the immediate area. Move to a safe position, note the location using a nearby landmark or phone map pin if it is safe to do so, and wait for police instructions.

For a non-urgent recollection, possible sighting or information about the 2016 disappearance, contact Greater Manchester Police on 101 or via https://www.gmp.police.uk. Tell the operator this concerns Jack Stewart, missing from Spotland on 8 February 2016, and provide the Missing People reference 16-000774 as an identifying aid. A charity reference is not necessarily a police incident number.

Please do not post photographs of potentially sensitive evidence, suspected remains, or unverified names online. Do not organise an unsupervised search of private land, woodland or waterways. Any possible discovery should go straight to police, who can preserve and assess evidence and contact families appropriately.

General official guidance on missing-person sightings and reporting: https://www.gov.uk/report-missing-person; UK Missing Persons Unit: https://www.nationalcrimeagency.gov.uk/missingpersons

WHAT IF YOU SIMPLY REMEMBER SOMETHING?

People who lived or worked around Ings Lane, Spotland or neighbouring areas in February 2016 might remember a morning journey, conversation or circumstance that they never associated with the disappearance. You do not need to be certain that a memory is significant before discussing it with police. Explain how confident you are, distinguish what you personally saw from what someone else told you, and do not guess to fill gaps.

The charity Missing People also accepts information confidentially. Call or text 116 000, or use the 'Report a sighting' link at https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774. Contacting the charity should not delay a call to police where there is an immediate danger or potential crime scene.

HELP FOR FAMILIES, FRIENDS AND ANYONE AFFECTED

The experience of an unresolved disappearance can affect loved ones and entire communities for years. Missing People offers free, confidential practical and emotional support to relatives, friends and people who are missing themselves. Call or text 116 000. Its family support team can also be reached at family.support@missingpeople.org.uk. Its helpline website lists current operating hours.

Missing People family help: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/help-services/family-support; helpline: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/helpline. If you are distressed by something you have encountered, the police or an appropriate health professional can advise on immediate support; Samaritans offers someone to talk to at any hour on 116 123.

ANY INFORMATION MAY MATTER

Jack Stewart was last seen in Rochdale on 8 February 2016. The clothing described in early appeals — a black quilted jacket, black jeans, striped socks and a dark check shirt — remains a potentially useful historical reference, but identification is the responsibility of trained police and forensic professionals.

For his loved ones, what matters is not speculation but a reliable answer. Ten years later, anyone with real information can still help by passing it to the right people. Rochdale Daily invites Greater Manchester Police and Jack's family, if they wish, to provide any verified updated details for a correction or follow-up; no family member is being asked to take part publicly.

Sources: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774; https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas; https://www.gov.uk/report-missing-person

Hobbies and family composition have not been independently verified. Potential evidence should be reported directly to police without being disturbed.

articles.title: Rochdale Pioneers Museum hosts archive sessions on local folklore
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will hold free drop-in sessions this weekend, exploring traditional and supernatural tales from the borough's archives, led by Mitch Robinson.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will host free archive creative drop-in sessions this weekend, focusing on traditional, unusual, and even supernatural tales from the borough's archives. The sessions, led by Mitch Robinson, aim to uncover hidden stories and records, ranging from folklore to magical narratives.

Scheduled for Saturday 15 October, the hour-long sessions will take place at 12.30pm and 2pm, with no prior booking required.

Participants will have the opportunity to engage with old books, documents, and letters that often remain stored away, providing a unique insight into the area's history.

The Co-op Heritage Trust, which is facilitating the event, encourages anyone interested in storytelling, history, or creativity to attend. The sessions are particularly suitable for families with older children, as they will delve into themes of folk belief, magic, and the supernatural.

This initiative is part of the 'Open with Care!' programme, designed to inspire and engage the community during the spooky season. Attendees can expect a creative and thought-provoking experience, whether they are history enthusiasts or simply looking for an intriguing activity this weekend.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.summary: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.body:
Anyone from Rochdale who’s ever limped away from a small mishap will recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” For many locals, cruckle means the particular half‑twist or awkward roll of the foot you can often walk off — not a full sprain but a sudden wobble that makes you wince. This usage is recorded in contemporary perceptual descriptions of Greater Manchester speech and has been listed by residents when describing Rochdale’s spoken character. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

The word itself, however, has deeper roots. Historical dialect lexicography gives us a family of related forms — crookle, crukle, cruggle, krukel — all clustered around meanings such as to bend, make crooked, stoop, huddle or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect sources and Scottish dialect records preserve these cognates, showing the same phonetic shape and similar senses across northern English and Scots varieties. In the Dictionary of the Scots Language you can see cognate entries (kruggle / cruggle / cruckle) used with senses like “to crouch or huddle,” and nineteenth‑century dialect glosses list crookle with senses such as “to make crooked; to bend, twist.” ([dsl.ac.uk](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd00075099))

How did a general sense of bending or crookedness come to mean the small ankle‑roll in Rochdale? Linguists point to ordinary, well‑attested word‑formation processes. A crook/crook‑ family root (suggesting bending, hooking or crookedness) plus a frequentative or diminutive ‑le ending can produce verbs that describe small, repeated, or imitative actions — crook → crookle. Comparable northern and Germanic dialect forms show similar semantic shifts from ‘bend’ or ‘stoop’ toward senses connected with awkward gait or limping; the broader comparative work on Germanic dialect vocabularies helps explain why these forms and meanings sit together. In short, cruckle is linguistically predictable as a local survival and narrowing of an older dialect verb family. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/The_semantic_development_of_words_for_%22walk%2C_run%22_in_the_Germanic_languages_%28IA_semanticdevelopm00ihririch%29.pdf))

Is cruckle uniquely Rochdalian? The short answer is: socially, yes — geographically, not absolutely. Perceptual dialect research carried out in Greater Manchester (2024) collected people’s mental maps and comments about local speech; among the keywords used to evoke Rochdale speech were “broad,” “flat,” “guinnel” and “cruckle,” showing that residents and neighbours associate the word particularly with Rochdale. That kind of folk‑linguistic visibility gives a strong local identity to a word even when related forms appear in older records elsewhere. At the same time, historical dictionaries and place‑name evidence show related spellings and senses across northern England and Scotland, so it would be misleading to claim the sound‑type has never occurred outside the area. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Large projects that collect lived speech and crowd‑sourced dialect entries also help explain how such words persist. When the British Library and other public call‑outs gathered regional words, contributors highlighted locally specific items that researchers had not always recorded in older printed dialect dictionaries; popular reportage of that work singled out “cruckle” as an example of a recognisably local term with onomatopoeic appeal. These crowdsourced attestations, together with formal perceptual surveys, are why small words like cruckle keep turning up in contemporary studies of regional identity. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? Cruckle matters because it shows how vocabulary anchors place: the word’s form and original sense are old and shared across northern dialects, but memory, everyday use and local attitude have made it feel distinctly Rochdale. Linguists view it as a useful data point — for historical contact between Lancashire and Yorkshire varieties, for small‑scale semantic narrowing, and for how people use language to say where they’re from. If you’ve got family pronunciations, old spellings or written examples from letters, keep them — local archives and dialect projects welcome material that helps trace exactly when and where words like cruckle shifted meaning and stuck to a place.

articles.title: Did Robin Hood really come to Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.summary: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.body:
There is a pulpit-shaped rock, a narrow pool and a name — the Fairy Chapel — at the base of Healey Dell’s steep gorge. The visitor centre and local heritage guides record a set of vivid stories: a King of the Fairies who turned a coven to stone, a ring lost in the river that cost a would‑be heir his title, and an origin tale that sends “Robert of Huntingdon” on the road to becoming Robin Hood. These versions are the ones you’ll see on site interpretation and in the Heritage Centre’s write‑ups. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

That is folklore, not archival evidence. The most systematic scholarly account of the Dell is an archaeological desk‑based assessment carried out for Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council by the University of Manchester Archaeological Unit in December 2004. It maps the valley’s mills, lodges, railway viaduct and later Victorian and industrial remains; it lists the local archives and printed sources consulted (John Rylands, Lancashire Record Office, Rochdale Local Studies and others) and documents the Dell’s long industrial and landscape history — but it does not produce contemporary medieval records linking a historical Robin Hood or a Robert of Huntingdon to Healey Dell. Put bluntly: the detailed desk‑based study records place, industry and later antiquarian interest, not a medieval outlaw’s itinerary. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

Healey Dell’s real, verifiable past is useful and interesting in itself. The site is a designated local nature reserve and a managed visitor attraction, with a Victorian railway viaduct that is Grade II listed and the valley’s surviving mill archaeology. Rochdale Borough Council describes the reserve, the visitor centre’s pictorial displays and the family‑oriented Fairy Grotto as part of the attraction visitors can find at Dell Road, Healey. The viaduct and the visible industrial remains are the kinds of things that the archaeological assessment and Historic England record in statutory listings. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

How did the Robin Hood story arrive here? Local legends often accrete around striking landscape features; caverns, pools and ravines attract tales of fairies, witches and enchanted tokens across Britain. The Healey Dell accounts appear in local storytelling and modern retellings by the Heritage Centre and local guides: they make no claim to derive from contemporary medieval documents but preserve a late tradition tying a Huntingdon name and a lost ring to the Chapel. Those popular accounts are part of the Dell’s cultural history and of local imaginative life — important for tourism and local identity — but they do not equal documentary proof. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

On the bigger question of Robin Hood’s historicity, mainstream scholarship treats Robin Hood as a legendary figure built from ballads and popular tales rather than a single, verifiable medieval person whose movements can be read off local court rolls. Modern reference works and folklorists stress the ballad tradition and its late medieval and post‑medieval formation; many local Robin Hood claims around England are later inventions, popular attributions or imaginative explanations for landscape oddities rather than recordable events. That does not make the stories worthless — it makes them folklore. ([books.google.com](https://books.google.com/books/about/Oxford_Dictionary_of_English_Folklore.html?hl=en&id=w2BMSAAACAAJ&output=html_text))

So what can a reader reasonably take away? If you mean “is there documentary, contemporary medieval evidence that Robin Hood or Robert of Huntingdon passed through Healey Dell?” the answer is: no such evidence has been produced in the local archival and archaeological surveys cited by the University of Manchester assessment and by the council’s heritage material. If you mean “are there stories that people tell about Robin Hood, witches and a magic ring here?” the answer is yes — they are recorded in local guides and on site interpretation, and they help make the place culturally lively. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

If you want to read more or check sources yourself: the University of Manchester archaeological desk‑based assessment (2004) is the most thorough published study of Healey Dell’s historic fabric; Rochdale Borough Council holds the reserve’s visitor information; the Healey Dell Heritage Centre publishes the Fairy Chapel story used in interpretation. None of these sources substitutes for a named medieval document placing Robin Hood in the Dell — and until such a record appears, the Robin Hood connection belongs to folklore rather than local history. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

articles.title: Andy’s Man Club Rochdale has four groups helping men talk
articles.excerpt: Andy’s Man Club has four groups meeting across the Rochdale borough, offering men a place to talk, listen and support one another.
articles.content_html:
Andy’s Man Club has four groups meeting across the Rochdale borough, offering men a place to come together, talk and support one another.

The groups meet at four locations:

### Rochdale-Heywood

Heywood Market, Church Place, York Street, OL10 1LT.

### Rochdale-Spotland

Rochdale AFC Community Trust Hub, Crown Oil Arena, Willbutts Lane, Rochdale, OL11 5DS.

### Rochdale-Milnrow

Milnrow Cricket Club Pavilion, Harbour Lane, Milnrow, OL16 4HF.

### Rochdale-Mayfield

Mayfield ARLFC, Keswick Street, Castleton, OL11 3AG.

The groups are part of Andy’s Man Club’s wider mission to help men talk and support one another.

More information about Andy’s Man Club and its work is available through its official website.

Source: Andy’s Man Club.

articles.title: Heywood Army Cadet Detachment opens its doors for National Cadets Week
articles.excerpt: Heywood Army Cadet Detachment is inviting young people and their parents or carers to an open evening on Thursday 8 October to discover what the Army Cadets has to offer.
articles.content_html:
Heywood Army Cadet Detachment is opening its doors as part of National Cadets Week, inviting young people and their parents or carers to come along and find out more about the Army Cadets.

The open evening will take place on Thursday 8 October from 7pm to 8.30pm at Heywood Detachment on Bamford Road, Heywood, OL10 4FT.

Visitors will be able to meet instructors and cadets, look around the detachment and find out more about activities available through the Army Cadets.

The programme can include adventure, fieldcraft, shooting, first aid, sport, the Duke of Edinburgh's Award, camps and leadership opportunities, as well as the chance to make new friends and try something different.

The detachment says no military experience is needed and that the open evening is an opportunity to see what Army Cadets is about and where participation could lead.

Young people and their parents or carers are invited to attend.

Christ Church Healey will hold its Harvest celebration on Sunday 18 October, with the church also welcoming the Rt Rev'd Bishop Mark for a special service to bless its bells later the same day.

The bell-blessing service will be followed by light refreshments in the church hall.

articles.title: Remembrance and reflection walks offer bereaved service families a place to connect at Denehurst Park
articles.excerpt: Get Together After Serving CIC invites families, partners and loved ones to a gentle weekly remembrance walk at Denehurst Park in Rochdale, with no pressure to talk about loss.
articles.content_html:
A weekly remembrance walk in Rochdale is offering families and loved ones of fallen service personnel a chance to find companionship, fresh air and a little space to reflect.

Organised by Get Together After Serving CIC (G.A.S-CIC), the Remembrance & Reflection Walk takes place every Wednesday at Denehurst Park. Participants are invited to meet outside Denehurst Café at 12.30pm before setting off together.

The gentle walk is expected to last between 30 minutes and an hour, depending on the weather. Dogs are very welcome, although there is no need to bring one to take part.

At the heart of the initiative is the understanding that grief does not always need words. Those attending can share memories of someone they have lost, chat about everyday life, walk quietly or simply enjoy being in the company of people who understand.

The event poster captures that sentiment: “Sometimes you don’t need a meeting or a support group. Sometimes you just need to get outside, walk, talk and spend some time with people who understand.”

After the walk, the group plans to return to Denehurst Café for a warm drink, a slice of cake and more time together for anyone who wishes to stay.

The invitation is aimed at families and loved ones remembering fallen heroes, with partners and friends also welcome. There is no expectation to discuss personal experiences or bereavement, and those who would prefer a quiet walk will be just as welcome as those looking for conversation.

The weekly gathering brings remembrance into the everyday: not only formal ceremonies or anniversaries, but a simple opportunity to come together, one Wednesday at a time.

Walk details: Every Wednesday at 12.30pm. Meeting point: outside Denehurst Café, Denehurst Park, Rochdale. The walk lasts 30 minutes to one hour, weather permitting. Dogs are welcome, but are not required. Participants can return to the café afterwards for optional refreshments and company.

articles.title: Rochdale’s Breaking Barriers secures core funding to expand its cultural work across Greater Manchester
articles.excerpt: Rochdale-based production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of GMCA core funding to expand cultural programmes, paid opportunities and creative development across Greater Manchester.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale-based multidisciplinary production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of core funding from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to strengthen the organisation and expand its cultural programmes across the region.

Over the funding period, Breaking Barriers plans to offer 42 paid placements through its Young Company programme, giving creatives aged 18–25 hands-on experience working on professional arts productions.

It will also provide 328 paid freelance roles and 45 in-kind artist residencies at its Rochdale base at Richard Street Studios.

Young Company participants will gain practical skills in producing, sound design, filmmaking and direction, with a focus on young people from underrepresented backgrounds who have had fewer opportunities to get into the arts.

A producer development programme will also support 36 creative producers a year to develop their own projects, secure resources and build sustainable careers.

Awarded through the Spirit strand of the GMCA Culture Fund, the investment will support Breaking Barriers to continue delivering theatre, film and immersive outdoor artworks, alongside training, mentoring and paid opportunities for emerging creatives.

Parvez Qadir, Artistic Director of Breaking Barriers, said: “Three years of core funding gives us the stability to plan ahead and grow as a company here in Rochdale. There’s so much creative talent locally, and we can now give more young people paid opportunities to work alongside experienced artists on our productions. It also enables us to keep building partnerships across Greater Manchester and develop projects shaped by local people, bringing their stories to life.”

Bev Craig, Mayor of Greater Manchester, said: “Culture has the power to connect communities, inspire creativity and strengthen pride in the places we call home.

“Through the Greater Manchester Culture Fund, we're investing in a diverse range of cultural organisations that help make our city region such a vibrant and inclusive place to live. Breaking Barriers is a fantastic example of a local company creating opportunities for young people to share their stories, develop their creativity and shape cultural experiences on their doorstep.”

Projects are currently planned to span the boroughs of Rochdale, Bury, Salford, Stockport, Manchester, Tameside and Bolton over three years.

Residents and local communities will help create outdoor artworks using sound, projection and light, alongside films and digital storytelling projects reflecting local experiences.

The funding will also help sustain and expand Breaking Barriers’ theatre in education work.

This includes multi-partnership delivery of Crossing the Line, a theatre and workshop programme tackling child criminal exploitation, which has already reached more than 15,000 young people across more than 220 schools.

Blind Side, exploring violence against women and girls, consent and healthy relationships, will continue to tour. Support from the Spirit strand will enable more time and resources to further expand its reach into other boroughs.

Source: Breaking Barriers.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway wins Community Hero Award for its volunteers
articles.excerpt: East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway has been recognised with a Roch Valley Radio Community Hero Award for the contribution of its more than 800 volunteers.

The awards celebrate people, groups, charities and businesses that go the extra mile to support others and strengthen their communities. The railway said the recognition reflects the commitment of its volunteers and the role the heritage line continues to play across the communities it serves.

The East Lancashire Railway operates heritage trains through the Irwell Valley, connecting communities including Bury, Summerseat, Ramsbottom, Irwell Vale, Rawtenstall and Heywood.

Diesel Driver and Head of the Signalling Department Linda Henderson said the railway could not exist without its volunteers.

"For almost 40 years, the ELR has operated Heritage trains through the heart of the Irwell Valley. Without volunteers, the ELR and Heritage Railways throughout the UK would not exist."

Henderson said the award recognised more than 800 current volunteers as well as those who had previously given their time to the railway.

Chairman Mike Kelly said he was "extremely proud" to accept the award on behalf of the railway and its volunteers, describing their work as generous and unselfish.

Kelly, who is also a volunteer, said the recognition highlighted the commitment and passion volunteers bring to organisations across local communities. He also thanked Roch Valley Radio for recognising volunteers and the contribution they make to charities and community organisations.

The award was collected by a group of volunteers representing several parts of the railway, including train operations, signalling, the guards department, the dining train team and a station café.

The East Lancashire Railway said the award was a recognition of the hard work and continued dedication of all its volunteers.

articles.title: Rochdale Sleepout 2026 returns to raise funds and awareness for people facing homelessness
articles.excerpt: Petrus is calling on Rochdale residents, businesses and community groups to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026 and help raise vital funds for local people experiencing homelessness and social exclusion.
articles.content_html:
Petrus Community is calling on people across Rochdale to get behind Rochdale Sleepout 2026, a fundraising and awareness event designed to highlight the realities faced by people experiencing homelessness while raising vital funds for local support services.

The Rochdale-based charity supports people experiencing homelessness, poverty and social exclusion across the borough. The Sleepout challenges participants to spend a night outdoors while learning more about homelessness and the support available locally.

Organisers are keen to stress that the event is not intended to replicate the experience of homelessness. Instead, it aims to encourage conversation, build understanding and raise money to support people accessing Petrus services.

Last year's inaugural Rochdale Sleepout brought supporters together from across the borough and raised £7,875.52 for Rochdale AFC Community Trust and Petrus.

The money raised has already helped launch Changing Lives, a partnership supporting people experiencing homelessness and those living in supported accommodation through football, wellbeing, education and employability opportunities.

According to Petrus, participants involved in the programme are rebuilding confidence, making new friendships, developing new skills and becoming more active members of their communities.

This year's event is also an opportunity for local businesses, community groups and individuals to get involved by taking part, sponsoring participants or making a donation.

Funds raised through the Sleepout will support Petrus' work across Rochdale, including homelessness prevention, housing support, wellbeing services, education and training opportunities, and practical support for some of the borough's most vulnerable residents.

Petrus is encouraging anyone interested in supporting the event to help spread the word and get involved.

articles.title: Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers take on 45-mile charity walk
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are taking on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October, to raise money for four causes close to their hearts.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers are swapping the rugby pitch for the road as members of the groups prepare to take on a 45-mile charity walk on Saturday, 31 October.

The challenge is being organised to raise as much money as possible for four causes close to the participants' hearts: Springhill Hospice, the Motor Neurone Disease Association (MND), Rochdale Masters and Rugby League Cares.

Organisers are expecting the walk to be a major physical challenge, but say they want it to become about more than completing 45 miles. They are also appealing to local businesses and members of the community to get behind the fundraising effort.

Businesses are being encouraged to support the challenge through sponsorship, donations, supplies for the day or simply by sharing the fundraiser with customers, colleagues and their wider networks.

The organisers said: "We're not playing rugby for this one… we're putting the boots down and walking 45 miles!"

The group hopes that local support will help raise as much money as possible for the four causes while bringing businesses, sports communities and residents together around the challenge.

Anyone who can help with sponsorship, donations, supplies or promotion is encouraged to get in touch with the organisers.

Mandy from Rochdale Masters and Mayfield Movers said the group would be happy to provide photographs, route details and further information about the charities involved, as well as speak about the challenge.

articles.title: Oliver Coldman crowned champion golfer at Rochdale Golf Club Captain’s Final
articles.excerpt: Oliver Coldman has won Rochdale Golf Club’s 2026 Captain’s Final with a two-round total of 133, four shots ahead of runner-up Steve Royle.
articles.content_html:
Oliver Coldman has been crowned Rochdale Golf Club’s Champion Golfer for 2026 after winning the Captain’s Final during a weekend of competition at the club.

Coldman recorded rounds of 69 and 64 for a combined score of 133 to take the Captain’s Final title. Steve Royle finished runner-up after rounds of 67 and 70 gave him a total of 137.

The weekend also saw a series of other prizes decided. Raymond Clegg claimed Best Nett on Saturday, while Tom Wilson took Best Nett on Sunday.

Aaron Buckley won the Darren Ogden Memorial Trophy, awarded for nearest the pin in two on the 18th, with a distance of 2.13 metres. Steve George was named the lowest qualifier at 10 under par.

Rochdale Golf Club said the weekend had produced some brilliant golf despite the threat of rain, and congratulated all of the finalists and winners. The club also thanked the volunteers and staff involved in staging what it described as a special annual event.

A charity raffle was drawn during the weekend, with the club thanking supporters who bought tickets as well as the donors who supplied prizes. A full list of raffle prize winners is expected to be emailed to members over the coming days.

The Captain’s Final is one of the highlights of the club calendar, bringing together qualifiers for the concluding competition and recognising performances across the weekend.
