articles.title: Wildfire emergency alert: an overreaction, or a sign of things to come?
articles.excerpt: Millions of phones across England and Wales sounded a Government Emergency Alert as wildfire risk reached exceptional levels. Was the intrusive warning proportionate, or are Britons being introduced to a hazard we will increasingly have to live with?
articles.content_html:
Millions of mobile phones across England and Wales emitted the unmistakable siren of the Government's Emergency Alerts system on Friday evening, carrying a warning about the risk of wildfires during exceptionally hot and dry conditions. People were urged not to light barbecues, campfires, bonfires or fireworks and to call 999 if they saw a fire.

For many people in Rochdale, where there was no wall of flame approaching their homes and no instruction to evacuate, the reaction was understandable: was this really what the country's most intrusive public-warning system was designed for? Emergency Alerts override ordinary phone settings and make a deliberately alarming noise intended to make people stop what they are doing immediately. Until recently, many people probably imagined receiving one only where there was a direct and imminent threat to life.

That makes the question worth asking. Was Friday's warning an overreaction, or was it an indication of how Britain's relationship with extreme weather is changing?

There is a reasonable argument that the Government must be careful not to overuse the system. Emergency warnings derive much of their effectiveness from their rarity. If people become accustomed to the siren being used for preventative advice that could have been distributed through television, radio, ordinary text messages and social media, warning fatigue becomes a real concern. A person who concludes that the alerts are unnecessarily dramatic may disable them and then miss a genuinely local warning about rapidly rising floodwater, an industrial accident or a fire approaching their home.

The Government should therefore be prepared to explain why this particular threshold was met and why an alert covering England and Wales was considered preferable to narrower regional warnings. Public confidence in an emergency system depends partly upon people understanding why its most intrusive warning mechanism has been activated.

However, dismissing the warning as hysteria would ignore the extraordinary situation confronting fire and rescue services this summer. Britain has experienced a succession of major wildfires during prolonged heat and drought. By Friday, national reporting indicated that the number of wildfires in England and Wales had already exceeded the 1,017 recorded during 2025, itself a record year. Dozens of fires were active around the country, major incidents had been declared, homes had been destroyed in the West Midlands and military personnel were being deployed to assist overstretched emergency services.

That changes the context considerably. Friday's message was not sent because somebody in Whitehall had suddenly discovered that dry grass can burn. It arrived during an active national wildfire emergency in which firefighters were already dealing with the consequences of repeated ignition in exceptionally dry landscapes.

The important distinction is between the probability of a fire starting and the severity of what may happen once one starts. Fire-danger measures do not necessarily predict that a particular patch of moorland will ignite. They indicate how easily vegetation may burn and how difficult a fire could become to control if ignition occurs. During ordinary British weather, carelessly discarded heat may produce a small scorched area. During prolonged heat, low humidity and very dry vegetation, the same ignition can develop into a fire requiring numerous appliances and many hours of firefighting.

Human behaviour therefore matters enormously. The Government cannot immediately cool the country, restore moisture to dried vegetation or remove weeks of accumulated heat from the landscape. It can, however, try to reduce avoidable sources of ignition. Disposable barbecues, bonfires, campfires, cigarettes, fireworks and other sources of heat can become much more consequential when the surrounding vegetation has effectively become fuel.

There is also a longer-term reason for taking the warning seriously. Britain is not becoming Spain, Greece or California overnight, and comparisons with those places can easily become exaggerated. Our climate, vegetation, housing patterns and emergency infrastructure are different. Nevertheless, the assumption that serious wildfire is an exotic problem belonging somewhere else is increasingly difficult to defend.

The UK has already experienced destructive moorland fires during previous hot summers, including the extensive Saddleworth Moor fires of 2018. For Rochdale this is not an abstract national concern. Moorland, grassland and countryside sit immediately beside settlements across the Pennine fringe, including areas around Littleborough, Wardle, Norden, Whitworth and the wider hills surrounding the borough. A serious moorland fire does not need to reach Rochdale town centre to affect Rochdale residents. Smoke, road closures, damaged habitats, exhausted emergency-service resources and threats to isolated properties can all spread consequences far beyond the flames themselves.

Climate science also points towards a future in which the weather conditions favourable to wildfire become more common. Research involving the Met Office and UK scientific institutions has concluded that human-caused climate change substantially increased the likelihood of the severe fire weather experienced during the 2022 heatwave. Climate-risk assessments anticipate more high fire-weather days as average temperatures rise, while longer periods of heat and drought can leave vegetation increasingly vulnerable to ignition.

That does not mean climate change can be blamed automatically for every individual fire. Fires still require ignition, fuel and conditions that allow them to spread. Land management, deliberate arson, accidental ignition and the speed of the emergency response all remain important. But the broader direction is difficult to ignore: a warmer climate can create more frequent periods in which an otherwise minor act of carelessness has much larger consequences.

This is why there is a sensible position between panic and dismissal. The Government should not turn the Emergency Alerts system into an electronic public-information poster. If the siren sounds too often for advice that is not genuinely urgent, its effectiveness may be weakened. Equally, a warning designed to prevent new fires during an already exceptional national wildfire situation is not obviously frivolous simply because no flames were visible from the recipient's window.

In fact, prevention may be one of the strongest arguments for using the system. Waiting until a wildfire is already moving towards houses means waiting until much of the opportunity to stop the emergency has disappeared. If a short national warning prevents even a small number of avoidable ignitions at a time when firefighters are already stretched, the intervention may prove proportionate despite its dramatic presentation.

The most interesting aspect of Friday's alert is therefore not the ten seconds of noise. It is what the noise was about. Britain has spent generations regarding wildfire principally as a rural inconvenience or an overseas catastrophe. Emergency planners are now treating it as a hazard capable of threatening homes, infrastructure and life on a sufficiently large scale to justify use of a national warning system.

For residents of Rochdale and the wider Pennine area, that deserves attention. Our landscape contains precisely the combination of moorland, grass, woodland and settlements that can make prolonged dry conditions problematic. The lesson is not that every warm weekend should cause millions of phones to scream. It is that the range of emergencies Britain prepares for may be changing.

If wetter summers return and warnings of this kind remain extremely rare, Friday's alert may ultimately be remembered as an unusually cautious intervention during an exceptional season. If periods of intense heat, drought and severe fire weather become more frequent, it may instead look like an early example of something the public later comes to regard as normal.

That is the uncomfortable possibility behind the alarm. The argument is not really about whether people were irritated by their phones. It is about whether Britain is entering a period in which hazards once considered unusual have to become part of ordinary civil protection.

Whether Friday's alert was perfectly calibrated is open to debate. The underlying wildfire risk is not.

articles.title: Homelessness, addiction and the cruelty of public condemnation
articles.excerpt: A disabled homeless man outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road has become the subject of photographs, insults and jokes online. The harder question is whether public humiliation solves anything at all.
articles.content_html:
There is a homeless man who regularly sits outside Tesco Express on Whitworth Road in Rochdale. He uses a wheelchair, has one leg, and appears to have longstanding problems with drug dependency. In recent days, photographs purporting to show him using drugs have been circulated in a local social-media group, accompanied by descriptions including ‘junkie’, ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’, together with jokes about his disability.

Those comments deserve more scrutiny than the man they were aimed at.

It is entirely legitimate for residents to object to public drug use, theft, abusive behaviour or intimidation. It is legitimate for shop workers to expect protection at work. It is legitimate for parents to dislike exposing children to distressing scenes. But there is a clear moral distinction between criticising behaviour and publicly degrading a vulnerable person. Calling a homeless, disabled man a ‘scruff’ does not protect children. Making jokes about his missing leg does not reduce drug use. Posting photographs of him at what may be one of the lowest points of his life does not help shop staff, improve public safety or increase the likelihood that he enters treatment. It serves a different purpose: humiliation.

The ease with which some people have participated in that humiliation should trouble us.

The editor of Rochdale Daily has spoken to this man several times. In those encounters, he has not demanded money. He has generally asked for a drink, usually a chocolate milkshake. Other residents have independently described similar experiences. A Tesco worker has, by contrast, said that staff sometimes experience him as abusive. Both accounts may be true. Addiction, withdrawal, mental distress and homelessness do not produce consistent behaviour.

That does not make abuse acceptable. But neither does difficult behaviour grant the public permission to strip somebody of dignity.

During one conversation, the man said he had previously been prescribed methadone but stopped collecting it because he felt demeaned and discriminated against when attending the dispensing pharmacy. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified that account. When asked whether he would consider restarting treatment if his medication could be dispensed somewhere he felt able to attend, he said yes.

That exchange should matter more than a photograph. It suggests that beneath the visible disorder is a person who can still discuss treatment, medication and the possibility of changing his circumstances. Yet this is precisely the sort of person whom public discussion can rapidly reduce to a caricature. Once the word ‘junkie’ has been applied, the individual disappears and only the label remains. That is not analysis. It is intellectual laziness.

Addiction is not a mysterious condition. It is extensively studied, medically recognised and strongly associated with homelessness, trauma, mental ill-health and social exclusion. National treatment statistics show that among people entering treatment for opiate problems in England in 2024–25, 41 per cent had no home of their own and 10 per cent were sleeping rough. Government research into rough sleeping published in 2025 found that 54 per cent of respondents reported a drug or alcohol misuse need during the preceding year.

These figures do not excuse criminal or antisocial behaviour. They do, however, make a mockery of the idea that addiction can be solved by simply telling somebody to ‘sort themselves out’. A person who is homeless must try to recover without privacy, stability, reliable sleep, secure storage, regular meals or often even basic hygiene. They may need to attend treatment, collect prescriptions, keep appointments, manage benefits, maintain identification documents and navigate housing applications while sleeping outside. To describe failure under those conditions as proof of moral inferiority is not toughness. It is ignorance.

One comment in the local discussion suggested that drug users should do these things ‘behind their own doors’. That statement is revealing precisely because the man in question does not have one.

Most people have the privilege of experiencing their worst behaviour privately. They can drink too much behind curtains, suffer mental-health crises in bedrooms, argue with family in kitchens, withdraw from medication under a duvet or make disastrous decisions without a stranger photographing them. A rough sleeper does not have a private sphere. His bedroom is public. His living room is public. His breakdowns are public. His addiction is public. And then the same society that has left him without a private space condemns him for failing to keep his problems out of sight. There is something deeply incoherent about that.

The man's disability makes the tone of some comments particularly ugly. Government research published in 2025 found that 80 per cent of people surveyed while sleeping rough reported a longstanding physical impairment, illness or disability. Yet a local discussion about a homeless man with one leg included jokes about his wheelchair. There is no serious public-interest argument for that. It is not community safety. It is not concern for children. It is not anger about shoplifting. It is mockery of disability, and adults should be capable of naming that for what it is.

The same applies to language such as ‘scruff’ and ‘down and out’. Such terms do not describe conduct; they reduce a person to a social category deemed beneath respect. The implication is that once somebody becomes sufficiently poor, addicted or visibly disordered, ordinary standards of human decency no longer apply to the way we speak about them. That proposition should be rejected. A person's entitlement to dignity cannot depend upon whether they are pleasant enough, clean enough, sober enough or useful enough to satisfy strangers on Facebook.

Rochdale also needs to confront the practical context. The borough is already under intense housing pressure. Under Places for Everyone, Rochdale's housing requirement for 2025 to 2030 is 616 homes per year. Council material from 2025 recorded 7,681 applicants on the housing register, while more recent council reporting has referred to approximately 20,000 people relying upon the register and nearly 7,500 meeting statutory ‘reasonable preference’ criteria. Rochdale Council declared a housing emergency in 2023.

So the instruction often directed at people like this man is effectively the following: become sober, become stable, engage with treatment, organise your paperwork, maintain appointments, secure benefits and compete for scarce housing, all while sleeping outside and managing a major physical disability. That is not impossible. But anyone describing it as simple has probably never attempted anything remotely comparable.

There are also legal considerations when photographs and allegations are published online. Taking a photograph in a public place is not automatically unlawful, and Rochdale Daily is not suggesting otherwise. Identifiable images can, depending on context, constitute personal data, while publishing a photograph alongside a serious allegation of criminal behaviour raises separate legal questions.

The Defamation Act 2013 provides protection against statements that cause or are likely to cause serious reputational harm. Truth may be a defence, but that is different from saying that anything alleged on social media is lawful merely because the publisher believes it. If an identifiable photograph is accompanied by an assertion that a person is committing a criminal offence, the publisher should be in a position to substantiate what is being alleged. Rochdale Daily is therefore not independently stating that the man was consuming a Class A drug based solely on photographs and comments circulated online.

There is an additional point that some contributors may wish to consider before reaching for the camera. Vulnerability does not make somebody public property. The fact that a person's suffering occurs on a pavement does not create an entitlement to turn it into entertainment, gossip or a community spectacle. There may be circumstances in which photographing suspected criminal behaviour serves a legitimate evidential purpose. There is a substantial difference between preserving evidence for police and distributing an image among neighbours so that strangers can compete to produce the most contemptuous description of the person depicted. One is potentially evidence gathering. The other can become a form of public shaming.

And public shaming has a cost. If a person already believes that institutions regard him as worthless, if he already feels humiliated collecting treatment, if strangers photograph him and hundreds of neighbours discuss whether he is a ‘scruff’, then it should not surprise anyone if disengagement, isolation and further drug use follow. People sometimes ask why addicts do not seek help while simultaneously creating a social environment in which admitting addiction results in contempt. They demand recovery while reinforcing shame. They demand engagement while making the person feel despised. They demand that somebody rejoin society while making it clear that society would rather not look at them. Those positions are difficult to reconcile.

There is also a tendency to present compassion as naïveté. Those who have defended the man have been dismissed as ‘Karens’ or ‘do gooders’, as though refusing to join in public degradation demonstrates some failure to understand the realities of addiction. The opposite may be true. It requires very little sophistication to dislike someone behaving badly in public. It requires considerably more maturity to condemn the behaviour without enjoying the destruction of the person.

Compassion does not mean giving unlimited money to somebody with an addiction. It does not mean ignoring theft. It does not mean expecting retail workers to endure abuse. It does not mean pretending crack cocaine is harmless. It means retaining the ability to distinguish a human being from his worst behaviour. That distinction is central to every serious approach to rehabilitation.

If society genuinely wants people to recover from addiction, then those people must eventually be able to imagine themselves as something other than an addict. If every interaction reinforces that they are disgusting, worthless and permanently defined by their dependency, society should not be surprised when they behave as though there is little left to recover.

Rochdale Council lists homelessness support, drug and alcohol treatment and specialist services including Turning Point. Those services are important, but complex cases require coordination. A homeless person with a major physical disability and drug dependency may simultaneously require healthcare, treatment, medication management, benefits assistance, housing support and persistent outreach. That is difficult work. Writing ‘absolute scruff’ beneath a photograph is considerably easier. Perhaps that is part of its appeal. It allows people to experience the satisfaction of condemning a social problem without undertaking any of the difficult work involved in solving it.

There is a legitimate debate to be had about public drug use in Rochdale. There is a legitimate debate about homelessness, shoplifting, antisocial behaviour, policing, treatment capacity and the availability of supported accommodation. Those are serious subjects. Wheelchair jokes are not. Photographing a visibly vulnerable disabled man for the purpose of ridicule is not. Describing somebody at the lowest point of his life as though he were vermin contributes nothing whatsoever to the safety or wellbeing of Rochdale.

Residents are entitled to expect streets that are safe and usable. Tesco staff are entitled to work without abuse. Children should not have to encounter dangerous drug paraphernalia. Police should deal with offences where offences occur. But none of those propositions requires cruelty.

The question for Rochdale is not whether this man is admirable. He may not be. The question is whether a civilised community applies standards of dignity only to people whose lives are already in order. Most of the people commenting about him will eventually put their phones down and return home. They will have a bathroom, a bed, heating, a front door and somewhere to make their mistakes privately. He will still be outside. That difference should produce some humility.

If a community cannot look at a homeless, addicted, disabled man without turning his circumstances into entertainment, then there is more than one social problem on display. One is sitting on the pavement. The other is holding the camera.

articles.title: Rochdale businesses urged to back Denehurst House in £30-a-month veterans challenge
articles.excerpt: A Rochdale veterans support organisation is asking 100 local businesses to pledge £30 a month to help keep Denehurst House operational and support former service personnel in need.
articles.content_html:
A Rochdale veterans support organisation has launched a drive to recruit 100 local businesses willing to pledge £30 a month towards keeping Denehurst House operational.

Get Together After Serving CIC, which is behind the campaign, says Denehurst House provides support for veterans including emergency housing, hot meals and mental health support. The organisation is promoting the appeal as the Rochdale 100 Businesses Challenge and is asking firms across the borough to make a regular monthly contribution.

If all 100 places are filled, the campaign would generate £3,000 each month in pledged support, equivalent to £36,000 over a full year if every business remained involved for 12 months. The appeal describes the contribution as a relatively small commitment for an individual business which, collectively, could make a significant difference to the service.

Campaign material highlights community spirit, warm meals and local businesses working together, with the message: 'Together, we keep Denehurst House operational.' It also says the project aims to provide a lifeline to veterans when they need it most.

The initiative is seeking support from companies of all sizes rather than relying on a handful of major donors. That model would spread the cost across the local business community while giving Denehurst House a more predictable stream of recurring income.

Local businesses interested in joining the challenge are being asked to contact Get Together After Serving CIC by emailing hello@gtascic.co.uk.

Rochdale Daily is publishing the appeal as today's front-page community story to help local firms understand what is being requested, how the funding model works and how they can take part.

articles.title: Can’t make it to church? Christ Church Healey invites community to join Sunday service online
articles.excerpt: Christ Church Healey is inviting people who cannot attend in person, are new to church or simply want to find out more to join its Sunday morning service online each week.
articles.content_html:
People across Healey and the wider Rochdale community who are unable to attend church in person are being warmly invited to join Christ Church's Sunday morning service online each week.

The church's weekly livestream is also open to people who may be new to church, curious about Christianity or who would simply feel more comfortable experiencing a service from home before deciding whether to attend in person.

Christ Church goes live at 9.55am every Sunday morning, allowing viewers to watch the service as it happens. Anyone who cannot watch at that time can catch up afterwards, with the service remaining available to view later.

The church said: “You are most welcome to join us for our weekly Sunday morning livestream from Christ Church. You can watch the service live as it happens, or at any time afterwards. We go live at 9.55am.”

For people who are housebound, unwell, caring for somebody, working on Sunday mornings or otherwise unable to be physically present, the livestream provides a way to remain connected with worship and the local church community.

It can also offer a gentle introduction for anyone who has never attended church before. There is no requirement to already be a member of the congregation — viewers can simply tune in from home and see what a Sunday morning at Christ Church is like.

The livestream runs each Sunday, with the broadcast beginning at 9.55am. Christ Church Healey welcomes both its existing congregation and newcomers joining online.

articles.title: MBF Cleaning sponsors Rochdale Foodbank van to support deliveries across the borough
articles.excerpt: MBF Cleaning has agreed to sponsor Rochdale Foodbank's van, helping the charity collect supplies and deliver food parcels to distribution points around the borough.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Foodbank has thanked local company MBF Cleaning after the business agreed to sponsor the charity's van, helping it continue moving supplies and donations and delivering food parcels across the borough.

The sponsorship followed a recent visit from representatives of MBF Cleaning, who wanted to understand how the company could best support local families and individuals in need.

Manuel and Janine from MBF Cleaning met with Ruth at Rochdale Foodbank to discuss the charity's work, share ideas and explore practical ways the business could make a difference.

The foodbank's van plays an important role in day-to-day operations, helping bring in supplies and donations before delivering food parcels to distribution points around Rochdale.

By sponsoring the vehicle, MBF Cleaning is helping the charity maintain that transport link and continue supporting people facing hardship across the borough.

Rochdale Foodbank is also encouraging other local businesses to consider becoming corporate partners. Companies interested in supporting the charity can find more information about partnership opportunities through Rochdale Foodbank's website.

The charity says it would welcome conversations with businesses interested in working together to support the local community.

Janine from MBF Cleaning is pictured with Ruth from Rochdale Foodbank in the original announcement.

articles.title: This week in Rochdale, 100 years ago: the town captured from the air in August 1926
articles.excerpt: Exactly a century ago this month, aerial photographers captured remarkable views of Rochdale's Town Hall, Yorkshire Street, railway station, Broadfield Park and industrial works — preserving the town as it looked in August 1926.
articles.content_html:
One hundred years ago this week, Rochdale was a very different town — but thanks to a remarkable series of aerial photographs taken in August 1926, we can still see it almost street by street.

The images, held by the Britain From Above archive, show a dense industrial town of mills, railway infrastructure, tramways, terraced streets and civic buildings. They provide one of the clearest surviving visual records of Rochdale in the inter-war period.

Yorkshire Street was photographed from the air in August 1926 under reference EPW016788. The view shows the familiar line of the street threading through tightly packed buildings, with factories, chimneys and terraced housing occupying much of the surrounding landscape. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016788

Rochdale railway station was also captured that month under reference EPW016784. The photograph shows not only the station but the extraordinary concentration of railway sidings, engineering works and industrial premises that once surrounded this part of the town. The archive identifies features including railway works, cotton mills, a goods shed and the Rochdale Canal terminal basin. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016784

Another image, EPW016791, looks across Town Hall Square. It records landmarks that remain instantly recognisable alongside features which have since vanished or changed beyond recognition. Archive annotations identify St Chad's, the Esplanade, Rochdale Post Office, Drake Street, tramcars and the Rochdale War Memorial while it was still under construction. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016791

Broadfield Park was photographed in the same month under reference EPW016782, giving another extraordinary perspective across the civic heart of Rochdale. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016782

The industrial scale of the town is perhaps most obvious in the August 1926 photographs of Fishwick Street. Image EPW016789 records the railway works there, reflecting the huge engineering and manufacturing presence which once surrounded Rochdale's rail network. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016789

Even before that August series, an Aerofilms photograph taken on 6 August 1926 captured Rochdale Road crossing the railway and Rochdale Canal at Slattocks. The image, EPW016440, preserves a landscape where canal, railway and road infrastructure sat side by side — the transport arteries which helped power the borough's industrial economy. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016440

What is striking about these photographs is not simply what has disappeared. It is how much remains legible. The Town Hall, St Chad's, major road alignments and parts of the railway landscape allow modern residents to orient themselves inside a town photographed from an aircraft a century ago.

The photographs also capture Rochdale during a period of profound change. The borough remained heavily industrial, public transport still included corporation tramcars, and mills and engineering works dominated huge areas which today contain housing, roads, offices and redeveloped land.

The Rochdale Observer itself was already a long-established part of town life by 1926, having first appeared in 1856. Its surviving archive means future editions of Rochdale Daily's '100 Years Ago' feature can go beyond photographs and recover the stories residents were actually reading — crime reports, council debates, sport, advertisements, court cases, births, deaths and the everyday incidents which made up life in the borough.

For this first edition, though, the photographs tell their own story. They allow us to look down on Rochdale exactly a century ago and recognise both the town we inherited and the one that disappeared.

Rochdale Daily intends to make 'This Week in Rochdale — 100 Years Ago' a recurring history feature throughout the centenary year.

IMAGE NOTE: The historic Aerofilms photographs referenced above are held by Britain From Above. Their terms do not permit commercial reproduction without a separate licence, so Rochdale Daily links readers to the original archive images rather than reproducing them without permission.

articles.title: Little'Pink'borough returns as businesses across Littleborough prepare to turn pink for Cancer Research UK
articles.excerpt: Businesses and organisations across Littleborough, Hollingworth Lake and Wardle are being invited to take part in Little'Pink'borough, a community campaign raising awareness and funds for Cancer Research UK.
articles.content_html:
Littleborough is preparing to turn pink once again as one of the area's colourful community fundraising campaigns returns in eight weeks.

Little'Pink'borough is inviting shops, pubs, clubs, cafés, restaurants, doctors' surgeries, dentists, hairdressers and businesses across Littleborough, Hollingworth Lake and Wardle to get involved in support of Cancer Research UK.

The campaign, organised by The Three Amigos FUNdraising Group, encourages local organisations to create their own pink-themed displays and help transform the area while raising awareness of cancer research.

Businesses are welcome to organise their own fundraising activities as part of the campaign, although organisers stress that in-house fundraising is appreciated rather than essential. Simply taking part and creating a display helps build the community-wide event.

Photographs from previous years are being shared to provide inspiration and get local businesses thinking about what they could create this time around.

There is also a competitive element. The organisation judged to have the best display will receive a bespoke trophy to keep for a year, with the winner's name engraved on it permanently as part of the event's history.

The campaign brings together businesses, community organisations and residents from across the wider Littleborough area around a common cause, while giving streets and shopfronts a distinctive pink makeover.

This year's Little'Pink'borough is being supported by Whittaker Golf Club, which is sponsoring the campaign. The club offers memberships and individual rounds of golf, with further information available through its website.

With eight weeks to go, The Three Amigos FUNdraising Group is encouraging organisations to start planning their displays and decide how they would like to take part.

Further details about the event and fundraising activities are expected as Little'Pink'borough approaches.

articles.title: Residents urge dog owners to clean up after pets amid fouling concerns in Milnrow and Newhey
articles.excerpt: Residents in Milnrow and Newhey are calling on dog owners to pick up after their pets following complaints about dog mess being left in public areas, alongside local concern about parvovirus.
articles.content_html:
Residents in Milnrow and Newhey are urging dog owners to take responsibility for cleaning up after their pets following growing frustration about dog fouling in local public areas.

Community members say the amount of dog mess being left behind has become unacceptable, creating an unpleasant problem for pedestrians, families and responsible dog walkers.

The message from residents is straightforward: if your dog fouls in a public place, carry a bag, pick it up and dispose of it properly.

Concerns have also been heightened by reports among local dog owners about canine parvovirus in the area. Parvovirus is a highly contagious viral illness affecting dogs and can be particularly serious for puppies and unvaccinated animals. The virus can be shed in the faeces of infected dogs and can persist in contaminated environments, making good hygiene and responsible disposal of dog waste especially important.

Rochdale Daily has not independently confirmed the extent of any current local parvovirus outbreak, so owners concerned about their dog's health should seek advice from a veterinary professional rather than relying on social-media reports.

Dog fouling is not simply an inconvenience. People should not have to navigate dog mess on pavements, paths, grassed areas and other shared spaces, while responsible owners should not have to worry about their pets walking through waste left behind by somebody else.

Residents are asking owners to remember that responsibility for clearing up belongs to the person in charge of the dog. It should not be left for council workers, other dog walkers or members of the public to deal with.

Picking up takes seconds and helps keep Milnrow and Newhey cleaner and safer for everyone using local streets and green spaces.

The message is simple: carry a bag, pick it up and bin it.

articles.title: New Whitworth venue Lillie's to serve kindness alongside cocktails with 'Be Kind' initiative
articles.excerpt: Guests at Lillie's in Whitworth will find anonymous handwritten messages of encouragement waiting at their tables as part of a new 'Be Kind' initiative designed to spread a little positivity from one visitor to the next.
articles.content_html:
A new Whitworth hospitality venue is planning to put kindness at the heart of its bottomless brunches by passing anonymous handwritten messages of encouragement from one guest to the next.

Lillie's, which is preparing to open in Whitworth, says its ambition has always been to create more than simply somewhere to enjoy cocktails, food and company. Its owner wants customers to leave feeling a little happier than when they arrived.

That idea has now developed into the venue's new 'Be Kind' initiative.

Every guest attending a Bottomless Brunch will be welcomed with a signature Lillie's cocktail and a sealed Be Kind envelope waiting at the table. Inside will be a handwritten message from a previous guest containing words of kindness, encouragement, positivity or support. The messages will be completely anonymous.

Each envelope will also contain a fresh piece of Lillie's stationery. While waiting for food, guests who want to participate can write their own anonymous message for somebody attending a future brunch. There is no obligation to take part.

The new note will be placed back into the envelope and passed on to another customer at a later brunch, while guests can take the message they received home with them.

The owner originally considered creating a communal 'Be Kind Box' from which anybody feeling low could select an anonymous uplifting message. Concerns that an unrestricted box might not always be used in the positive spirit intended led to the more controlled table-envelope idea instead.

The concept is based on a simple recognition that people rarely know what somebody else may be dealing with behind the scenes and that a small act of kindness, including a few thoughtful words from a stranger, can sometimes make a significant difference to someone's day.

Lillie's says the initiative is its own small way of spreading kindness one message at a time, built around the message: 'In a world where you can be anything, be kind.'

The initiative will launch as part of Lillie's Bottomless Brunch offering when the Whitworth venue opens.

Alcohol is for adults aged 18 and over. Please drink responsibly.

articles.title: Newhey Gardening Gang volunteers transform churchyard in latest community clean-up
articles.excerpt: Volunteers from Newhey's Gardening Gang have completed another major session in the local churchyard, cutting grass, tending shrub beds and cremation plots and clearing pathways.
articles.content_html:
A team of community volunteers has continued its work keeping a Newhey churchyard looking its best after another strong turnout for the local Gardening Gang.

Volunteers were back at work yesterday, tackling a substantial list of jobs across the churchyard and continuing the improvements made during previous sessions.

The group's 'buzzy bee strimmers' were out in force and completed the mammoth task of cutting all of the grass areas. Other volunteers weeded and cut back shrub beds and cremation plots, while a number of pathways were also cleared.

The work is part of an ongoing community effort to maintain and improve the churchyard, with local volunteers giving their own time to care for a space used by families, visitors and the wider Newhey community.

Organisers thanked everyone who took part, saying the churchyard continues to look great thanks to the efforts of the Gardening Gang.

Volunteer-led projects like this can make a significant difference to shared spaces, particularly where regular maintenance involves large areas of grass, established planting and paths which need repeated attention throughout the growing season.

The Gardening Gang is expected to announce another volunteering date, with residents being encouraged to watch for details of the next session.

Rochdale Daily would like to thank all of the volunteers giving their time to help look after Newhey's community spaces.

articles.title: Full house for National Emergency Briefing screening in Falinge
articles.excerpt: A community screening of the National Emergency Briefing attracted a full room in Falinge, with Rochdale councillors Tricia Ayrton and Shah Wazir joining residents for the event and discussion afterwards.
articles.content_html:
A community screening of the National Emergency Briefing attracted a full room in Falinge, with two Rochdale Council portfolio holders joining residents for the event and subsequent discussion.

Organisers have thanked everyone who attended the screening, saying it was encouraging to see such a strong turnout for the film and the conversation which followed.

Rochdale Borough Council portfolio holders Councillor Tricia Ayrton and Councillor Shah Wazir were among those attending.

Organisers thanked both councillors for remaining after the screening to listen to residents, take part in discussions and consider how the issues raised by the film could be discussed more widely.

They said the councillors left the event with a plan to help ensure the film and its message reach a broader audience.

The National Emergency Briefing brings together scientists, campaigners and public figures to discuss climate change and the risks they believe the UK faces, with contributors associated with the project including environmental campaigner Chris Packham.

The Falinge event gave residents an opportunity not only to watch the presentation together but to discuss its arguments and what they could mean at a local level.

Following the strong turnout, another community screening has already been arranged.

The next screening will take place on Thursday 4 September at 6pm, giving residents who were unable to attend the latest event another opportunity to see the film and join the discussion.

Organisers thanked residents, guests and councillors for supporting the event and helping create what they described as an important community conversation.

articles.title: Prehistoric survivor growing in Syke herb garden has roots stretching back 300 million years
articles.excerpt: Residents picking herbs from a community garden in Syke are being invited to help tackle horsetail — a persistent weed whose ancestors grew locally more than 300 million years ago.
articles.content_html:
A troublesome weed growing in a community herb garden in Syke has a remarkable connection to the landscape's prehistoric past — with its ancestors dating back more than 300 million years.

Residents are being encouraged to help maintain the community herb garden while collecting fresh herbs to take home.

The garden is open for people to pick herbs for their own use, but volunteers are asking visitors who have a few spare minutes to lend a hand with some weeding at the same time.

One plant in particular is proving difficult to control: horsetail, also commonly known as mare's tail.

While modern gardeners may regard it as a persistent nuisance, horsetail belongs to an extraordinarily ancient group of plants whose history stretches back to long before dinosaurs walked the Earth.

During the Carboniferous period, more than 300 million years ago, relatives of today's horsetails grew across the landscapes that would eventually become northern England.

Among them were Calamites — tree-like plants related to modern horsetails which could grow many metres tall and formed part of the vast Carboniferous vegetation.

Evidence of that lost landscape can still be found locally. A fossil discovered in a quarry at Tonacliffe shows the distinctive remains of Calamites, providing a physical connection between the plants growing here hundreds of millions of years ago and the much smaller horsetails residents battle in gardens today.

Carboniferous plant fossils can also be found within rocks across the surrounding moorland, reflecting a period when the area's environment looked dramatically different from the Pennine landscape residents know today.

People remain welcome to collect herbs from the community garden, but anyone visiting is being encouraged to pull a few weeds while they are there.

As the volunteers joked, nobody wants today's horsetail growing to the size of its Carboniferous grandparents.

The community garden is maintained for local people to enjoy, and even a few minutes of weeding can help keep it productive and accessible for everyone.

articles.title: Plans for 45 homes behind Greenvale unanimously deferred after more than 290 objections
articles.excerpt: Councillors have unanimously deferred a planning application for 45 homes on land behind Greenvale in Bamford after campaigners raised concerns over transport, drainage, biodiversity, design and the absence of a wider masterplan.
articles.content_html:
A controversial planning application for 45 homes on land behind Greenvale in Bamford has been unanimously deferred after a packed Planning Committee meeting and more than 290 public objections.

The application had been recommended for approval by planning officers, but strong public interest saw it moved to the first item on the committee agenda.

Claire, chair of Bamford Green Belt Action Group, Dr Barry Lewis and Councillor Steve Anstee addressed the committee, asking councillors either to refuse the proposal or defer a decision while outstanding issues were examined further.

Campaigners raised a wide range of concerns, including the absence of a comprehensive masterplan for the wider allocation of around 450 homes and the lack of an infrastructure phasing and delivery strategy.

Transport was another major issue. Objectors highlighted Transport for Greater Manchester's position that effective transport mitigation could not yet be determined, while concerns were also raised over the proposed access through Greenvale and Norford Way rather than Norden Road.

Existing drainage and pedestrian-safety problems were raised during the meeting. Dr Lewis highlighted drainage issues already experienced on Norford Way and also questioned proposals relating to affordable and social housing beneath power lines.

Environmental concerns included a reported 39 per cent biodiversity net loss, rather than the 10 per cent biodiversity net gain required under current rules. Campaigners also pointed to outstanding concerns from ecology and urban-design officers.

United Utilities was said to have requested an allocation-wide drainage masterplan, while further concerns were raised about design, affordable housing, recreational facilities and the absence of what campaigners considered appropriate pre-application public consultation.

More than 290 objections have been submitted by members of the public.

Following debate, councillors voted unanimously to defer the application until September to allow further work and clarification.

The decision does not amount to a refusal of the proposed development. The application remains live and is expected to return to councillors once the outstanding matters have been considered.

Bamford Green Belt Action Group described the deferral as an important result and thanked residents who attended the meeting, submitted objections or supported the campaign.

Rochdale Daily will report further developments when the application returns to the Planning Committee.

articles.title: Hundreds of families join Holiday Hive fun in the parks - and it's back in libraries next week
articles.excerpt: Lawn games, bubble stations and free books drew hundreds of families to the parks this week. The Holiday Hive moves back into libraries next week, starting with a ballerina craft at Spotland.
articles.content_html:
Hundreds of families joined Rochdale Borough Libraries' Holiday Hive in parks across the borough this week, making the most of the sunshine and the borough's green spaces.

The libraries service thanked everyone who came along, with families enjoying lawn games, bubble stations, music stations, parachute play and musical crafts - and well done to everyone who managed to find a free book hidden amongst the activities.

The Holiday Hive returns to library buildings from next week, starting with a ballerina craft at Spotland Library.

There's an extra incentive to keep reading through the summer too. The Holiday Hive will be giving away more free books to any child who completes the Summer Reading Challenge whilst attending a Holiday Hive session - while stocks last, so families are urged not to delay.

The Summer Reading Challenge encourages children to keep reading through the long break, when many pupils' reading otherwise slips back before September. Signing up is free through the borough's libraries.

articles.title: Got a Uniform For All order waiting? Balderstone Library needs the shelf space
articles.excerpt: The school uniform reuse scheme says its collection point is 'busier than Amazon's warehouse' - and is asking families with ready-to-collect orders to pick them up to make room for new deliveries.
articles.content_html:
Families with a school uniform order waiting at Balderstone Library are being asked to collect it as soon as possible - because the shelves are full and new deliveries are arriving fast.

Uniform For All, the borough scheme that gives pre-loved school uniform a second life, says anyone who has received an order-ready-to-pick-up email from www.uniformforall.co.uk should call in and collect it promptly to make space. "It's busier than Amazon's warehouse at the Uniform For All office right now," the scheme said.

What is Uniform For All?

Uniform For All collects donated school uniform - the coats, jumpers, polo shirts, trousers and PE kit that children outgrow long before they wear out - checks and sorts it, and passes it on to families across the borough. Orders are placed through the website and collected locally, with Balderstone Library serving as a collection and donation point.

The idea is simple but the impact is real. Kitting a child out for September can cost families well over a hundred pounds per child, and for households already stretched by rent, bills and food, uniform costs land at exactly the wrong time of year. A reuse scheme means good clothing goes to a child who needs it instead of landfill, families keep money in their pockets, and children start term dressed the same as everyone else.

With the summer holidays in full swing and the new school year only weeks away, demand is at its annual peak - hence the plea for prompt collections.

How to donate

If you have school uniform your children have outgrown, you can drop it off at Balderstone Library too. Clean, wearable items are what the scheme needs most. And if your child needs uniform for September, orders can be placed at www.uniformforall.co.uk.

articles.title: Shoppers donate 368 kilos of food at Rochdale Foodbank's Morrisons Kingsway drive
articles.excerpt: Generous shoppers added extra items to their trolleys over two days at Morrisons Kingsway, donating 368kg of food. How the foodbank works, how to get help - and how to give it.
articles.content_html:
Shoppers at Morrisons Kingsway have donated a remarkable 368 kilos of food to Rochdale Foodbank after a two-day food drive at the store last Thursday and Friday.

The foodbank thanked all the generous shoppers who added extra items to their shopping, saying donations came in all shapes and sizes and included many of its most needed items. The charity also paid special tribute to the volunteers who staffed the collection and made the event a success, adding that every single item received will make a big difference to its clients.

Rochdale Foodbank has been part of life in the town for more than a decade. Registered as a charity in its own right in 2017, it operates as part of the Trussell network of food banks and is run almost entirely by volunteers - around 70 of them - who sort, date-check and pack donated food into emergency parcels at its base off Newgate in the town centre.

How the foodbank works

The foodbank operates on a referral system. Care professionals - including GPs, health visitors, social workers, Citizens Advice staff, welfare officers, the police and probation services - identify people in crisis and issue them with a foodbank voucher. That voucher can then be exchanged at a foodbank session for an emergency parcel containing at least three days of nutritionally balanced food. Volunteers meet clients over a cup of tea and can signpost them to agencies able to help with the longer-term problem, from debt advice to benefits support.

Alongside its main sessions, the foodbank has expanded in recent years. A Saturday morning session runs at Branches Christian Fellowship in Smallbridge, where clients can collect parcels between 10am and 12pm, and the charity has also opened Rochdale Central Pantry in the Rochdale Exchange Shopping Centre - a membership pantry for people who have recently needed foodbank support and could use a little extra help each week.

If you need help, you can call the foodbank on 0300 102 1646 or visit rochdale.foodbank.org.uk, which lists the organisations able to issue vouchers.

How to donate

More than nine in ten items given out by Trussell network food banks are donated by the public, which is why collections like the Morrisons drive matter so much. There are permanent donation points in Rochdale's larger supermarkets, including Tesco, Asda and Morrisons, intended for food purchased in-store. Larger donations can be dropped off at the foodbank's warehouse via the Newgate service area - ring ahead on 0300 102 1646 for big deliveries - and the foodbank publishes a shopping list of the items it most urgently needs on its website. Money donations, which help cover running costs and fill gaps in donated stock, can also be made through the website.

As the foodbank itself puts it: even if it's just one tin every week, every tin helps.

articles.title: Lord-Lieutenant's visit, a surprise inspection passed and a packed cafe: quite a week for Whitworth's Stronger Together
articles.excerpt: The Whitworth carers' group welcomed the King's representative in Lancashire, retained its 5-star hygiene rating in a surprise inspection, and saw its Community Cafe overflow into the main hall — all in one week.
articles.content_html:
A remarkable week for Whitworth carers' group Stronger Together began with a royal representative at the door and ended with a cafe so busy it spilled into the main hall.

On Monday the group welcomed the Lord-Lieutenant of Lancashire, Amanda Parker, and her husband Robert. Mrs Parker is His Majesty The King's personal representative in Lancashire and the first woman to hold the role in the county in almost five hundred years, and her visit is a mark of how far the volunteer-run group has come.

The same day brought a test of a different kind: an unannounced visit from environmental health officers just before lunch service. The inspectors found everything in order and the group retained its food hygiene rating of 5, the top score, which it has held since Rossendale Borough Council first awarded it in December 2024.

By Tuesday the group's Community Cafe was packed, with every table full and half of the main hall pressed into service to seat everyone.

Stronger Together was founded in 2023 by Angela Forster and Kathleen Proctor, both unpaid carers themselves, after they found there was nowhere locally for carers to turn for support. What began as a weekly coffee morning has grown into something much bigger, now based at The Ashcroft on Market Street, where volunteers serve more than 70 fresh, home-cooked meals every week alongside cakes and unlimited drinks, all free of charge with donation pots for those who wish to give.

The group describes itself as a warm, safe space offering advice and emotional and practical support, with activities including prize bingo, crafts and quizzes, and it runs entirely on fundraising, raffles, donations and grants. A crowdfunded project launched last year added gentle exercise sessions with a qualified trainer, healthy eating advice and a singing group open to all ages and abilities.

Recognition has followed. The founders received a Mayor's Special Award at the Whitworth Business and Community Awards in 2023, with the then Mayor of Whitworth describing the pair as truly inspirational to the community. The group went on to win the Not-for-Profit category at the Rossendale Business Awards, and this summer it was shortlisted for Community Group of the Year at the Pride of Rossendale Awards.

Reflecting on the week, the founders thanked the group's volunteers and supporters, saying the group is truly blessed in the people around it.

Anyone who would like to support Stronger Together, volunteer or find out about its sessions can contact the group through its Facebook page.

articles.title: Elderly lady found after incredible community effort
articles.excerpt: A woman in her 70s who went missing in Newhey has been found after hundreds of residents joined Greater Manchester Police in an extraordinary community search.
articles.content_html:
An elderly woman who went missing in Newhey has been found following an extraordinary community effort involving hundreds of local residents.

Christine, who is in her 70s, was reported missing earlier in the evening, prompting an urgent response from Greater Manchester Police and a huge mobilisation across Newhey and the surrounding area.

As concern grew, residents left their homes to help officers search on the ground. People walked streets, paths and open spaces, checked nearby areas and shared information rapidly across community groups in an effort to bring Christine home.

The response was remarkable. Hundreds of people are understood to have assisted either directly with searches or by sharing appeals and helping coordinate information alongside GMP.

At around 11pm, local woman Charlotte Rigby found Christine. In a touching detail after hours of worry, Christine was found clutching a bunch of flowers.

News that she had been located was met with enormous relief across the community, bringing a frightening evening to the best possible conclusion.

Tonight demonstrated Newhey and the wider Rochdale borough at its very best. Residents did not simply share a post and hope for good news. They put on their shoes, went outside and actively helped search for someone who needed them.

Credit must also go to Greater Manchester Police and everyone who supported the search, but special recognition is due to the countless members of the public who gave their time and refused to give up.

The borough should be very proud tonight. This was community spirit in its purest form, and the outcome is the great news everyone had been hoping for.

Out of respect for Christine and her family, no further personal or medical details should be shared unless released through official channels.

articles.title: Heywood singer-songwriter releases heartfelt debut single 'Rewind'
articles.excerpt: Twenty-year-old Heywood singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson has achieved a lifelong ambition with the release of her debut single, Rewind, a soulful pop track inspired by heartbreak, hope and moving forward.
articles.content_html:
A young musician from Heywood has realised a lifelong dream with the release of her debut single.

Twenty-year-old singer-songwriter Rhiannon Thompson released her first original song, Rewind, on 31 July. The soulful pop track draws on her own experience of heartbreak and the realisation that someone she believed was 'the one' ultimately was not the right person after all.

Music has always played a central role in Rhiannon's life, and releasing her own song is something she says she has dreamed about since childhood.

"Having my own song has always been my biggest dream, so finally releasing Rewind is such an emotional and proud moment for me," she said.

Rhiannon worked alongside her friend, songwriter and producer Jack Carroll, who helped write and produce the track in his studio. She cites Sienna Spiro as one of her biggest musical inspirations.

The response to Rewind has already been overwhelming.

"Seeing people say they love my song means everything to me. I hope when people hear it, they remember there is always a light at the end of the tunnel and that things do get better with time."

Looking ahead, Rhiannon hopes to release an EP and continue sharing her music with the world.

"One of my biggest dreams is to hear my music played on the radio. If people enjoy Rewind, I would be so grateful if they could share it and help more people discover my music."

She added: "Thank you to everyone who has supported me so far. I appreciate every listen, every comment and every share — it truly means the world to me."

Rewind is available now on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube. Rhiannon can also be followed on Facebook, Instagram at rhiannon_t05 and TikTok at @rhiannonthompsonxx.

articles.title: Veterans invited to weekly breakfast club as Rochdale continues to support Armed Forces community
articles.excerpt: Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being encouraged to attend a free weekly breakfast club at the Flying Horse Hotel in Rochdale town centre, offering friendship, support and an opportunity to reconnect with fellow servicemen and women.
articles.content_html:
Military veterans from across Rochdale Borough are being invited to attend the weekly Rochdale Veterans Breakfast Club held every Thursday morning at the Flying Horse Hotel on Packer Street, Rochdale.

Supported by Rochdale Borough Council, the breakfast club has become a welcoming meeting place for former members of the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force. Breakfast is served between 9am and 10.30am every Thursday, with organisers reporting that thousands of breakfasts have now been served since the initiative began.

While the event offers a free breakfast, its real purpose is bringing veterans together. Leaving military service can often mean leaving behind the camaraderie and close friendships built over years of service. The breakfast club provides an opportunity to reconnect with fellow veterans, share experiences and offer informal peer support in a relaxed environment.

Rochdale has a proud military heritage stretching back generations. The borough has long been associated with the Lancashire Fusiliers and today remains home to a significant Armed Forces community, including serving personnel, reservists, veterans and military families. Many continue serving their communities long after leaving the military through volunteering, public service and local charities.

Research has consistently shown that social connection can play a vital role in improving wellbeing, particularly among veterans who may experience loneliness or find the transition to civilian life challenging. Community initiatives such as breakfast clubs provide an important opportunity to maintain friendships, reduce isolation and ensure no veteran feels forgotten.

The club is open to any military veteran, regardless of how long they served or when they left the Armed Forces. Whether someone completed a full career or served for only a short period, organisers say everyone who has worn the uniform is welcome.

The Rochdale Veterans Breakfast Club takes place every Thursday between 9am and 10.30am at the Flying Horse Hotel, Packer Street, Rochdale.

Rochdale has always been a borough that values those who have served. While remembrance services rightly honour military sacrifice each November, supporting veterans throughout the year is equally important. Initiatives such as the Rochdale Veterans Breakfast Club demonstrate how something as simple as sharing breakfast can strengthen friendships, improve wellbeing and remind those who have served that their contribution continues to be appreciated by the community.

Corrections and clarifications

This article was amended on 9 November 2026. This article originally placed the Flying Horse Hotel in Heywood and gave the finishing time as 10am. The hotel is on Packer Street, Rochdale, and breakfast runs until 10.30am, according to Rochdale Borough Council's events listing. The club's name and the photograph have also been corrected.

articles.title: Late-night fireworks return to Shawclough and Healey as residents' frustration grows
articles.excerpt: Residents in Shawclough and Healey have reported a second consecutive evening of fireworks after 11pm, with growing frustration over disrupted sleep, distressed pets and concerns for wildlife near Healey Dell Nature Reserve.
articles.content_html:
Residents across Shawclough and Healey have once again reported being disturbed by late-night fireworks, with explosions heard at approximately 11.21pm on Sunday evening. The latest incident marks the second consecutive night of reports, leaving many residents questioning when meaningful action will be taken to tackle the ongoing nuisance.

For many households, the issue extends far beyond a brief display. Parents have described children being woken after bedtime, pet owners report anxious and distressed animals, and residents working early shifts say repeated interruptions to their sleep are becoming increasingly difficult to tolerate.

The repeated use of fireworks late at night has also prompted renewed concerns for local wildlife. Healey Dell Nature Reserve, together with the surrounding woodland, provides important habitat for nesting birds, bats and other protected species. Wildlife organisations have long warned that unexpected loud explosions can disturb feeding, nesting and breeding behaviour, particularly during sensitive periods of the year.

Residents have increasingly questioned whether existing legislation is sufficient to prevent repeated anti-social use of fireworks. While fireworks can be legally purchased and used subject to restrictions, businesses selling them must comply with licensing and storage regulations. However, any decision to suspend or revoke a retailer's licence would require evidence that they had breached those legal requirements. Simply because fireworks are being misused by individuals does not automatically mean a retailer has acted unlawfully.

Enforcement remains difficult, particularly when fireworks are discharged from private property under the cover of darkness. Identifying those responsible often relies on witness evidence, CCTV or reports made at the time of the incident.

Nevertheless, residents say patience is wearing thin. After another evening of disrupted sleep, many are calling for stronger enforcement, tighter controls on sales and greater action against those repeatedly using fireworks in residential neighbourhoods late at night.

Fireworks remain an important part of many cultural and community celebrations when used responsibly. However, repeated displays after 11pm in quiet residential areas are a very different matter. Communities should not have to endure nightly disruption, frightened pets, exhausted children and unnecessary disturbance to local wildlife. As complaints continue to mount, many residents are asking a simple question: when will enough finally be enough?

articles.title: Residents raise concerns over anti-social behaviour around Kingsway
articles.excerpt: Residents and businesses are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour around Kingsway, with police identifying retail crime, ASB and road safety as neighbourhood priorities.
articles.content_html:
Residents and businesses around the Kingsway area of Rochdale are calling for continued action to tackle anti-social behaviour, saying a minority of offenders are affecting what is otherwise one of the borough's busiest retail and employment destinations.

Kingsway has undergone significant regeneration over the past two decades, transforming into a major business and retail hub with national retailers, industrial estates, distribution centres and hundreds of jobs. Thousands of people visit the area every day to shop, work and access nearby facilities.

However, some residents and businesses say issues including nuisance behaviour, shoplifting, groups congregating outside retail premises, dangerous driving and road safety concerns have become increasingly noticeable in recent years.

Greater Manchester Police has identified retail crime at Kingsway Retail Park, anti-social behaviour and road safety as neighbourhood policing priorities for the area. Officers say they have carried out targeted operations against shoplifting, increased patrols and undertaken road traffic enforcement to tackle motorists committing offences.

Police have confirmed that numerous arrests have been made for shoplifting at Morrisons in recent months, while dedicated traffic operations have also been carried out along Kingsway to improve road safety. Regular police surgeries are also being held at Kingsway Retail Park to allow residents and businesses to discuss local concerns directly with neighbourhood officers.

For businesses operating on Kingsway, anti-social behaviour can have a wider economic impact. Retailers say persistent shoplifting, disorder and nuisance behaviour place additional pressure on staff while affecting customer confidence. Many businesses have invested heavily in CCTV, security staff and crime prevention measures, working alongside Greater Manchester Police to identify prolific offenders.

Residents have also highlighted concerns over speeding, dangerous driving and the use of modified vehicles on Kingsway, particularly during evenings. Although the vast majority of motorists use the road responsibly, police say road safety remains one of their key neighbourhood priorities alongside tackling retail crime and anti-social behaviour.

Community safety experts say anti-social behaviour often requires more than enforcement alone. Alongside visible policing, long-term solutions typically involve youth engagement, support for vulnerable individuals, environmental improvements, partnership working with businesses and swift action against repeat offenders.

There have been encouraging signs elsewhere in Rochdale. Greater Manchester Police recently reported significant reductions in anti-social behaviour and wider crime within Rochdale town centre following the introduction of Operation Tetbury, a partnership initiative combining targeted policing with regeneration and community engagement. Officers say anti-social behaviour in the town centre fell by more than 30 per cent during the first year of the operation.

Many residents hope a similarly proactive approach around Kingsway will continue to improve the area, ensuring it remains an attractive destination for shoppers, businesses and investors.

The overwhelming majority of people visiting Kingsway do so without experiencing any problems, and local businesses continue to invest confidently in the area. Nevertheless, residents say continued police visibility, partnership working and prompt action against those responsible for anti-social behaviour will be essential to protecting one of Rochdale's most important commercial centres.

Greater Manchester Police encourages anyone witnessing anti-social behaviour or criminal activity to report it online, by calling 101, or by dialling 999 if there is an immediate risk to life or a crime is in progress.

articles.title: Milnrow author helping children cope with grief through heartfelt storybooks
articles.excerpt: Milnrow author Jane Somers is helping children understand bereavement and pet loss through two beautifully illustrated storybooks, while donating hundreds of copies to hospitals and hospices.
articles.content_html:
A Milnrow author is helping children navigate some of life's most difficult moments through a pair of beautifully illustrated books exploring bereavement and the loss of much-loved pets.

Jane Somers has written two children's books, *Look For The Robin* and *Over Rainbow Bridge*, with the aim of providing comfort, reassurance and hope for young readers experiencing grief.

Drawing on gentle storytelling and colourful illustrations, Jane's books tackle subjects that many families find difficult to discuss, helping children understand loss in an age-appropriate and compassionate way.

Her first book, *Look For The Robin*, tells the story of a friendly robin who reminds grieving children that the special people they have lost are still watching over them and that they continue to be loved. The book has resonated with families, schools and support organisations, with Jane using proceeds from sales to give something back to the community.

Thanks to the support of readers, she has now donated more than 200 copies of the book to hospitals, hospices and other worthy causes, helping children facing bereavement access the story free of charge. Customers ordering directly from her website also receive a handmade robin clay heart trinket as a keepsake.

Jane's second book, *Over Rainbow Bridge*, focuses on another form of grief that is often underestimated – the loss of a family pet. Written in rhyme and accompanied by warm illustrations, the story follows the bond between children and their beloved animals, reassuring young readers that although their pet has crossed Rainbow Bridge, the love and memories they shared remain forever.

The book aims to help parents start conversations about pet loss in a gentle, positive way, recognising that the death of a much-loved animal is often a child's first experience of bereavement. Every copy purchased through Jane's online store includes a complimentary bookmark.

Child psychologists have long recognised the importance of helping children understand grief through honest but reassuring conversations. Books can provide a safe and accessible way for young readers to explore difficult emotions, ask questions and recognise that feelings such as sadness, confusion and loss are a normal part of bereavement.

Jane says her ambition has always been to create stories that offer comfort while giving families practical tools to support children during challenging times. By combining uplifting messages with beautiful illustrations, she hopes her books provide reassurance that love continues even after someone, or a cherished pet, has gone.

Both books retail at £9.99, excluding postage and packaging, and are available directly through Jane's website. As well as supporting an independent local author, every purchase helps her continue donating copies to hospitals, hospices and organisations supporting bereaved children.

Jane's work is another example of the creativity found within Rochdale borough, using the power of storytelling not only to entertain but to make a genuine difference in the lives of local families and children across the country.
